title_en: Why Does Secondhand-Clothing Chain 2nd Street Have More Stores in Japan Than Uniqlo?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Why Does Secondhand-Clothing Chain 2nd Street Have More Stores in Japan Than Uniqlo?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: This episode breaks down 2nd Street, the Japanese secondhand-clothing chain that runs over 900 stores across Japan and more than 1,000 worldwide, outpacing Uniqlo's Japan count. The winning formula combines three things: a country where the idle-economy soil is deep, parent company GEO's nationwide store network, and a human-buyer pricing system. Together they turned apparel — the hardest category to standardize — into a scale-model direct-operated chain that few rivals have matched.

blocks.label: Light Analysis: How 2nd Street Built a Thousand-Store Chain in Secondhand Apparel
blocks.text: 2nd Street buys used clothes from consumers, processes them, and puts them back on shelves. As of March this year it had over nine hundred stores in Japan, covering all forty-seven prefectures, and more than one thousand worldwide, including the US, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. The key insight: most Japanese secondhand players with over a thousand stores concentrate on easily standardized categories like gold, bags, and electronics, and rely heavily on franchising. 2nd Street does apparel in a direct-operated model, which is rare globally; its parent company ranks first in Japan's secondhand industry by revenue, seventy percent ahead of the runner-up. For comparison, North America's Goodwill has over three thousand stores, but it's a nonprofit whose inventory comes from donations. 2nd Street is a commercial buy-and-resell model. As the episode puts it, "It has opened more than nine hundred stores in Japan, while Uniqlo has fewer than eight hundred stores there." Yet despite more stores, its profit is less than a tenth of Uniqlo's. The deep soil behind it: rapid postwar economic growth created mass consumption and idle goods; when the economy slowed, people started selling them off. Japanese households hold idle items worth roughly ninety-one trillion yen — about five hundred seventy billion dollars — and fashion apparel makes up more than a third of that. 2nd Street buys used clothes from consumers, processes them, and puts them back on shelves. title_en: 3T Ghost Stories Night 9: Mountain Legends — The Smiling Man, the Double-Faced Curse, Mushroom Picking, and the Guide in the Rain

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: 3T Ghost Stories Night 9: Mountain Legends — The Smiling Man, the Double-Faced Curse, Mushroom Picking, and the Guide in the Rain

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Host Xiao Wu's solo climb up Mount Huangshan in a downpour sets the mood for four Japanese mountain ghost stories from "Mountain Spirits": the smiling man on the ridge who lures you off a cliff, the double-faced curse that squeezes your tent, a mushroom picker lost near an abandoned cable car, and the kind spirit guide in the rain. Storyteller Antan Junpei reworks the fear of mountain accidents through modern climbing experience — folklore's luring spirits mirror the real-world dangers of hypothermia and fatal falls.

blocks.label: Prologue: Xiao Wu Solo-Climbs Mount Huangshan in a Storm
blocks.text: Let's start with the real atmosphere. The mechanism: northerners underestimate the rainy season. On that stormy day the trailhead was completely empty — thick fog and heavy rain the whole way, limited visibility, soaking wet, and colder with every step up. The key insight: an unfamiliar environment amplifies the unease — afraid of getting lost, afraid of meeting anyone. Your senses go hypersensitive in the white noise, and your brain automatically plays back the ghost stories you've heard. A typical scene: Tiandu Peak's vertical stairs loomed through the fog like a monster surrounding a city; the phone was soaked and useless; only after four hours did he finally see people at the cable car station. The original line: "You're afraid of taking the wrong path, and afraid of not meeting anyone... then again, afraid of meeting someone — you don't know what you might run into." This sets the emotional tone for the four mountain tales that follow, and it strongly resonates with the mindset behind "the guide in the rain." And the reason: slippery trails, lightning, hypothermia, getting lost, no rescue — Xiao Wu himself admits it was "highly dangerous." The mechanism: northerners underestimate the rainy season. The higher I climbed, the more the fear closed in. My brain started feeding me ghost stories. I kept imagining every shadow was something.

blocks.label: The Book: Mountain Spirits and Antan Junpei
blocks.text: Now, who is behind these stories. As a mountaineer: he knew the Hida Mountains of Japan — the Northern Alps — deeply; after a cerebral hemorrhage in 1999, he shifted from conquering high peaks to documenting low-altitude village culture. As a storyteller: he runs a website called "Wind of the Northern Alps," collecting oral stories from mountain huts and villagers. As a genre founder: from 2004 he serialized "Mountain Spirits" in ghost-story magazines, a new category grounded in modern mountaineering. The boundary: the stories come from midnight talks in mountain huts, village fieldwork, and personal experience; in 2018 he had manga artists including Junji Ito adapt them into comics. His own words: "The horror of the mountains is not monsters eating people — more often, it's disaster brought on by humans who ignore nature's rules." And the mechanism: the range stretches over 100 kilometers, with volatile weather, frequent fog, and violent ridge winds — it ranks among the top mountain ranges in Japan for accidents and missing persons. He stopped chasing summits and started documenting villages. The peaks gave way to oral histories. It's not monsters — it's humans ignoring the rules. Nature punishes the careless, not the believers.

blocks.label: Tale One: The Smiling Man on the Ridge and the Double-Faced Curse
blocks.text: Tale one, the smiling man and the double-faced curse. The story: five years ago, Ishida was ridge-hiking; after rounding a boulder, his whole group vanished, and a tall, thin man in red came toward him — mouth smiling, brows knitted, gait and speed mismatched, a "spirit moonwalk." It even caught up and touched his backpack from behind. The key insight: around the same time, a 50-year-old woman died in a solo climb, slipping on the snow line just a dozen meters off the ridge trail. Ishida suspects she didn't backtrack like he did — she was pushed toward the ridge's side and fell into the valley. What to do: if you see an abnormal figure on a ridge, backtrack to a sheltered spot first — never step sideways off the trail. The original line: "The mouth was shaped like a smile, but there was no warmth in it... the gait and speed didn't match at all, like a moonwalk in the mind." The lore: spirits of accident victims can't leave the mountain; they use illusions to disturb climbers' judgment and cause accidents, seeking a "body double" to escape. Red clothes stand for the mountain god's color and the red of blood; the stiff smile is a vengeful spirit's failure to mimic human faces; and smiley carvings on ridge stone markers are one source of the face. As the narrator puts it: "It won't harm you directly, but it puts psychological pressure on the climber, which then leads to an accident." Don't engage — just backtrack. Ignore it and walk back the way you came.

blocks.label: Tale Two: Mushroom Picking — Lost After Finding Matsutake
blocks.text: Tale two, the mushroom picker. The cause: mushrooms grow in damp, shaded spots, so you have to leave the trail; after spotting matsutake, greed drove him deeper — the bell contact broke off, and the phone had no signal. The solution: when foraging, stay within earshot of the bell; don't be greedy, and don't push into unmarked areas. Longchuan's annual warning: "Never let a beginner find a matsutake — once they've found one, they lose interest in every other mushroom." The story: lost, Antan saw the abandoned cable car suddenly start running, carrying a mummified body — white hair, a mushroom basket at its waist. As he squeezed his eyes shut, Longchuan's shouts broke the spell. The key insight: following the cable car downhill could mean a point of no return on a hillside washed out by storms — the missing old man may have walked exactly that route. Once reclaimed by the forest, abandoned buildings become a border zone where "malignant spirits" are most easily met. What to do: when lost, return along your original route or a known trail — don't be lured by abandoned structures that look like shortcuts. Greed kept pulling him off the trail. When in doubt, turn around. The safest route is the one you came from.

blocks.label: Tale Three: The Guide in the Rain — A Kind Spirit
blocks.text: Tale three, the guide in the rain. In late-summer fog and rain, Antan climbed a cliff with fear swelling; he met a heavy-gear man in blue sitting on a rock. The man refused to hike together, pointed the opposite way, and said "six minutes to the hut" — when in fact Antan had already lost his way. In the hut's drying room, the same rain boots peeked out under a clothes rack; the crouching man looked up and said, "I made it in 30 minutes — you owe me a beer." On a stretcher in the living room lay the same man's body, dead from hypothermia hours earlier. The original line: "He walked the opposite way... following that path would have meant getting lost — and without reaching the hut in time, hypothermia." The related concept: he matches the "kind spirit" — hunter and mountain-keeper souls under the mountain god's protection; many in the Hida Mountains have seen a hiker in white, leaving no footprints, who points the way. Why it matters: an open, unobstructed ridge marks the boundary between worlds, where the "barrier" is weakest; camping alone marks you as an intruder; and foraging off-trail means leaving protected ground. And the boundary: on developed park routes in good weather with a group, risk is manageable; on wild mountains, in storms, in winter, or solo, you need maximum caution. blocks.text: Out in the mountains on a rainy night, hypothermia is a real risk. Don't hesitate when you see something off — just backtrack. Following that abandoned cable car downhill could be a point of no return. His partner's shout broke the spell.

title_en: The Oral History of SpaceX: Musk's Hiring Philosophy, the Biggest IPO, Space and AI

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: The Oral History of SpaceX: Musk's Hiring Philosophy, the Biggest IPO, Space and AI

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Lewis Hong, a former chief rocket manufacturing engineer at SpaceX, tells the inside story of the Falcon 1, Falcon 9, and Starship development at a historic moment when SpaceX went public and acquired xAI. He reveals how Musk's 'first-principles thinking plus extreme manufacturability' overturned the aerospace industry — cutting the cost of putting a kilogram into orbit from 20,000 dollars to 3,000 (with an ultimate target below 100) — and argues that the fusion of space and AI will open a new chapter in the expansion of human civilization.

blocks.label: The SpaceX IPO and the xAI Acquisition: The Logic Under the Space Data Center
blocks.text: The core logic revolves around the space data center. America's AI computing build-out faces two bottlenecks. Starlink started in 2015 — the moment the rocket was recovered, Musk immediately thought of the 'second step.' SpaceX never does things without a purpose: Starlink exists to raise the enormous funds needed to go to Mars. Lewis's judgment: this is no accident. In 2014 Musk registered X.com, and Zeus, xAI, SpaceX, Neuralink, and the Boring Company — each company serves a larger master plan, which may eventually consolidate into an 'X' holding group like Alphabet. Space has natural advantages: first, no permission needed — whoever gets there first takes the spot; second, unlimited solar power — conversion efficiency more than ten percent higher than on Earth; third, information in a vacuum travels twice as fast as the fastest optical fiber, derived from first principles; fourth, a distributed architecture is not constrained by any single region's power grid. The AI giants each have their positions: Gemini has Google Search, Claude goes the B2B coding-tool route, OpenAI goes mass consumer — and Grok has the massive physical-world data of Musk's ecosystem: Tesla's self-driving, robots, and SpaceX's space data. xAI's mission 'Understand the Universe' may mean understanding the physical world rather than the universe in a vague sense. No one needs a permit to stake a claim in orbit.

blocks.label: The Extremely Introverted Musk and His Counterintuitive Hiring Philosophy
blocks.text: At the 2013 all-hands meeting, Musk was extremely introverted — standing on stage was deeply uncomfortable for him, and the audience was more uncomfortable than he was. He isn't a bad speaker; his style is just entirely different. But one thing never changed: he is extremely sincere, exactly the same inside and out. That's the core reason he can hold a team together. As Lewis said with resignation, 'Musk talks recklessly on X — I wish he'd talk a little less.' But today's 'performativeness' was practiced over more than a decade. SpaceX deliberately does not hire people from traditional aerospace backgrounds. When they scaled up the Falcon 9 production line, the first team they brought in was the Mini Cooper team — because Mini Cooper has the most SKUs of any car line: seven roof colors, multiple mirror colors, countless interior combinations — exactly the 'high volume + high variation + stable quality control' requirement. The underlying logic: Musk believes the aerospace industry hasn't changed in decades precisely because of the people who made it. To overturn it, you must bring in fresh thinking from outside the industry. SpaceX values how fast a person can absorb, grow, and adapt in a short time — not decades of past experience. Lewis happened to join while Musk was traveling, becoming one of the few exceptions who got in without a personal interview — he could only write a self-introduction letter. Facing the question 'you did food, why rockets?', he wrote: food is the hardest product in the world — you must produce an enormous quantity in an explosive burst of time, and every single unit passes 'humanity's highest quality review,' your own mouth. The essence of mass production and supply-chain management is exactly what rocket production lacks most. Musk reportedly made the decision within a minute of reading the letter. blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: After walking the 2026 Beijing Auto Show, Sandao shares a deep recap: at 380,000 square meters it's the world's largest, and suppliers have stepped from behind the curtain onto center stage. Consumers now pick cars by supply chain rather than badge; smart driving pushes in two directions at once; the cockpit ecosystem will split into camps like phones; and BBA fight back with Chinese solutions, but their brand premium is hard to sustain.

blocks.label: Show Scale and How to Tour It
blocks.text: The exhibition area doubled from 220,000 to 380,000 square meters, old and new halls merged into one, and parts suppliers and finished cars share the same halls for the first time: 17 halls, 1,451 cars, 181 world premieres, and 71 concept cars. In previous years you had to take a shuttle between the new-car halls and the supplier halls; this year you can see CATL's booth in the car halls and complete cars in the parts halls — like visiting Apple and Huawei, then walking over to the chip and screen booths at a phone show. A real car fan should spend at least two days. At closing time, 16:30 to 17:30, the taxi queue can have 200 people — leave early, or ride the subway a couple of stops before hailing a cab. Related terms: media day for reports and launches where you can't see cars in the morning, pro-audience day with concept cars still up and industry matchmaking, and public days that only sell current production models. Sandao didn't reach the halls until noon this year and only toured key models — when homogeneous content is supplied without limit, traffic dies and quality drops. Better to sit with your first-hand impressions and turn them into deep content for the podcast and videos. The suppliers stepped out from behind the curtain. Parts makers are now center stage, not backstage. At closing, you're 200 people deep in the taxi queue. Escape early — the cab line at closing is brutal.

blocks.label: Choosing Logic: From Badge to Supply Chain
blocks.text: In the past you chose a car by first trusting a BBA badge; now, buying a new-energy car, the first questions are which cockpit chip, an 8295, which driving solution, Momenta R6 or R7, and which battery, CATL or Sunwoda. The supply chain's brand weight now outweighs the car brand's. Leapmotor's sales ride on a systemic dividend: buyers don't care if it's a Leapmotor — they care whose chip, whose driving compute, whose battery cells are inside. Once you've owned one new-energy car, brand preference shrinks fast. It's like buying a laptop: first pick Intel or AMD, then ignore the other camp entirely. Car buying now works the same way — lock the battery, chip, and driving supplier, then pick the model. At the store they ask how many lidars, why it's on the roof, whose battery, what the charging plan is, and how much compute — miss any answer and your professionalism rating drops to near zero. The fix: 4S stores have turned into experience centers — Huawei calls theirs user centers — and salespeople must master the full specs of the three-electric system, smart driving, and cockpit, not just length, width, height, and wheelbase. The first question is now which chip is inside. Buyers open with 'what's the compute under the hood?' Lock the camp first, then pick the model. Choose the ecosystem, then browse within it.

blocks.label: Ecosystem Camps: Cars Splitting Like Phones
blocks.text: The car is evolving from a means of transport into a mobile terminal and then into an embodied intelligence robot. From now on you won't ask which brand will survive — instead, like Android versus Apple, cars will split into camps, where the cockpit, smart driving, and smart home unify into one ecosystem. The closed camp: Huawei, which doesn't build cars itself but serves automakers, locking partners into its closed system, and BYD, which self-develops driving, infotainment, manufacturing, and chips. The open camp: most automakers working with Momenta, CATL, and others. There's a boundary: users with special needs like foldable screens can cross ecosystems — Sandao uses a vivo foldable purely because he needs the two-app drag-and-drop to post on Weibo. Before buying a car, check whether your home appliances and phone are already inside an ecosystem, Huawei or Xiaomi; otherwise pick hardware and OS by experience. If not, choose hardware and system by experience — a few hundred yuan of price difference doesn't matter. Related idea: from now on the cockpit defines who allies with whom — most car-infotainment ecosystems will die, and only two or three will survive in the end. Cars are splitting into camps, just like phones. Pick your car the way you pick Android or Apple. There's the closed walled garden and the open camp. Closed ecosystems lock you in; open ones let you mix and match.

Smart driving will become standard equipment just like air conditioning and stereo — back in the day you could live without ESP, today impossible. BYD fired the first shot popularizing the God's Eye system; Leapmotor fired the second and pinned it to the floor. blocks.text: Once L3 spreads, your hands won't hold the wheel and your feet won't touch the pedals — so the seat doesn't have to face forward anymore. You could sit sideways, backward, even work out in the car. Interior designers are told to drop the old logic; many outlandish designs are preparing for the post-autonomous era. AI models turn the human-car relationship from driver-plus-tool into owner-plus-butler. Sandao jokes though: people dreaming of running on a treadmill or clocking in for sleep in a self-driving car — 'that's a thought we shouldn't have.' Brands are also rushing to build 9-series and 8-series flagships, not because the market truly needs that many giant cars, but because the latest tech — three or six lidars, Thor chips, 900-volt 5C charging — needs flagship bodies to land on. title_en: Why a Bull Market Makes You Anxious: Desire Is a Triangle

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Why a Bull Market Makes You Anxious: Desire Is a Triangle

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: A bull market — especially a structural one — makes people more anxious than a bear market because "someone always earns more than you": that desire-mediator ignites what René Girard called mimetic desire. Girard's desire triangle of subject, object, and mediator explains that most desires aren't born within us but copied from the people around us. The antidote from Graham, Buffett, and Munger: recognize the difference between authentic desire and mimetic desire, actively distance yourself from the mediators, and embrace the slow compounding of getting rich gradually.

blocks.label: Structural Bull Market: Why Rising Prices Make People More Anxious
blocks.text: First, the structural bull market — why rising prices make people more anxious. In a bull market, the people making money are always the minority. In a structural bull market, hot sectors like AI from late February to late June this year monopolize the capital inflow, while the rest of the market suffers a capital-bleeding effect: you miss the joy of gains and endure the anguish of being banned from printing money. A bear market tests one dimension — patience; but an extremely polarized structural bull market tests your greed and envy at once. Typical scene: watching AI-chasers double their money while your holdings stagnate — and since July, tech corrected sharply while value and dividend stocks bounced, so those who chased the rally got hit on both sides. The stock market is an amplifier of human nature, and in a structural bull market, that amplification is on full display. In a bull market, the people making money are always the minority. In a structural bull market, hot sectors — like AI from late February to late June this year — monopolize the capital inflow, while the rest of the market suffers a "capital-bleeding" effect: people not on the hot side not only miss the joy of gains but endure the anguish of "being banned from printing money." The key insight: a bear market tests a single dimension — patience; but an extremely polarized structural bull market tests your greed, envy, and other instinctive desires at once. Fail to see through and manage those desires, and you sink into endless anxiety, your investing moves distort, and you end up pleasing nobody. A typical scene: watching the people chasing AI double their money while your holdings stagnate; since July, tech stocks have corrected sharply while value and dividend "old-guard" stocks bounced — investors who couldn't hold out and chased the rally are now suffering a double hit. "The stock market is an amplifier of human nature, and in a structural bull market that amplification is on full display." Related concept: the anxiety isn't handed out by the market — it comes from the mediator of "others earning more than me," which is exactly the ticket into the desire-triangle theory in the next section. American economist Charles Kindleberger wrote a piercing line in his classic Manias, Panics, and Crashes — said before Girard invented his geometry of desire, this was the intuitive conclusion from watching countless financial bubbles in history. My anxiety comes from seeing others earn more. It's not the market that stresses me — it's my neighbor's gains. A bull market amplifies human nature. The market turns your instincts up to eleven.

blocks.label: The Desire Triangle: Girard's Geometry of Desire
blocks.text: Second, the desire triangle. The triangle has three vertices: the subject who desires, the object desired, and the mediator the subject imitates. We crave something not because it's inherently valuable, but because others want it too, or someone else owns it. Before Girard, academia used a straight-line model — desire born from your own needs and instincts. But the straight line can't explain the contradictions: people often don't know what they want and just frantically chase whatever others chase; something worthless becomes instantly attractive once it's someone else's object of desire. Think of dating rituals or designer bags — you want the bag because influencers and friends have it. As Girard said, desire, like gravity, never exists alone inside anything; it's born in the space where we influence each other. All our desires are essentially projections of other people's. And literature proves it: Don Quixote imitates knightly novels, Madame Bovary imitates romantic ones — and ends in tragedy. The triangle has three vertices — the subject (the person who desires), the object (the thing or person desired), and the mediator (the model the subject imitates). We crave something not because it's inherently valuable, but because others want it too, or someone else owns it. The key insight: before Girard, academia generally held a straight-line model from subject to object — desire born from your own needs, instincts, and tastes. But the straight line can't explain a mass of contradictions: people often don't know what they want and just frantically chase whatever others chase; something worthless becomes instantly attractive once it becomes someone else's object of desire. A typical scene: in dating, the "must" of gifting a certain present or eating a certain meal; wanting a certain designer bag often because you see influencers or friends doing the same. "Desire, like gravity, never exists alone inside any thing or person — it is born in the space where we can influence each other. In other words, all our desires are essentially projections of other people's desires." The mechanism: apart from basic physiological needs like eating when hungry, the vast majority of human desire isn't original — it's acquired by imitating others. The key insight: literature is the best evidence — Don Quixote, obsessed with chivalric novels, desires to become a knight-errant, an imitation of the knightly model; Flaubert's Madame Bovary endlessly imitates the romantic heroines of novels, producing endless desire for luxury and romantic love, ending in tragedy. You want it because someone else wants it, not because you do. Desire is contagious — it spreads through models. All desire is a projection of other people's desire. We borrow our wants from the people around us.

blocks.label: The Inevitability of Bubbles and the Cost of Evolution
blocks.text: Third, the inevitability of bubbles and the cost of evolution. From the first tulip bubble to the South Sea, canal, railway, and internet bubbles, every bubble's fuse is usually new technology — it sparks imaginings of new seas and new land. But what turns the bubble into a roaring fire is the greed of human desire. Consider the periodical cicada: larvae burrow underground for 17 years feeding on root sap, then billions of adults emerge in the second week of May, mate frantically, lay eggs, and all die before the end of June. It's a predator-saturation effect so wildly successful that no predator can eat that much food in a few weeks — and predator saturation is the bubble effect. From the big picture, bubbles push technology forward, and that may be evolution's basic law — but evolution comes at a cost, and nobody wants to be the cannon fodder. From the first tulip bubble to the South Sea, canal, railway, and internet bubbles, the fuse of every bubble is usually new technology — it sparks imaginings of "new seas and new land." But what turns the bubble into a roaring fire is the greed of human desire. The key insight: there's an insect called the periodical cicada whose larvae burrow underground for 17 years, feeding on tree-root sap; when their time comes, billions of adults emerge in the second week of May, mate frantically, lay eggs, and all die before the end of June. This "predator-saturation effect" is wildly successful — no predator can eat that much food in a few weeks. Predator saturation is the bubble effect. A typical scene: at a major industry conference, an investor said flat out, "if I don't make a hundred times, I'm letting down this era." In the AI bull market some people truly made a fortune — the ten-fold, hundred-fold rags-to-riches stories happening around you are exactly what Girard calls desire mediators. "Moving forward within bubbles may be the basic law of evolution, or its paradox. That paradox clearly shows: evolution comes at a cost." The boundary: from the big picture of human progress, it's bubbles that pushed new technology to grow and society forward; if everyone were perfectly rational, no one would pay for highly uncertain futures. So we shouldn't simply define bubbles as pejorative — in a sense they may be "synonymous with evolution." The reason: on the Serengeti, every year the wildebeest migration crossing a river triggers terrible stampedes — some die as sacrifices while the survivors walk over their kin's bodies. Investing objectively helps technology, the economy, and society, but nobody wants to be "cannon fodder of evolution." New tech lights the fuse, but greed burns the house down. Innovation starts the bubble; human desire inflates it. Evolution comes at a cost — and the cost is paid by some. Progress has a body count.

blocks.label: The Masters' Desire Management: Slow Wealth, Discipline, and Distance from Mediators
blocks.text: Fourth, the masters' desire management. Benjamin Graham lived through the epic 1929 bubble and crash — then entered the market too early in 1930, his fund lost 70% overall, nearly going bankrupt, and that bitter experience taught him the dangers of leverage and speculation. He published Security Analysis in 1934, drawing a strict line between investing and speculating, and gave us equity mindset, margin of safety, and Mr. Market — earning the title father of value investing. Buffett later added the circle of competence. His lesson: every time you think 'this time is different, I must add leverage,' remember that Graham's trouble wasn't failing to see value — it was failing to manage desire. Value investing is hardest on temperament, because it goes against human nature. That's why Buffett moved back to the remote town of Omaha in 1956, and Templeton to the Bahamas in 1968 — physical distance is the first line of defense against desire mediators. Benjamin Graham lived through the epic 1929 bubble and crash. After the crash, he entered the market too early in 1930, and his fund lost 70% overall, nearly going bankrupt — that bitter experience taught him the dangers of leverage and speculation. The key insight: learning from the pain, he published Security Analysis in 1934, drawing a strict line between investing and speculating, and distilling three core ideas — equity mindset, margin of safety, and Mr. Market — which earned him the title "father of value investing." Buffett later added the circle of competence onto that foundation. A typical scene: every time you feel "this time is different, I must add leverage and get on," think of Graham's 1930 bottom-fishing lesson — his trouble wasn't failing to see value, it was failing to manage desire. "The hardest part of value investing isn't technique — it's temperament, because it's a philosophy that goes against human nature." The mechanism: in 1956, 26-year-old Buffett left New York for the remote town of Omaha — where the density of desire mediators is clearly much lower; in 1968, 55-year-old Sir John Templeton moved from Wall Street to Nassau in the Bahamas, where the Wall Street Journal arrived a week late. The key insight: both were like "hermits living quietly inside the market," good at blocking outside noise. Value investing is hardest on temperament, and Mr. Market builds a "get rich overnight" desire mediator right in front of your eyes every day — physical distance is their first line of defense against desire. Value investing is 10% technique and 90% temperament. The hardest thing to manage isn't the portfolio — it's yourself. Physical distance is their first defense against temptation. Sometimes the best trade is moving to a quieter place.

blocks.label: Defeating the Inner Bandit: A Practical Framework for Bull-Market Anxiety
blocks.text: Finally, defeating the inner bandit. The Tao Te Ching, chapter 9: hold a cup full and it spills — wealth accumulating to the brim is a cue to stop; what's too sharp cannot last. Chapter 46: no disaster is greater than not knowing contentment. Buffett and Munger live simply and champion delayed gratification, yet ended up enormously wealthy — the sage's maxims and the compounding path are cut from the same cloth. So whenever a 10% annual return stops feeling tasty, remind yourself: that instant of disdain is the voice of mimetic desire, not the judgment of authentic desire. blocks.text: Here's why it matters: phones default to brightening dark scenes, so the image gets oversaturated and bright. Lower the exposure a bit and the algorithm recognizes the highlights and restores them — you actually get more contrast and texture. But don't apply it one-size-fits-all: in very dark night shots or moody frames where you want shadow detail, brighten up a little. The practical move: in most daytime scenes, press and hold the screen and drag down the exposure compensation; you can also lock in a fixed exposure value in settings. For daily shooting he uses auto mode, with the zoom reaching as far as 8.6x; when a foreground object blocks focus, he switches to pro mode and uses manual focus with focus peaking. For editing, the built-in album editor is enough: favorite and filter, apply a soft black or white diffusion filter around thirty percent, pull the curve to press highlights and lift shadows, adjust mono saturation, and paste the edit points across the batch. title_en: E16 How to Eat Carbs Smartly? Meat First or Rice First? A Nutrition PhD's Glucose-Control Lab

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: E16 How to Eat Carbs Smartly? Meat First or Rice First? A Nutrition PhD's Glucose-Control Lab

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Metabolic-nutrition PhD Lu Lu joins the show with real data from continuous glucose monitors. Together they systematically break down the chemistry of carbohydrates — from monosaccharides to starches — glycemic index and glycemic load, food ordering, diabetes subtypes, and the Asian paradox of visceral fat. They also reveal that sleep deprivation wrecks blood sugar far more than any single meal. The bottom line: controlling added sugar matters more than cutting all carbs, and seven to eight hours of sleep beats any dietary tweak.

blocks.label: Carb Chemistry: From Molecule to Table
blocks.text: Let's start at the molecular level. The mechanism: sugar is the everyday word for carbohydrates, which split by chemical complexity into monosaccharides — glucose, fructose, galactose, which enter the blood directly — disaccharides like sucrose, lactose, and maltose, which can be hydrolyzed, and polysaccharides like starch, glycogen, and cellulose, which are only absorbed after enzymatic breakdown. The key insight: monosaccharides spike blood sugar fastest. Fiber counts as a carb but isn't absorbed, so treat it separately. For Chinese diets, starchy foods — rice, noodles, potatoes, sweet potatoes — are the real blood-sugar drivers, not just milk tea and cola. A typical scene: when reading nutrition labels, separate total carbs, fiber, and added sugar. Imported snacks sold in China often skip the added-sugar line, which gutses the label's value. The original line: "What we should be controlling is added sugar... if the added sugar is high, you should try to avoid it." The related concept: controlling sugar means limiting added sugar first — not blindly cutting all carbohydrates. And a reality check on the table: southern breakfasts of soup dumplings and wontons, northern ones of noodles and fried dough sticks — it's really "carbs on carbs." Shredded potato over rice and Basque sweet-potato wraps work the same way. Potatoes are usually treated as a vegetable, but their main nutrient is starch. Cut added sugar first, keep the rest of the carbs. The first target isn't all carbs — it's added sugar. It's carbs on top of carbs. Two starch-heavy foods, one meal.

blocks.label: Diet Patterns: Low-Carb, Keto, and Mediterranean
blocks.text: Then the diet patterns. The mechanism: with the same calorie deficit, low-carb and high-carb diets show no significant weight-loss difference over 6 to 12 months — "a calorie is a calorie." But the low-carb group had lower triglycerides, higher HDL, and lower fasting insulin — better metabolic markers. The key insight: low-carb helps most when you already have blood-sugar issues. For healthy people, long-term keto demands heavy fat and protein, a drastic shift in diet; ketones strain the kidneys, and the brain mainly runs on glucose. The boundary: the weight lost in the first one to two weeks of keto is glycogen from the liver — each gram binds three to four grams of water — not fat. Keto has a therapeutic role for children with epilepsy, but for ordinary people the cost may not be worth it. The original line: "In the short term, one to two weeks, you'll see weight loss... it mainly comes from liver glycogen depletion and water loss." And the self-experiment: while wearing a CGM, one week of low-carb shed one kilogram — which came right back after returning to a normal diet. That confirms it was water plus glycogen, not real fat loss. As Lu Lu puts it: "That kilogram wasn't from fat loss — it was liver glycogen and water after I cut sugar... once I ate normally again, the kilogram came back." "That kilogram wasn't from fat loss — it was liver glycogen and water after I cut sugar... once I ate normally again, the kilogram came back." Low-carb and high-carb lose the same amount of weight. A calorie is a calorie for weight loss. That's water weight, not fat. It comes off fast and comes back faster.

blocks.label: Glycemic Index and Food Ordering
blocks.text: Now the glycemic index and food ordering. The mechanism: GI, the glycemic index, measures how fast a fixed amount of carbs raises blood sugar — glucose is 100. GL, the glycemic load, is GI times total carbs. High-GI foods include white rice, white bread, potatoes, and grapes, at 70 or above; medium ones like sweet potato, brown rice, and oats sit between 56 and 69. The key insight: watermelon has a high GI but is mostly water with low total carbs, so its GL stays low; white rice is high on both GI and GL, making it the bigger offender. The area under the curve captures both the peak height and how fast it falls back. The boundary: people with diabetes should focus on GI because of the insulin response; everyone else can manage both GI and total intake through GL. The original line: "Five bites of watermelon might fill you up... but five bites of rice bring a lot more carbs." And the ordering mechanism: in a controlled study of type 2 diabetes patients, with the same Western-style meal, eating protein and vegetables first, waiting 15 minutes, then eating the carbs, lowered post-meal blood sugar by more than 20 percent at every time point versus the carbs-first group. The key insight: the 15-minute gap is essential — a bite of chicken followed immediately by rice doesn't work. Eating slowly and social meals, where you chat between bites, help control sugar almost by accident. Protein and veg first, carbs 15 minutes later. Front-load the fiber and protein.

blocks.label: Diabetes Subtypes and the Asian Metabolic Paradox
blocks.text: Then the diabetes subtypes. The mechanism: type 1 is an autoimmune attack on beta cells — absolute insulin deficiency, onset in youth, unrelated to obesity, patients often slim. Type 2 is insulin resistance — the lock is rusted; the key is still there but can't turn. Obesity, especially visceral fat, is the main trigger. The key insight: the hormones that manage blood sugar — insulin lowers it, while glucagon raises it during hunger or stress. Type 1 requires lifelong insulin injections; for type 2, injected insulin helps much less. The related concept: Sana BioTech's allogeneic islet-cell transplants — knocking out HLA and boosting CD47 — bring hope for type 1 patients, but they're costly and carry immune and cancer risks. Then the Asian paradox: Asian subcutaneous fat is more fibrotic; once it can't expand further, surplus energy is forced into visceral fat. An Asian with slim limbs and a round belly — the apple shape — may carry very high visceral fat, putting type 2 risk above evenly obese Westerners. As the doctor puts it: "Asian subcutaneous fat has been put in shackles... surplus energy can only take the road of visceral fat." And the flip side: the pear shape — gaining weight around hips and thighs — is actually the healthier one metabolically. Slim on the outside, fatty on the inside. The apple shape hides visceral fat even in thin people.

blocks.label: Special Groups: Pregnancy, Menstrual Cycle, and Birth Control
blocks.text: Next, special groups. The reason: the placenta's hormone HPL deliberately creates insulin resistance, keeping blood sugar a bit high to feed the fetus. But overly high sugar causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, then a large baby, then difficult delivery or newborn hypoglycemia. The solution: apply the food-ordering principle, keep your usual exercise within a safe range — don't suddenly ramp up — and note that Asian women pass the first glucose screening less often, possibly because of lower muscle mass and standards built around Western bodies. Severity: for both mother and baby, this is a life-threatening level that needs medical management. As one guest says: "With the glucose tolerance test, you rarely hear of a Chinese woman passing on the first try." Then the menstrual cycle. In the follicular phase, before ovulation, estrogen is high, insulin sensitivity rises, and blood sugar is at its most stable — a good window for high-intensity training. In the luteal phase, after ovulation and before the period, progesterone rises with mild insulin resistance — bigger appetite, cravings for sweets: "the body isn't getting the glucose; most of it stays in the blood." Pregnancy raises sugar on purpose — to feed the baby. The body keeps glucose high for the fetus. Blood sugar swings with your cycle. Stable before ovulation, hungry and craving sweets after.

blocks.label: Sleep and Stress: The Underrated Blood-Sugar Killer
blocks.text: And finally, the underrated killer. Why it matters: in the host's CGM data, staying up late affected blood sugar more than any dietary factor — sleep badly one night and the next day's sugar spirals out of control; sleep well and the whole day stays stable. The boundary: occasional late nights are reversible; chronic sleep deprivation needs systematic intervention. As the host puts it: "The biggest thing affecting my blood sugar... mine was always stable, but if I stayed up late the night before, the next day it spiked uncontrollably." How to apply it: prioritize seven to eight hours of sleep — it delivers faster results than obsessing over what you eat. The mechanism: in one study, 11 healthy young adults were split into two groups — six days of four-hour sleeps versus eight-hour sleeps, with diet and activity fully controlled. The sleep-deprived group cleared post-meal glucose 40 percent slower and cut insulin response by 30 percent — beta cells secreted less, and cortisol suppressed insulin's action. The original line: "In just six days of sleep deprivation, you can already see this response in healthy young adults." Get your seven to eight hours — no shortcuts. Sleep first, diet second.

blocks.text: When it comes to sugar control, start with added sugar. The first two weeks on keto are mostly water weight, not fat. Front-load the fiber and protein, and save the carbs for last. Prioritize seven to eight hours of sleep — it beats obsessing over every meal.

title_en: Finding a Coherent Life When You're Stuck Inside the Factory

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Finding a Coherent Life When You're Stuck Inside the Factory

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Mengmeng, a former product manager at Baidu, Ctrip, and Meituan, walked through 15 years of the internet's golden age and retired in 2024. She paid a 6-million-yuan tuition bill when Chinese tech stocks crashed, and evolved from Duan Yongping-style stock conviction to David Swensen's asset allocation, then iterated again to Taleb-style options hedging — building an investment system to fund a FIRE life. Retiring early wasn't escaping; it was finding coherence on both the financial and the psychological dimension.

blocks.label: From Inside the Factory to Retirement: 15 Years on the Big-Tech Assembly Line
blocks.text: Mengmeng started in the industry in 2012: Baidu, then Lvping.com, a Ctrip-owned travel community startup modeled on TripAdvisor that ultimately failed, then Ctrip's travel-guide community, then Dianping and Meituan — working on recommended dishes and offline-to-online services. It spanned the golden growth years of product management. In the early days, the internet ran on a 'make-shift crew' model; the demand for product managers was huge, and switching jobs was easy. But by 2024, growth had slowed, repetitive work increased, team culture turned into internal competition, and interest-driven work no longer sustained itself. When the positive returns — the sense of achievement — keep declining while the negatives — no freedom, failing health — keep piling up, that's your signal to reconsider. As she said, the joy and satisfaction work gave her declined year after year; the positives shrank and the negatives stacked up. And this isn't age panic at 35 — it's the organizational friction and stunted growth exposed once growth slowed. Mengmeng quit four times at Meituan; the first three times her boss talked her into staying. The fourth time, at the end of 2024, Hashimoto's thyroiditis flared up — yoga and brisk walks, yet she'd lie awake at three a.m. unable to even turn over. In the end, her body made the decision for her. Core path: Mengmeng entered the industry in 2012 — Baidu (internationalization / Japanese products) → Lvping.com, a Ctrip-owned travel community startup benchmarked against TripAdvisor that eventually failed → Ctrip's travel-guide community → Dianping/Meituan (recommended dishes, offline-to-online). She rode the golden growth years of product management. Key insight: the early internet was the 'make-shift crew' era — product managers were scarce and job hopping was easy. By 2024 growth slowed, repetitive work multiplied, team culture turned inward, and interest-driven work was no longer sustainable. Typical signal: when work no longer brings positive returns (shrinking sense of achievement) while negatives (no freedom, declining health) keep stacking up, it's time to re-examine your career choice. Direct quote: 'The sense of achievement and joy work gave me declined year by year. Positive returns kept shrinking while the negatives kept stacking up.' Related concept: the link to '35-year-old anxiety' — it's not age itself but the organizational friction and personal-growth ceiling exposed once growth slows. Mengmeng resigned four times at Meituan; the first three times her manager persuaded her to stay. The fourth, in late 2024, Hashimoto's thyroiditis worsened — yoga and brisk walks, yet she still couldn't sleep past 3 a.m. and could barely turn over in bed. Her body made the final call. The job's positives kept shrinking while the negatives piled up. Work was costing more than it was giving back. It was never about age — slowing growth exposed the cracks. The ceiling showed up once the elevator stopped going up.

blocks.label: Investment Evolution: The System Paid for with 6 Million Yuan
blocks.text: Starting in 2015 she went all-in on Chinese tech ADRs, heavily weighted on Meituan. The logic: 'I understand this company better than any other, so why would I expect other stocks to make me money?' Individual stocks are spectacular in a bull market, but when Chinese ADRs crashed from the top, the 'hang in there' strategy broke — after 2008 the US market always recovered within six months, while Chinese ADRs fell from 406 and never got back. So in 2021, planning retirement, she borrowed the Yale model: A-shares (CSI 300 / CSI 500), US stocks (Nasdaq / S&P 500), Hong Kong stocks, bonds, and gold — each index capped at 20 percent, rebalanced dynamically by PE percentile. She set aside three to five years of living expenses and let the rest roll, keeping any single asset class under 30 to 40 percent. The catch: you'll miss a lot of gains in a bull market. When the Nasdaq PE sits above the 80th percentile, the discipline means you skip most of the upside of the rally. Core mechanism: from 2015 she traded US-listed Chinese tech stocks, heavily weighted on Meituan. The logic: 'I know this company better than anyone, so I have no reason to expect other stocks to make me money.' Key insight: individual stocks pay off spectacularly in a bull market, but after the Chinese ADRs crashed from their peak, the 'just wait it out' play failed — after 2008 US stocks always recovered within six months, while Chinese ADRs fell from 406 and never came back. Direct quote: 'What reason do I have to believe I can make money on other stocks? Chinese ADRs fell from 406, and no matter how many years you wait, they never got back to 406.' Core mechanism: planning retirement in 2021, she borrowed the Yale model: A-shares (CSI 300 / CSI 500), US stocks (Nasdaq / S&P 500), Hong Kong stocks, bonds, and gold — each index capped at 20 percent, rebalanced dynamically by PE percentile. Typical allocation: keep 3–5 years of living expenses aside and roll the rest into investments; keep any single asset class under 30–40 percent. Boundary: in a bull market you will miss a lot of gains — when the Nasdaq PE sits above the 80th percentile, strictly following the discipline means you skip most of the rally's upside. Betting on one stock leaves you no escape when it crashes. Single-stock conviction is a one-way bet with no floor. Strict discipline means giving up part of the bull-market rally. Following the rules costs you upside when everything goes up.

blocks.label: The FIRE Decision Framework and What Life After Retirement Looks Like
blocks.text: Why it matters: if the money isn't sorted out, you'll be anxious every day — the day before she resigned she recalculated 'will I go broke' a dozen times. And if your sense of achievement comes from the wrong place, you'll soon be back in the office. The boundary: some people can FIRE without doing the math — one of her friends did — but she's a planner who has to see the numbers. Of the FIRE cases she's seen, only one person went back to work, and it was for a loss of achievement, not money. Her framework: first, run the numbers — what you'll spend, what return rate you can expect, what risks under different environments. Second, where does your achievement come from? If it comes from leading a group of people to pull something off, FIRE might not feel great. Concretely: list your household expenses, estimate a return range, stress-test whether you can survive a bear market, and honestly judge whether your achievement runs on solo creation or teamwork. Mengmeng admitted she's a bit disappointed to have missed the AI-layoff severance windfall, but her logic: inside a company, your attention must go to what the company cares about — foot spas, say — while as an independent person you can use AI to dig into what you actually care about, like psychology. Is it 'missing the windfall' or 'gaining attention freedom'? The guests clearly lean toward the latter. And if your source of achievement isn't right, you'll soon be back in the workforce. So far she's met only one 'FIRE failure,' and that person went back to work for loss of achievement, not money. title_en: Why Are the Chinese Afraid to Spend? Jia Kang on Consumption, Housing, and Economic Confidence

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Why Are the Chinese Afraid to Spend? Jia Kang on Consumption, Housing, and Economic Confidence

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Host Xiaowu and economist Jia Kang start from the "quietest 618" and May's 0.6% year-on-year drop in retail sales, unpacking the K-shaped divergence and weak expectations behind sluggish consumption — income pressure, shrinking household assets, and rising precautionary savings make ordinary spending more cautious by the day. The way out: fast variables — loose fiscal and monetary policy — to prop things up, and slow variables — reform — to cure the root. They also debunk common myths about handing out cash and saturated investment, landing finally on the support chain of consumption → income → employment → effective investment.

blocks.label: The Phenomenon: What's Wrong with Consumption — Quiet or Uneven?
blocks.text: First, the phenomenon. Carnival-style shopping festivals like 618 and Double 11 have been getting quieter every year, and platforms no longer publish transaction figures. Consumers have moved from herd-following to careful budgeting after years of experience — festivals have become a barometer of changing consumer psychology. But a quiet festival doesn't mean no one is spending; it means purchase decisions turned rational, weighing whether it's worth it before whether it's exciting. May's retail sales fell 0.6% year-on-year, contrasting with a bright first quarter — that's the real turning-point signal. And the market is K-shaped: first-tier cities saw bigger consumption drops, yet Shanghai's housing transactions hit their best May in six years, and middle- and high-income people keep pouring into Universal Studios, while mass consumption data falls. One end down, one end up. Carnival-style shopping festivals like 618 and Double 11 have been getting quieter every year, and platforms no longer release transaction figures. Consumers have shifted from herd-following to careful budgeting after years of experience — promotional festivals have become a barometer of shifting consumer psychology. The key insight: a quiet festival doesn't mean no one is spending — it means purchase decisions have turned rational, weighing "is it worth it" before "is it exciting." May's 0.6% year-on-year drop in retail sales, contrasting with the first quarter's bright spot, is the real turning-point signal to watch. A typical scene: the 618 ended "silently," platforms published no transaction records, and consumers quietly watched from the sidelines. "Consumption is increasingly about being more careful and rational. But May was a phenomenon that goes against our wishes." Related concept: it goes hand in hand with "precautionary savings" and "K-shaped divergence" — the temperature of shopping festivals is a leading indicator of structural change in consumption. The mechanism: first-tier cities saw a bigger consumption drop than the national average, yet Shanghai's housing transactions hit their best May in six years; middle- and high-income people keep pouring into Universal Studios — spending one to two thousand yuan per person — while mass consumption data falls. The market shows a "K-shaped" split: one end down, one end up. The festival hype keeps dying down year after year. Shopping festivals are getting quieter — and that says something. Consumption is splitting into a K shape — one end up, one end down. The market is diverging: premium spending up, mass spending down.

blocks.label: The Causes: Why People Won't Spend — Where Weak Expectations Come From
blocks.text: Second, why people won't spend. Spending power is set by income, but expectations matter just as much. Falling housing prices shrink household net assets — a house worth 10 million dropping to 8 million is like losing 2 million — and even without selling, that on-paper feeling suppresses the willingness to spend. The rebound so far only covers prime locations and quality projects in first-tier cities; third, fourth, and fifth-tier cities still feel the pressure, so the threat hasn't lifted broadly. And expectations of rigid future spending on education, healthcare, and retirement keep rising — especially the child's future fund. Parents pinch their own pennies but keep the kids' reserve solid. Shrinking assets, precautionary savings, weak expectations — they compound and tame consumption. Spending power is set by income, but expectations matter just as much. Falling housing prices shrink household net assets — "a house worth 10 million dropping to 8 million is like losing 2 million" — and even without selling, that on-paper feeling suppresses the willingness to spend. The key insight: shrinking assets change your "sense of wealth," not your cash flow — but it still affects real spending. The housing rebound is so far limited to prime locations and quality projects in first-tier cities; third, fourth, and fifth-tier cities still feel the pressure, so the threat of shrinking assets hasn't lifted broadly. A typical scene: income stays the same, yet the willingness to spend clearly drops — "simply because the precautionary-savings motive has invisibly risen." "My house was worth 10 million, now it's 8 million — that's like losing 2 million. That feeling affects people's motivation to spend and their actual spending behavior." Related concept: shrinking assets → precautionary savings → tamed consumption, the same roots as the K-shaped divergence. The mechanism: expectations of rigid future spending on education, healthcare, and retirement are rising. Especially the "child's future fund" — parents would rather pinch their own pennies than loosen the reserve for their kids, "making that fund more solid." What shrank wasn't your income — it was your sense of wealth. The loss is on paper, but it still hurts your confidence to spend. The precautionary-savings motive has quietly gone up. People are saving for a rainy day without realizing it.

blocks.label: The Way Out: Fast Variables Prop Up, Slow Variables Cure
blocks.text: Third, the way out. Fast variables: proactive fiscal policy plus moderately loose monetary policy — swapping debt to resolve local hidden debt, special bonds and treasury bonds supporting major projects, stabilizing the real-estate pillar, and activating capital markets, with stocks back above 4,000 points since late September. Fast variables can show real effect within months or be scaled up further; their role is to stop things from getting worse and push toward better — a stopgap. Real GDP hit about 5% for three straight years, impossible without policy support. Slow variables: the Third Plenum's 300-plus reform tasks, cultivating new productive forces from "Internet Plus" to "AI Plus," strengthening from 1 to 100 and breaking through from 0 to 1, so creativity is no longer suppressed. Fast variables buy the time window for slow ones — they relay, not replace. Proactive fiscal policy plus moderately loose monetary policy: swapping debt to resolve local hidden debt — a five-year program focused on the identified 14.3 trillion yuan of hidden local debt — special bonds and ultra-long-term treasury bonds supporting major projects, stabilizing the real-estate pillar, and activating capital markets, with the stock market back above 4,000 points since late September. The key insight: fast variables "can show real effect within months, or be scaled up further" — their role is to "stop things from getting worse and push toward better," a stopgap; the double easing is already at extraordinary intensity. A typical scene: real GDP hit 5.2% in 2023, 5% in 2024, and 5% in 2025 — three straight years on a roughly 5% plateau, impossible without policy support. "Without such policies, the economy would definitely be worse now… the relay and combined force of fast and slow variables is where the effort must continue." Related concept: fast variables buy the time window for slow variables — they must relay, not replace, each other. The mechanism: the Third Plenum outlined more than 300 reform tasks, cultivating new productive forces — advancing from "Internet Plus" to "AI Plus" — strengthening from 1 to 100 and breaking through from 0 to 1. Reforming education and tech systems so creativity is no longer suppressed. Fast variables are the stopgap — they keep things from getting worse. It's first aid, not surgery. Fast and slow variables have to hand off to each other. The quick fix buys time for the real fix.

blocks.label: The Cash Debate: Helicopter Money, Consumption Vouchers, and Ration Coupons
blocks.text: Fourth, the cash debate. Musk argues that as long as the supply of goods and services grows faster than the money supply, you can hand out cash per person without inflation. But Jia Kang points out: China's population base is too large — 3,000 yuan per person is about 400-plus US dollars, and nationwide that's over 4 trillion yuan, exceeding the 2008 four-trillion stimulus, plus governments are already in debt with the deficit ratio raised to 4%. Money isn't the only constraint. Drawing the line is hard: household sizes differ wildly, income verification tangles with underreporting, and the management cost is huge. Then there's social acceptability: even Ma Yun would get a check — what's the point? The US actually drew an income line covering about half the population at two to three thousand dollars each, and nobody quibbled. Differentiated payments in China would sink into disputes over how to draw the line and who gets it. Musk argues that as long as the supply of goods and services grows faster than the money supply, you can hand out cash per person without inflation. But Jia Kang points out: China's population base is too large — 3,000 yuan per person is about 400-plus US dollars, and nationwide that's over 4 trillion yuan, exceeding the 2008 "four trillion" stimulus; plus governments are already in debt, with the deficit ratio raised to 4%. The key insight: money isn't the only constraint — there are two hard ones. First, drawing the line is hard: household sizes differ wildly, income verification tangles with underreporting, and the management cost is huge. Second, social acceptability: "even Ma Yun would get a check — what's the point?" A typical scene: the US "cash for everyone" during the financial crisis actually drew an income line covering about half the population at 2,000 to 3,000 dollars each — socially accepted, nobody quibbled about the line. If China issued differentiated payments, it would sink into disputes over "how to draw the line and who gets it." "No differentiation, no policy… the total pressure plus what the public finds acceptable — put together, the decision becomes very hard to make." Related concept: along with consumption vouchers and ration coupons, they're all tools in the "demand-side stimulus toolbox," each with its own boundaries. The mechanism: China's consumption vouchers are essentially "government-plus-merchant joint promotions," targeting lower- and middle-income groups and young white-collar workers who are motivated; trade-in programs focus on durable goods like electronics, appliances, and cars. The total bill for cash handouts is simply too big. Spread across 1.4 billion people, the money just doesn't stretch. Drawing the line between who gets it and who doesn't is a minefield. Income checks and household sizes make targeting messy.

blocks.label: The Root Cure Chain: Consumption → Income → Jobs → Effective Investment
blocks.text: Finally, the root cure chain: consumption → spending power → income → jobs → effective investment. Consumption's root is income; income depends on stable, substantial, predictable jobs; and jobs come from effective investment. You can't only talk about consumption — you have to work upstream along the chain. When corporate investment is depressed, government investment steps in — that's the most important entry point. The "two-major" areas — national security-critical infrastructure plus strategic infrastructure like disaster reduction, sponge cities, underground utility tunnels, and rail networks — directly create jobs and orders, and turn excess capacity into effective capacity. Fast variable and slow variable finally join at the point of employment. The complete support chain: consumption → spending power → income → jobs → effective investment. Consumption's root is income; income depends on stable, substantial, predictable jobs; and jobs come from effective investment. The key insight: "you can't only talk about consumption" — you have to work upstream along the chain. When corporate investment is depressed, government investment steps in — that's the most important entry point. A typical scene: when private-enterprise investment is low and jobs are under pressure, government "two-major" investment directly creates positions and orders, driving income and the consumption environment. "The most fundamental support for consumption is spending power, and spending power is income. Where does income come from? It depends on jobs." Related concept: the fast variable (government investment) and the slow variable (reform) join at the point of "employment." The mechanism: the "two major" areas are national security-critical infrastructure plus strategic infrastructure: disaster reduction, sponge cities, underground utility tunnels, and rail networks. Government investment directly creates jobs and orders, and can turn excess capacity into effective capacity. Consumption is rooted in income — everything upstream of that is where you intervene. You can't boost spending directly; you boost income first. When private money sits idle, public investment steps in. Government spending backstops the gap private capital left.

blocks.label: Why Clawdbot Blew Up: The Soul of a Phenomenon Product
blocks.text: The core mechanism: long-term memory lets it remember conversations and preferences across sessions; initiative shows in daily greetings, pre-researching tasks, and life reminders — it can joke and tease like JARVIS. AI initiative isn't a new concept, but Clawdbot is the first product to nail memory plus initiative plus IM all at once, so ordinary people can feel the progress. A typical scene: you murmur 'the beef won't last much longer,' and the agent adds a reminder on its own and nudges you about the right cooking time in the afternoon. Users describe it as 'that kind of super-proactive subordinate… once you use it, you can't go back.' And because it lives inside familiar messaging apps like WeChat and Feishu, talking to it feels like chatting with a colleague, not typing in a terminal. Once you use it, you can't go back. It's addictive in the best way — the old way feels broken now. It feels like messaging a coworker, not operating a tool. The IM wrapper makes it feel human.

blocks.label: Impressive Use Cases: The Boundaries of Agent Autonomy
blocks.text: Zhixian asked the agent to test the macOS local-model API. After testing, it automatically wrote an article in the user's voice, published it to his bilingual blog, and set the tags and categories itself. The agent read the whole repo's rules and figured out the configuration on its own, without any follow-up questions — the publish took about ten seconds and it tossed back two links. The practical tip: give the agent a clear goal, like write and publish, and let it explore the repo rules itself — this suits developers with custom blog setups.
