title_en: The '8 Carmakers Summoned' Story Was Fake — But Battery Locking Is Worth Discussing

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: The '8 Carmakers Summoned' Story Was Fake — But Battery Locking Is Worth Discussing

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Three-Dao takes apart the fake news that 'eight carmakers were summoned for battery locking,' then digs into the real issue: how OTA software quietly caps battery capacity, the BMS 'happy gauge' that shows full even when it isn't, the eight-year warranty deadline pushing automakers to play safe, and where owners' rights actually end. He closes with practical ways to protect your rights — keeping evidence and filing collective complaints with the regulators instead of rushing into lawsuits.

blocks.label: Part 1: The Battery-Locking Storm and the Boundary of Power
blocks.text: Let's talk about battery locking. Carmakers can modify the battery management system's parameters through over-the-air updates or the OBD port, capping the charging limit, depth of discharge, fast-charging power, and motor output — pushing the battery into a conservative operating state. The BMS is the battery's brain. The maker sells you a 100-liter bucket; years later the gauge still shows 100 percent full, but it may only hold 90 liters. That's a happy gauge. Why now? EVs bought around 2018 are passing their eight-year warranty, and mass degradation means real claim costs and brand damage, so carmakers use software to make batteries lazier. Just remember: battery locking is different from natural degradation and from hardware neutering. The mechanism: via over-the-air updates or the 4S shop's OBD port, carmakers modify the battery management system's parameters to cap the charging limit, depth of discharge, fast-charging power, and motor output — pushing the battery into a more conservative operating state. The insight: the BMS is the battery pack's 'brain' — it decides how far it can charge, how far it can discharge, and when to limit power. The maker sells you a 100-liter bucket; years later the gauge still shows 100% full, but it may only hold 90 liters. That's the 'happy gauge.' Typical case: EVs bought around 2018 are about to pass their eight-year warranty. To avoid mass claims and bad publicity, carmakers may tighten the battery strategy through OTA. As the host says: 'The maker tells you the bucket holds 100 liters. After a few years the gauge still shows 100% full — but it's not really holding 100 liters. The gauge is a happy gauge.' Related concepts: battery locking versus natural degradation versus hardware neutering — like the smart #1 charging you to unlock a feature that's already installed. 2026 is exactly when the 2018 EV boom turns eight, and the eight-year, 120,000-kilometer battery warranty runs out. Mass degradation failures mean real claim costs and brand damage, which pushes carmakers to use software to make batteries more conservative — lazier, if you will. Carmakers tighten the battery through software. They quietly cap the usable capacity. The gauge says full, but the bucket is smaller. It's a happy gauge — it tells you what you want to hear. The warranty expiring pushes them to play safe. As the warranty window closes, the incentives shift.

blocks.label: Part 2: Regulation and How to Fight Back
blocks.text: Here's the regulatory picture. Since 2021, China's MIIT has required safety-impact assessments, testing, implementation records, and full disclosure for every OTA update, and 2025 rules tightened further — changing major technical parameters now needs a product-change permit and full filing. Last year's delayed OTA pushes were exactly a filing-approval problem. So if carmakers get 'summoned' only after mass complaints, the real question is whether the filing review is strict enough. Open, compliant updates for safety recalls are fine; silently forced updates and repackaged 'optimizations' violate consumer rights. The hard part is that OTA is a black box — you can feel shorter range but can't prove locking. The practical route is keeping evidence and filing collective complaints with 12315 and the regulators, not lawsuits. The mechanism: in 2021, China's MIIT required carmakers to run safety-impact assessments, test and verify, ensure implementation, and keep records for every OTA — and to disclose the purpose, content, duration, cautions, and result of each update. In 2025 it tightened further: changes to major technical parameters require a product-change permit plus full filing. The insight: last year several carmakers delayed their OTA pushes precisely because filing approval broke their schedules. Since a filing system already exists, if carmakers are 'summoned' only after mass complaints, the logical thing to question is whether the filing review is strict enough. Boundaries: open, compliant OTA for safety recalls is fine; silently forced updates, vague disclosure, and repackaging cuts as 'optimization' infringe on consumer rights. As the host says: 'Carmakers can't use software to hide hardware problems. Regulators must be strict in reviewing filings — if a recall is being dodged, the update must not be pushed.' Why it's hard to prove: OTA is a black box — owners never see the BMS parameters before or after an update. You feel shorter range and sluggish acceleration, but you can't prove it's locking rather than temperature, highways, rain, mountain roads, fast-charging habits, or natural degradation. The fix: lawsuits are the most expensive route with the least certain results; social-media discussion threads plus collective complaints to 12315, the market regulator, or the MIIT tend to work better. OTA is a black box to owners. You never see what the update actually changed. You can't prove it's locking, not natural wear. Too many variables make the cause impossible to pin down. Collective complaints work better than lawsuits. Numbers give you leverage with regulators.

blocks.label: Part 3: Industry Ripples — Supply-Chain Shifts
blocks.text: Finally, the industry ripple. The battery industry has few suppliers, nowhere near a healthy '2-2-2-3' mix of premium, mid, and budget players, but Tesla's five battery suppliers is already an unusually large roster for an automaker. A listener makes a sharp point: a healthy supplier pool should have four makers competing for high-end quality, and Tesla adding Sunwoda signals a shift away from CATL. And notice the double standard — when a Chinese EV uses Sunwoda, people question it; when Tesla uses Sunwoda, it's read as a quality endorsement. It's just consumers looking through tinted glasses. After all, the iPhone already uses Sunwoda components. The mechanism: the battery industry has few suppliers, nowhere near a '2-2-2-3' mix of two premium, two mid, and three budget suppliers — yet Tesla's five battery suppliers is already an unusually large roster for an automaker. The insight: listener Wuzhucaomeiyu notes that a healthy supplier pool should have four makers competing for high-end models to keep quality, with mid-tier and budget players competing for the lower end. Tesla following that logic to add Sunwoda signals a supply-chain shift away from CATL. As the listener puts it: 'When a Chinese EV uses Sunwoda, people question it; when Tesla uses Sunwoda, it's read as a quality endorsement — it's just consumers who don't understand batteries, looking through tinted glasses.' Related point: Sunwoda was picked by Tesla, yet it's often labeled a 'second-tier brand' — even though the iPhone already uses Sunwoda components. People look at it through tinted glasses. There's a double standard at play. Tesla picked them, yet they're still called second-tier. Same factory, two different reputations depending on who buys. Adding Sunwoda signals a shift from CATL. It's a quiet message to the dominant supplier.

Too many variables make it impossible to pin down the cause. Consumers judge second-tier brands through tinted glasses.

title_en: E227 The Economics of Exhaustion: Why Are We More Tired as Technology Improves?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: E227 The Economics of Exhaustion: Why Are We More Tired as Technology Improves?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Host Yu Bai opens with the shock of seeing 'single-threaded' work in European restaurants and, together with economist Wen Yifei, explores a paradox: the more technology advances, the busier and more exhausted we become. Food delivery and productivity tools make money off 'tired money'; the eight-hour workday came from Cold War labor compromises, not a gift of productivity; and AI serves first as a supervisor before it becomes a tool. Exhaustion has structural causes — it isn't just personal laziness.

blocks.label: Where the Fatigue Comes From: European Observations and 'Tired Money'
blocks.text: In a European restaurant, Yu Bai stood for ages without being served — the host only seats people, and everyone else sticks to their own job; nobody has 'eyes for work.' Paying the bill took twenty minutes from asking to finishing. Locals take it for granted: each person has a fixed role, single-threaded work, and it's easier on the worker. Back in China for a week, she was back to fast-paced habits: order delivery, get one missing side dish, and immediately think about leaving a bad review. As consumers we demand faster and better; as workers we're pinned to instant messaging, online 24/7. Technology and efficiency improved, yet the legitimacy of rest has vanished. A lot of businesses are essentially making money off people's exhaustion — isn't food delivery exactly that? In a European restaurant, Yu Bai stood for ages without being served — the host only seats people, and everyone else sticks to their own job; nobody has 'eyes for work.' Paying the bill took twenty minutes from asking to finishing, and locals take it for granted: each person has a fixed role, single-threaded work, and it's easier on the worker. Back in China for a week, she slid right back into the fast pace: order delivery, get one missing side dish, and immediately think about a bad review. As consumers we demand faster and better; as workers we're pinned to instant messaging, online 24/7. Technology and efficiency improved — yet the legitimacy of rest has vanished. A typical case: no time for a proper lunch — that's how the food delivery industry was born. Too exhausted to rest — that becomes the business model of 'making money off exhaustion.' The original quote: 'A lot of businesses are essentially making money off people's exhaustion... isn't food delivery exactly that?' Related concept: the economics of exhaustion means society sees everyone exhausted, and instead of eliminating the exhaustion, it exploits it to create new demand and new industries. Every industrial revolution — steam, electricity, information — was supposed to bring a productivity leap, and people expected job losses and shorter hours. The data says the opposite: labor intensity was often at its peak in those very eras. In China since 2015, average annual working time has grown by about a month, roughly 20 extra working days per person. Everyone has their own fixed job. Each person sticks to their lane. Food delivery cashes in on your exhaustion. These apps profit off tired people.

blocks.label: The Eight-Hour Day: Not a Gift from Technology
blocks.text: From the Ford era through the 1970s, benefits grew and hours shrank; after the 1980s information revolution, intensity climbed back. The eight-hour day was not a natural perk of rising productivity — it was the result of proletarian revolutions forcing capitalism to give ground. When the Soviet Union was thriving, top income tax rates for Western capitalists ran at 80 to 90 percent — don't pay and workers might flip the table. Heavy taxes came back to workers as welfare, and hours and labor relations improved. The danger here: everyone wants AI to replace work, but nobody expected AI to watch your work — slack for five minutes and it nudges you; slack again and it reports you to the boss. So recognize that tighter monitoring is a certain trend, and build judgment and life experience in your main career that AI can't replace. Heavy taxes flowed back to workers as welfare, while hours and labor relations improved. Once it was eight hours before and after the revolution, the incentive for revolution faded. A typical case: understanding today's overtime culture means you can't just wait for AI to mature and make life easy — you have to look at the power structure and the substitute bargaining chips. The original quote: 'The eight-hour day wasn't a natural benefit won by productivity gains — it was because proletarian revolutions were happening in some places at the time.' The cause: everyone wants AI to replace the work, but nobody expected AI to watch the work — slack for five minutes and it nudges you; slack again and it reports you to the boss. In China, AI entered through the B2B side, where companies will pay for efficiency, so AI interviews, meeting analysis, and performance quantification arrived first. The fix: recognize that tighter monitoring is a certain trend, and build judgment and life experience in your main career that AI can't replace. The eight-hour day was fought for, not gifted. It came from labor organizing, not from productivity. AI landed first as a supervisor, not a tool. Before it does your job, AI is watching you do it.

blocks.label: Boss Economics: The 996 Math
blocks.text: Take a worker earning 20,000 a month, eight-hour days, two days off — about 174 working hours a month. If the work doesn't get done, you hire a second person: two people cost about 57,000 with social insurance, for 348 hours. Or let one person work 996 to cover those 348 hours: double overtime pay is about 7,300, and with social insurance the total cost is about 35,000 — saving over 20,000, plus no recruiting, no training, no desk space, no extra management layer. It's not that bosses are born evil; it's market elimination. If your competitor's employees each do the work of five people and you don't keep up, you disappear. A normal boss, thinking in pure operating efficiency, would rather pay double overtime than hire. blocks.text: In this episode, Pan, Bai Xiong, and Seven from Photo Reason dig up their reject-photo shame files, breaking down each failure from technical mistakes to aesthetic misfires. blocks.label: 1. What Is a "Reject Photo"? The Hosts' Shame Files
blocks.text: A reject photo isn't a universal standard — it's a shot that's ineffective or outdated relative to who you are now. Seven sees it as outdated taste, form over substance. There's a telling coincidence: all three picked rejects from their transition period, when they were switching from digital to film or messing with early digital post-processing. Transitions are exactly when you're most likely to make photos that felt great then but don't hold up now. The classic scene: scrolling through old cloud drives and Moments archives — every file you open is a horror show. But as they say, "reject photo" sounds like an insult, yet every one of them is a stepping stone. Being able to recognize a reject already means your taste has moved forward. One friend sent thirty-odd rolls of expired film, some two years old, some ten, and it created the illusion that pressing the shutter was nearly free. The key difference from her old portraits: this photo feels natural and real — you can sense the person's emotion, while the old studio work was people striking pretty poses, all form and no soul. blocks.text: Pan walks through his milestones: at sixteen or seventeen, a guesthouse commercial taught him tripods and indoor post-processing; at Aranya, copying great work online made things click; his first Hasselblad scan after the Rolleiflex revealed what film could really do; starting a podcast forced him to study photobooks and quietly broadened his vision; Jerome's high-pressure workshop pushed him out of his comfort zone; and swapping the Rolleiflex for a Mamiya 6x7 gave his compositions more tension. title_en: Podcast Anniversary Special: We Tried Answering a French Philosophy Bac Exam Question

blocks.label: 英文标题

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: The one-year anniversary special of Iambus: two hosts improvise answers to a French philosophy baccalauréat question — 'Is truth always convincing?' From whether the Earth is round or flat, phenomenological evidence, and the violence of Platonic truth, to Descartes' evil demon and the 'trivial truths' of street-corner chat, this is a deep conversation about truth, imagination, power, and everyday life.

blocks.label: The Format and the Core Question
blocks.text: The producer Achai picks a question at random; the hosts get only about fifteen minutes to prepare, then answer it impromptu as a conversation — it's like a game. There's no scoring; whoever violates the rules too often — abusing jargon or name-dropping philosophers — has to buy books out of their own pocket. Academic words like '-ism,' '-ity,' and 'tradition' are deliberately banned, forcing them to discuss philosophy in everyday language and testing their dialogue and improvisation skills. This is modeled on the French baccalauréat philosophy essay — the prompt being 'La vérité est-elle toujours convaincante?' — is truth always convincing? As they said, they were answering a philosophy exam, but they couldn't answer in an overly academic, scholarly way. The French philosophy exam is famous for open-ended essays: define the concept, argue, then answer the counterarguments — but this show deliberately breaks that rigid template. And everyday experience shows why: some people are convinced the Earth is flat and argue about wrong arithmetic answers on Douyin — even the most 'obvious' truth can't convince everyone. Money is persuasive, lies are persuasive — but is a triangle persuasive? Is one plus one equals two persuasive? blocks.label: Is the Earth Round? Three Paths to Understanding
blocks.text: Andy argues with Occam's razor — the 'razor principle,' as they call it. If the Earth were flat, you'd need to invent elaborate conspiracies; the simpler explanation is to accept a spherical Earth. But we never actually ran the shadow experiment ourselves — what we call 'verification' is really a hermeneutic inference made in a specific historical and social context. Scientific truths are established through peer review, yet ordinary people believe the Earth is round not because they've read the papers, but because they've been told so since childhood. Yutong, by contrast, stresses imagination and power. To her, truth is boring, theoretical, unrelated to her — she believes the Earth is round not from scientific verification but because language and childhood education have implanted a 'spherical Earth' in her imagination; imagining a flat Earth is extremely hard. As she said, the proposition 'the Earth is round' is convincing because it seizes me through imagination, not because truth itself seizes me. Andy pushes back: it's not so much truth that's persuasive as power — schools and the scientific establishment drill 'the Earth is a sphere' into you, and these institutions of knowledge transmission sustain the belief. In the Middle Ages, people believing in a flat Earth was likewise the work of particular institutions of power. What convinces is often power, not truth. Authority repeats, and repetition becomes belief.

blocks.label: Attempts in the History of Philosophy to Find 'Persuasive Truth'
blocks.text: First, phenomenology: don't ask whether red is 'really' red — just confirm 'I clearly saw red.' What is seen is itself persuasive; that's the self-evident standard phenomenology tries to establish. This works for everyday perceptual judgments, but evidence can't cover the complex web of interests in real arguments. As they said, what did we actually see... when a thing is merely seen, it is quite persuasive. Second, formalizing science — like one plus one equals two — so everyone can verify truth under the same rules. Yutong points out that a circle, as a theoretical entity, can be given form through imagination, but concepts like wave-particle duality resist being imagined. Formal logic works for mathematics, but it can't capture the complexity and emotional dimension of real-world facts. And then there's Plato's cave: truth is the sun that you see — and seeing it 'blinds' you, you're completely conquered and silenced. This truth isn't a comfortable everyday perception like seeing a red coat; it's a forceful persuasion whose result is the total overturning of your existing beliefs. What you see is persuasive simply by being seen. Evidence doesn't ask permission — it's just there. Platonic truth hits you like staring into the sun. Some truths conquer rather than comfort.

blocks.label: Descartes: The Ontological Argument and the Evil Demon
blocks.text: The ontological argument infers from the idea of perfection that a perfect being — God — must exist. Descartes, a top-tier mathematician, insisted this proof was as indubitable as 'the angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees' — yet almost nobody accepts it today. The feeling of 'being pierced by truth' is deeply dependent on historical context and cannot serve as an absolute standard. As Yutong reads it, what's truly powerful about Descartes is the 'evil demon' image — a crimson, bat-winged demon that jams everyone's vision; believing in God may stem from an existential predicament rather than logical necessity. But there's a caution: reducing a believer's sincere pursuit to natural causes like fear and desire can disrespect the other person — Descartes would 'angrily' deny that his belief in the ontological argument wasn't genuine. The resolution: admit both sides may be equally caught in the age's 'demon' — the Zeitgeist — and neither is superior. The tension between hermeneutic reduction and respect for sincerity always remains. Core mechanism: from the 'idea of perfection' infer that a perfect being — God — must exist. Descartes, a brilliant mathematician, insisted this proof was as indubitable as 'angles of a triangle summing to 180 degrees' — yet almost nobody accepts it today. Key insight: the feeling of 'being pierced by truth' is heavily dependent on historical context and cannot serve as an absolute standard. Yutong's reading: what is genuinely powerful in Descartes is the 'evil demon' imagination — a crimson, bat-winged demon that confounds everyone's vision. Believing in God may spring from an existential predicament rather than logical necessity. Why it can offend: reducing a believer's sincere pursuit to natural causes such as fear and desire may fail to respect them — Descartes would 'angrily' deny he didn't genuinely believe the ontological argument. The resolution: admit both sides may be equally under the spell of the age's 'demon' (the Zeitgeist) — neither is smarter than the other. Severity: be careful — the tension between hermeneutic reduction and respect for sincerity is always there. He treated his proof as self-evident as a math theorem. To him, God's existence was as obvious as 180 degrees. The sense of being pierced by truth varies across eras. What feels self-evident in one age looks odd in another.

blocks.label: Everyday Truth: The Power of Trivial Truths
blocks.text: Trivia comes from the Latin for 'three-way crossroads' — the 'this and that' people exchange when they run into each other at the corner. Archives can be rewritten, but a passing remark or a nod in an encounter on the street often preserves a reality that can't be erased. As they said, in everyday conversations between people, a great deal of truth is preserved. Under limited conditions like large-scale deployment and stable model architectures, the TPU's total cost of ownership can challenge Nvidia. blocks.label: TPU vs GPU: The Fundamental Architectural Difference
blocks.text: The core mechanism: GPUs come from gaming graphics cards and use a SIMT multi-thread architecture — like a kitchen full of independent chefs, each grabbing ingredients, cooking, and plating on their own, with massively parallel compute. The TPU is a custom accelerator built for matrix computation, like an assembly-line relay: the first person grabs ingredients, the second processes, the third plates, with minimal scheduling in between and higher device utilization. The key insight: modern pretraining has shifted from compute-bound to memory-bound. GPUs idle while waiting for data movement when computing grain by grain; TPUs use software-hardware co-design to stay at full power — either reusing cached data or saturating memory bandwidth. A typical scene: large-scale Transformer pretraining and Gemini-class custom model training. As the episode put it, GPUs are like multiple chefs working in parallel independently; TPUs are like a pipeline relay, pumping results to every corner like a heart pumping blood, with far less scheduling in the middle. Compared with Groq's LPU: Groq is a compiler company, and its hardware serves deterministic low latency; the TPU is a system-level cluster solution that excels at high throughput rather than tail latency. When deeply customized for Google's own Gemini or frontier models from big labs, once all assumptions are fixed, the TPU beats the GPU in training efficiency and total cost of ownership. The core reason is better utilization: software tells the hardware what to do at every tick, the hardware layer adds no complex control units, and all complexity goes to XLA. blocks.label: The XLA Black Box and the Ecosystem War
blocks.text: The core mechanism: XLA is a static compiler. When the workload is known, it can do system-level optimization across the global TPU pod — operator fusion, avoiding repeated memory round-trips for intermediate states, and customizing memory allocation for the hardware architecture. The upper layers support PyTorch, JAX, and TensorFlow, all translated into TPU assembly instructions. The key insight: compared with CUDA's open ecosystem, XLA is a black box — it can squeeze out performance, but developers can't easily control it; debugging requires understanding both hardware and software, and external customers can hardly fix bugs independently. A typical scene: Anthropic, whose team comes from Google and understands XLA; and Apple, where Pang Ruoming took the whole stack to train Apple Intelligence. As the episode put it, XLA is a black box and the secret sauce; external developers can hardly handle or fix a bug on their own and must reach out to Google engineers. Compared with CUDA: CUDA's ecosystem is mature and independently debuggable; XLA's performance ceiling is higher but the barrier is extremely high, and you must migrate to JAX plus XLA to unlock the TPU's advantages. blocks.text: Early MoE didn't run well on TPUs, because in a 2D topology a chip can only talk to its neighbors, and routing to different experts required many detours. The V4 introduced a 3D Torus with an OCI optical switch, letting software program the communication paths, solving the MoE all-to-all pain point in one shot with a clear efficiency gain. As the episode noted, it takes at least two to two-and-a-half to three years from chip design to mass production; but model algorithms can change every six months. The reason: aggressive customization can boost efficiency 30-40% on Gemini models, but if the algorithmic paradigm shifts — beyond the core Transformer logic — rolling back is extremely painful. The fix: from V6 onward, training and inference split into two versions, with modular matrix units to fit different workloads; the software group's say has far exceeded the hardware group's. blocks.label: The Supply-Chain Lifeline: Broadcom and Datacenter Costs
blocks.text: The core mechanism: the TPU team designs the chip's front end — the schematics; Broadcom handles the ICI interconnect, back-end signal layout, and mixed-signal work combining analog and digital — extremely high-barrier dirty work. Everything goes to TSMC for mass production. The key insight: Broadcom runs like a 2B business locked to its biggest customer, helping secure CoWoS and TSMC capacity; but its pricing power keeps growing, squeezing the TPU's margin. Without a backup plan — like Nvidia's bargaining position with TSMC — costs are hard to control. A typical scene: GPU clusters need a lot of expensive NVSwitch switches; the TPU uses barrel chips with direct connection plus a small amount of optical switching, and the datacenter build-out cost gap has already widened. As the episode put it, the GPU's main cost is switches; the TPU's main costs are liquid cooling and SerDes signal stability — and Broadcom is a very core link. Henry's conclusion: there's no absolute answer, but under the limited conditions of large-scale deployment, relatively stable models, and massive user bases sharing costs, the TPU can absolutely challenge the GPU. As the episode put it, TPUs aren't well-suited for local deployment; they're great for operator-level use — scenarios like Gemini or ChatGPT with millions of daily users. title_en: It's an MPV, but They Call It an SUV — What Is Great Wall Thinking?

blocks.text: It's an MPV, but They Call It an SUV — What Is Great Wall Thinking?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Sandao takes apart the Wey Gaoshan 7 'SUV Edition' in depth: the ride height up 3 centimeters, new off-road styling kits, an added four-wheel-drive mode, and a guide price of 285,800 yuan that stays put. The real story isn't the specs — it's Great Wall using an 'SUV narrative' to give an MPV a fresh mental entry point, borrowing the off-road DNA of Haval and Tank to dip into the SUV traffic pool with the 7 series. Get it right, and it's pure upside; if it doesn't sell, they can quietly kill the variant without hurting the main line.

blocks.label: Part 1 · Product Breakdown: What Changed in the Gaoshan 7 SUV Edition
blocks.text: The mechanism: it adds an 'SUV Edition' configuration on top of the standard Gaoshan 7, with the guide price still at 285,800 yuan, currently 278,800. It's not a stretched version — the wheelbase stays at 3,085 millimeters, and the length changes to 5,050 due to the body kits. The key insight: the ride height rises 30 millimeters, from 155 to 185, which takes chassis reinforcement and a full re-tuning, not just a simple spacer; side skirts and a new front bumper make it look tougher; and a dedicated four-wheel-drive mode is added, optimized for rough roads, gravel, and slippery surfaces. Who's it for? Bed-and-breakfast owners commuting between town and countryside, campers hitting rural lanes on weekends, construction bosses running mountain roads — people who need more capability than a traditional MPV but don't need real off-roading. As Sandao puts it, it's not just about ground clearance — it's about whether you dare to drive, not whether the car can go anywhere. And the regular Gaoshan 7, 8, and 9 all come with Hi-4 four-wheel drive anyway. blocks.text: The mechanism: Great Wall's strongest label is SUV — the Haval H6, Tank 300 and 500, the Lanshan — but the Gaoshan is an MPV. Wey, as the underdog chasing the pack, has no legacy baggage, so it opens a new path: make the MPV more outdoorsy and all-scenario, and plant the 'SUV' name into buyers' minds — you're not buying a traditional business MPV; you're buying an MPV with Great Wall SUV DNA. Traditional MPVs like the GL8 and Sienna are built on low floors, low profiles, and business composure; raising the chassis means redoing the engineering and possibly pleasing no one, so the incumbents won't bother. Wey, arriving late with no baggage, is betting on differentiation. The target: buyers of big SUVs like the Li L8 and L9 or the AITO M7, M8, and M9 — an MPV's third row beats a similarly priced SUV, and the 250,000-to-350,000 bracket overlaps heavily. As Sandao says, the SUV market is a layer cake, and even a trickle of its volume could double MPV sales. title_en: Greenlights: A Vibrant Life Matters More Than a Rising Career

title_en: Two Years of World Travel: I Am Definitely Not the NPC of This World ｜ VOL.233

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Two Years of World Travel: I Am Definitely Not the NPC of This World ｜ VOL.233

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Daxi quit her job and visited 28 countries over two years, starting with the lowest-threshold route of visa-free destinations. She transformed from a checklist tourist into a 'walking anthropologist' — no guides, no review apps, no social media accounts. In a seaside cemetery, on the Nile, at a Peruvian funeral, and against the New York skyline, she confirmed that she is not the world's NPC, but a living person who can actively choose her life's track.

blocks.label: Getting Started: The Lowest-Threshold Launch Method
blocks.text: Like running, choose the easiest thing to start with — search social media for visa-free country routes in Eastern Europe, Thailand, and so on, and don't get intimidated by visas, gear, or guides. The first trip wasn't 'world travel' at all — she just wanted to see abroad after quitting her job. Only after the first trip through seven or eight countries over two or three months did she confirm she fits the backpacker life. This is for when you have the travel itch but always feel unprepared, and the plan feels too big to start. As she says, she never set out under the label of 'world travel' — she just wanted to go out and play, and only slowly did she become someone who had completed a world trip. It contrasts with 'save up enough first' and 'finish the perfect plan before leaving' — action before the label. Many people think of world travel as a complicated big deal and never move; Daxi, simply 'out of work for now, going out to play,' started from places that need no visa and made it work. The core mechanism: like starting to run, pick the easiest thing to begin with — search social platforms for visa-free country routes like Eastern Europe and Thailand, and don't get scared off by visas, gear, or guides. The key insight: the first trip wasn't 'world travel' — she just wanted to go abroad after quitting her job; only after covering seven or eight countries over two or three months did she confirm she fits the backpacker life. A typical scene: you have the travel itch, but you always feel underprepared, and the plan feels too big to start. 'I never set out with the world-travel label — I just wanted to go out and play… only slowly did I become the person who finished a world trip.' Related concept: it contrasts with 'wait until I've saved enough' and 'perfect the plan before leaving' — action before the label. Many people see 'world travel' as a complicated big deal and keep postponing it; Daxi, simply 'no job for now, let's go play,' started from places that need no visa — and made it work. Act first, earn the label later. The title came after the journey, not before. Start with the easiest possible version. Pick the lowest barrier and just go.

blocks.label: Travel Method: A Walking Anthropologist
blocks.text: On arrival she reads no guides — just wanders freely through tourist and residential streets, and when something looks curious, she goes and looks. Let the destination surprise you. She evolved from following companions to popular checkpoints to 'natural occurrence' travel; only afterward did she summarize it as 'walking anthropological observation.' It suits slow travel with plenty of time and a relaxed mindset; a five-day business-style trip may still need guide-based guarantees. She doesn't check review apps either — she observes street restaurants instead: if it's in a non-tourist area and locals — old people, families with kids, off-duty workers — are eating there, it's cheap and authentic. A budget backpacker's funds are limited; if one meal fails, find another tomorrow. She doesn't photograph or post to social media — just for the experience itself. Let the destination surprise you. The boundary: this suits slow travel with abundant time and a relaxed mindset; a tight five-day business-style trip may still need a guide for guarantees. 'I like to arrive and read no guides at all… wander wherever the road goes, and go see whatever catches my curiosity.' The key insight: a budget backpacker has limited funds, so a failed meal just means trying again tomorrow; she doesn't photograph or post to social media — the experience itself is the point. Let the place surprise you. Show up with zero expectations and let the city write the script. Where locals eat is where it's good. Follow the lunch crowd, not the reviews.

blocks.label: Highlights: The Power of Random Encounters
blocks.text: At the seaside cemetery of Pontarenas, a white-haired man in a red cotton coat came holding red roses to visit Rachel, who passed on September 11, 2022 — exactly three years to the day of the visit. Red roses in various stages of wilting lay before the tombstone, suggesting he comes often. It's an incredibly moving love story, something she never expected before coming. On a wooden boat, a group of backpackers from the US, France, Malaysia, Egypt, and China put on music from a phone and started dancing, while a girl sat on the gunwale watching an Egyptian leading a donkey into the sunset — an oil-painting-like cross-cultural resonance. The joy didn't come from a luxury ship or a famous band, but from music and dance breaking through language to the most basic delight. After watching American dramas for over twenty years, she entered Manhattan on an ordinary backpacker visa, watching the night skyline through dirty glass — not as a Wolf of Wall Street, but with the awe of 'I don't understand it, I just came to play.' blocks.label: Backpacker Culture and the Identity of a 'Living Person'
blocks.text: Travelers leave behind clothes they don't want for newcomers to take for free or swap; Daxi traded a summer T-shirt for a winter sweater. She picked furniture from secondhand markets and scavenged trash with roommates — a German roommate joked it refreshed his view of Asian girls. Someone told her, 'I'm sure you're not an NPC' — and yes, she's not an NPC; she's pretty special. In Thailand she traveled solo; after a border official in Azerbaijan warned her to be 'careful,' she felt downcast, but landing and finding a Chinese backpacker at the same hostel brought the sense of safety back instantly. French siblings, an Argentine guy, and a Finnish traveler all became unforgettable companions. In a foreign land it's easier to 'pick up' like-minded people — but the core is daring to set off alone first. blocks.label: People on the Road, and Seeing Yourself in the Mirror
blocks.text: When she set out, she thought 'everything outside is good' — until foreigners asked her about traditional Chinese medicine, Taoism, and history, and she found she knew nothing. After traveling, she actively studied her own culture, and started introducing herself by her Chinese name. As she says, we go out thinking we're here to absorb, but in their eyes we're an extension of a mysterious Eastern kingdom — and realizing we have nothing to offer feels regretful, even hollow. Her words: 'We went out thinking we were here to absorb — but in their eyes, we are an extension of a mysterious Eastern kingdom… when we find we have nothing to offer, it feels regrettable and hollow.' Travel revealed how little I knew about my own culture. It took strangers to show me my blind spots. I had nothing to offer in return. The exchange felt one-sided — and I was the empty side.

blocks.label: Parents, the Social Clock, and Choosing Your Track
blocks.text: Feijie sums it up: whether parents interfere depends on whether they feel you're more capable and better off than them. Daxi took her father to Shanghai, booked a good hotel, and he moved from 'too expensive' to recognizing her ability — she even rode an electric bike around her home village with him. What evidence do parents use to prove their child is really living a happy life? The premise is whether it's genuinely real happiness. Parents are more bound to the social clock, projecting expectations of marriage, a house, and promotions; Daxi's parents, with limited money, only hoped she'd have a steady income and support herself. She 'brainwashed' her father with a globe — in a few decades of life, who are you completing the marriage-and-kids task for? After traveling, her father verbally accepted: marriage and kids are one way to live; world travel is another. Verified actions — income, taking parents to experiences — beat arguments. She used to think she could only live by leaving the village for the center; now she actively chooses to come back, and both the people and the scenery of home deserve anthropological curiosity. blocks.label: Two Years Later: From Experiencing to Creating
blocks.text: Her original answer would definitely be to keep traveling. Now she wants to invest in a field continuously — creating and producing something, whether back in her old industry, a vintage business, or a new interest. She discovered that what makes her happiest is 'finishing something with my own idea in it,' even if it's just a piece of writing. She admits she's someone who gives up easily — but she feels she needs to practice persistence; it's her challenge, and she wants to complete it. NPCs follow the script; a living person, after enough experience, actively chooses to go deep or to return. Before traveling, daily life felt boring; after returning, the ordinary became precious. Feijie concludes: only with enough experience can you turn options into your own and make deliberate choices — even if, ten years from now, the choice is to go home and stay with your father. The key insight: photography didn't change him by teaching technique first — he first learned to see himself through the lens, to release feelings, anchor memory, and find identity, and only then hoped others would feel the same. blocks.label: Photographic Power: Mazi, Consent, and Intimate Boundaries
blocks.text: This is the sharpest part of the conversation — photographic power. The core mechanism: holding the camera means holding the power to narrate. The subject exposes themselves; the power is unequal. In intimate relationships this violence is most hidden — think of Araki, Fukase photographing Yoko, and similar cases. The key insight: the danger isn't having power — it's forgetting that you have it. As he says, it's not the power itself that's the problem; it's when the photographer forgets he has it that it gets truly frightening. He shared his own case: after two years of commercial wedding shoots, he reflexively used sales-pitch directions to pose Mazi. Mazi felt like not a girlfriend but a client, and the shoot ended in an argument. Qu Luoma later admitted this was a kind of violence he hadn't recognized early on. blocks.text: Listener Stella noticed gold-award coffee beans on every street corner, so the show takes apart the IIAC and ICT judging mechanism. blocks.label: Part 1: Business & Tech News Briefs

The same day its stock jumped over 14 percent, making it the second Asian company after TSMC to pass a trillion dollars in market value, powered by AI demand for memory. Meanwhile Moonshot is closing a 2-billion-dollar round at a post-money valuation above 20 billion, pivoting to model performance after DeepSeek stole the spotlight. And Google DeepMind bought a minority stake in the EVE Online developer to train AI for long-term planning — games are an ideal sandbox for AI training. The mechanism: Google DeepMind bought a minority stake in the EVE Online developer, using this massive multiplayer game to train AI for long-term planning and continual learning — a path already validated with games like StarCraft. blocks.label: Part 2: The IIAC Gold-Award Coffee Bean, Explained
blocks.text: Now the coffee. The IIAC — International Institute of Coffee Tasters — was founded in Italy in 1993, runs non-profit on membership fees, and its International Coffee Tasting has scored coffees in anonymous blind tastings since 2006. The gold award needs two conditions at once: at least 85 out of 100, and a top-25-percent finish. There are only gold and platinum tiers — no silver, no bronze. And the entry bar is low: pay about 2,000 yuan per product, ship samples, and any brand can compete. That's the institutional root of the gold bloom. The insight: the gold award needs two conditions at once — a score of 85 or higher out of 100, and a finish in the top 25% of that session's tasting. As the show says: 'Any brand that pays the entry fee and ships samples can compete' — that's the institutional root of gold awards blooming everywhere. Why: the word 'gold' carries built-in rarity in Chinese, but the ICT has no knockout rounds and no entry barrier, and the 85-point plus top-25% bar isn't strict once tasting sessions grow large. Since August 2024, more than ten sessions have been held in China, with over 40 entries winning at a single event. The fix: when buying coffee, tell 'certification pass' apart from 'competition champion' — the first means 'pretty good,' the second means 'one in ten thousand.' blocks.label: Sensory Design: The Underrated Power of Touch
blocks.text: The core mechanism: design isn't just about looking good — it systematically considers touch, smell, taste, and hearing to create a more immersive experience. In home settings, texture often outranks visuals. The key insight: wood brings warmth and a natural feel, metal brings rationality and coolness, and velvet connects to intimacy and softness. Materials shape users' psychology in systematic ways, backed by plenty of research in industrial design. A typical scene: Starbucks uses coffee aroma to guide purchases; Jellycat plush toys prioritize tactile safety in their design; a rug's softness extends through the entire visual evaluation system, even if your feet never touch it. As the episode put it: nobody buys a rug to use it — but a rug is the stabilizer of the living room's atmosphere, and home is the space where we can embed ourselves gently. Compared with the visually-driven Bauhaus steel tube chair — which gives off that cold 'businessman' vibe — Nordic design pulls people back into the natural forest. And in practice: you hesitate about laying a rug while renovating — cleaning is a real pain, but the rug's soft comfort can color the whole home. Sensory cues strongly steer our perception; this is an underestimated dimension of design. blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: The Japanese convenience store isn't just a place that sells food and drinks — it's a 24-hour government counter, a cardless ATM, a parcel station, and a gateway to digital life. blocks.label: How the Store Evolved Into a 24-Hour Government Window
blocks.text: The self-service printer at Japanese convenience stores evolved in three stages. First, you had to bring a USB drive or cable and plug it in to transfer files. Then each brand launched its own app, and you had to manually pair your phone with the machine — the connection was unstable, especially at FamilyMart. This machine is a microcosm of a digitalizing society: every new technology that rolls out — the apps, the My Number card — upgrades the printer right along with it. For international students, printing a certificate of residence used to mean taking a day off work to visit the ward office. Now they just swipe their My Number card at the store. And since paper insurance certificates are being phased out from December, students basically have no choice but to get the card. title_en: Currency Crash, Prices Soaring: Japan's Price Changes Over a Decade

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Currency Crash, Prices Soaring: Japan's Price Changes Over a Decade

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Two Chinese who have lived in Japan for a decade — Lao Fan and Shirley — trace their journey from the study-abroad era of a 6.7 exchange rate and thirty years of frozen prices to today's yen below 4 and prices doubling overnight. Using their own food, clothing, housing, and transport bills, they capture the surreal rift of Japan's shift from the deflationary "lost three decades" to an era of rising prices: tourists find Japan cheaper and cheaper, while residents earning and spending in yen feel squeezed from all sides — wages lagging prices, tax rates pressing down, and welfare perks being stripped away.

blocks.label: Exchange Rate & Identity: The "Measuring Stick" for Money Has Changed
blocks.text: Let's start with the exchange rate. When the hosts first arrived in Japan as students, the rate was around 6, even up to 6.7, so they converted every purchase into yuan. Today it's fallen to the low 4s, and briefly approached the 3s. A monthly salary of 250,000 yen was about 15,000 yuan at 6.7, but barely more than 10,000 yuan at 4-point-something. The exchange rate isn't an abstract macro number — it directly rewrites your value chart priced in yuan. You did nothing, and your salary automatically lost 30%. For residents earning and spending in yen, daily life feels the same — until you go home or exchange money. There's also the identity shift: as students they had tax-exempt status, so every government payout included them, but after graduation, income tax, residence tax, pension, and insurance already take nearly a third of the paycheck. "At today's rate of 4-point-something, I did nothing, and my salary automatically lost 30%." Related concept: this is two sides of the same coin as the "cheap for tourists" perspective — the exchange rate is the root of the rift. The reason: as a student she had tax-exempt status, so every government payout included her — over the three pandemic years, she received nearly 600,000 yen in total (a national 100,000 plus the school's 50,000 plus city payouts of 30,000 to 100,000). While working part-time, even when Fast Retailing closed stores, they still paid 60% to 80% of wages, and with perfect attendance she earned over 300,000 yen a month. After graduation, she became a taxpayer: income tax, residence tax, pension, and insurance already take nearly a third of her paycheck. The exchange rate silently rewrote how much my salary is worth. My paycheck shrank 30% without me doing anything. If you earn and spend in yen, nothing feels different — until you go home. The gap only shows up when you exchange currency or return to China.

blocks.label: Food: Inflation Shows Up in Your Stomach First
blocks.text: Inflation shows up in your stomach first. A five-kilogram bag of rice went from about 2,000 yen to over 4,000 yen, supermarket shelves got cleaned out, and households were limited to one bag. The government released reserve rice, but the agricultural cooperative, JA, fiercely opposed it — and JA isn't just a farm organization; it also runs banks, hospitals, and insurance, making it a monopoly-level player. The price surge isn't simple supply and demand — it's a three-layer structure of monopoly pricing, blocked reserve rice release, and import substitution locked out by tariffs of 300 percent or more. And the rescue hack is the hometown tax program: turn part of your tax bill into shopping credit on designated sites, offset it next year, and only pay a 2,000-yen processing fee. People grab it the moment it's stocked.

blocks.label: Housing & Transport: Tokyo Prices Double and Tenant Tactics
blocks.text: Next, housing and transport. After the bubble burst, prices stayed flat for over thirty years, but in the last three to five years they've risen about one hundred percent — the average new Tokyo home has broken past 100 million yen. The weak yen has pulled in global property speculators, and new units sell out almost instantly. The key insight: prices rise while wages don't — a mismatch between asset-side inflation and income-side stagnation. So second-hand homes have risen more gently and become the safe harbor for first-time buyers; the hosts now only look at resale properties. And a useful tip: in Japan, rent can be renegotiated at lease renewal. Many people from China are used to just accepting a raise, but Japanese law actually leans in the tenant's favor — you can push back. blocks.text: The money-saving playbook. Japan's points ecosystem is massive: different apps can be linked to different credit cards, so people research which app-plus-card-plus-store combo is most profitable, then use points at checkout. The key insight: as prices rise, points become a "second currency" that only grows more valuable — some people literally live off their points, stacking up millions of them, with a quality of life that might even beat ours. The host has set her sights on being a "million-points" player, treating points research like a family finance project. And when shopping, don't lock into one supermarket: eggs, meat, and shrimp at Costco; Chinese ingredients at specialty stores; frozen vegetables and canned goods at business supermarkets; and half-price bentos at night. It's all an information-gap dividend — it rewards people who study the system. title_en: Slowly Living Out Our Own Summer in Japan

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Slowly Living Out Our Own Summer in Japan

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Two Chinese long-term residents of Tokyo, Lao Fan and Shirley, start from "midsummer day" heat and unfold the differences between how China and Japan get through summer — watermelon freedom versus air-conditioning freedom, indoor cooling systems, summer food, cicada song, wind chimes, and fireworks festivals. They land on a shared conclusion: Japan's seemingly superfluous rituals turn summer from a piece of weather into a rhythm of life with colors, tastes, and sounds — and turn them from merely living into actually starting to live.

blocks.label: Under the Heat: Watermelon Freedom and Air-Con Freedom
blocks.text: Let's start with the heat. Japan officially names days above 30 degrees midsummer days. This year the rainy season dragged on, so early July was still 23 to 24 degrees — but the moment it ended, temperatures jumped to 35 to 36. It feels like the in-between temperatures got eaten up, and people barely had time to adapt. On this island nation, real summer only runs from early July to late August, and sudden heat is harder to guard against than a long hot stretch — more than 10,000 people were taken to hospital by ambulance for heatstroke in half a month. But here's the hosts' gem: you may have lost watermelon freedom, but you gained air-conditioning freedom. Two Chinese in Japan traded ludicrously expensive watermelons for the freedom to run the AC without being nagged. Japan officially names days above 30 degrees "midsummer days." This year the rainy season dragged on, so early July was still 23 to 24 degrees — but the moment the rain ended, it jumped to 35 to 36. Sudden heat is harder to guard against than a long hot stretch — nationwide, more than 10,000 people were taken to hospital by ambulance for heatstroke in half a month in July. A typical scene: in early July you still sleep under a blanket; by mid-month you can't survive without air conditioning. Under the same roof, Tianjin's humid heat feels like a steamer, while Japan's dry heat is a completely different sensation. "This year, early July was 23, 24 degrees; then mid-month, as soon as the rainy season ended, it went from 23, 24 to 35, 36 — it feels like the temperatures in between got eaten up." Related concept: midsummer day → sudden heat warnings → heatstroke risk management — the link where weather meets health. The gem: "You may have lost watermelon freedom, but you gained air-conditioning freedom." Two Chinese in Japan traded ludicrously expensive watermelons for the freedom to run the AC without being nagged. It felt like the in-between temperatures just vanished. There was no gradual warm-up — it jumped straight into midsummer. We traded watermelon freedom for AC freedom. They gave up cheap watermelon for worry-free air conditioning.

blocks.label: Indoor Cooling Systems: AC, Fans, and Shade
blocks.text: Next, the indoor cooling system. Japan's dehumidify mode lowers humidity while gently cooling — once the humidity drops, your body feels fresh, sometimes even colder than cooling mode set at 26 degrees, and without the hot-cold swings. Lao Fan admits he only learned to use dehumidify after moving to Japan, because back home, without AC freedom, he never knew what the function was for. And keeping the AC running all the time is actually more power-efficient than blasting it on and off. One catch though: wooden houses insulate poorly, so the second floor can hit 32 degrees by day, and wherever the AC is installed, the cool air stays trapped in that room — even with the door open, it's like there's a barrier at the doorway, and the cool air just cycles inside, never reaching the next room. Cooling mode is also unstable — set at 26 degrees, it sometimes blows hotter and hotter, turning into "heating" — while dehumidify stays steadier. A typical scene: both floors of their home run dehumidify all summer. Lao Fan's old habit — cranking the AC to the lowest temperature and highest fan, then turning it off when cold and on again when hot — wasted power and felt terrible. "With dehumidify running constantly, I feel it's a bit colder than cooling mode at 26 degrees." "I only recently learned that keeping the AC running all the time is actually more power-efficient." The mechanism: Japanese wooden houses insulate poorly, so the second floor can hit 32 degrees by day. Wherever the AC is installed, the cool air stays "trapped" in that room — even with the door open, it's like there's a barrier at the doorway; the cool air circulates inside but never flows to the next room. Keeping the AC on is actually more energy-efficient. Constant cooling beats blasting it on and off. The cold air just cycles inside the room. The cool air is stuck there — it never reaches the hallway.

blocks.label: The Taste of Summer: From Cold Noodles to Eel
blocks.text: The taste of summer. The staple logic is the same — both are cold noodles — but the seasoning is completely different: Japan's sweet-and-sour taste is hard for northerners used to sesame sauce, and its refreshing feel comes more from plain flavor plus icy texture, like cold soba. Then there's the eel tradition. Before each season starts — beginning of spring, summer, autumn, winter — there's a two-week window called doyo, a transition period; every 12 days cycles an ox day; and when the two meet, it's the doyo ushi day. The custom stacks three layers of logic: one, seasonal change kills your appetite, so eat something nourishing; two, 'ushi' sounds like 'u,' so foods starting with 'u' — unagi eel, udon, ume plum — are considered lucky and nourishing; three, commercial marketing made eel win among all the 'u' foods and bind it into a national summer habit. blocks.label: Fireworks and Summer Festivals: From Tourist to Resident
blocks.text: Fireworks and festivals. The gap in fireworks experience isn't about scale — it's about how you "open" it: free venues mean crowds and blocked views; ticketed venues give you open views and a transformed experience; and rural field venues feel like your own private show. Lao Fan's first unticketed attempt was terrible — "why did I even come?" — and the Sumida River show, supposedly a million people, was his worst fireworks night in ten years in Japan. But field shows in Ibaraki, at the foot of Mount Fuji, and in Nagaoka — the nation's largest, running two hours — have open views, and inconvenient transport actually keeps the crowds away. His strategy: pick only one or two premium shows a year, buy tickets or choose the countryside, and treat fireworks as a proper send-off for summer rather than a checkpoint-counting game. And community festivals beat public ones: in the danchi, neighbors know each other, residents are the organizers, and you truly participate — at a public festival, you're just an outside spectator. The key insight: the first time Lao Fan watched fireworks on his own, he didn't buy a ticket and it was terrible — "why did I even come?"; the Sumida River show, supposedly a million people, was his worst fireworks night in ten years in Japan. Meanwhile, field shows in Ibaraki, at the foot of Mount Fuji, and in Nagaoka — the nation's largest, running two hours — have open views, and inconvenient transport actually keeps the crowds away. A typical scene: sitting on a chair in the middle of a field, watching for free with nothing blocking your view; Nagaoka runs two hours — most shows run 1.5 hours, short ones half an hour — and they happened to be nearby when it went on air. The pitfall diary: "Too many people, too many buildings, you can't see anything — in free spots there's always something blocking the view"; "I ended up with heatstroke, it was physically miserable." The strategy: pick only one or two premium shows a year, buy tickets or choose the countryside, and treat fireworks as "a proper send-off for summer" rather than a checkpoint-counting game. The mechanism: community festivals and public festivals feel completely different. Community festivals — held in the public-housing complex — have neighbors who know each other, residents who are the organizers and committee members, and real participation. At a public festival, you're just an outside spectator. Free spots are packed — you can't see a thing. The free section is always blocked by something. Treat it as a proper send-off for summer. One great show beats ten mediocre ones.

title_en: Vol.44 What Happens When You Get Old? A Look at Japanese Elders' Daily Life

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Vol.44 What Happens When You Get Old? A Look at Japanese Elders' Daily Life

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: From Uniqlo's front-opening underwear to the Long-Term Care Insurance system, UDF foods, Panasonic's home renovation line, and the plight of the "shopping-vulnerable," Salad and Tomo break down Japan's super-aged society across clothing, food, housing, and mobility. They explore both finely tuned solutions and structural dead ends — and ask whether China, before its own super-aging wave hits in 2035, can first learn to treat old people as people.

blocks.label: Clothing: Age-Inclusive Wear From Function to Dignity
blocks.text: Let's start with clothing. The mechanism: in 2018, a nurse with cancer wrote to Uniqlo complaining that pullover underwear was hard to put on and take off in the hospital, and that care-specific styles were ugly. Uniqlo responded with Velcro front-opening T-shirts and snap-fastening bras, folded in HEATTECH and AIRism tech, and marketed them to all genders and all ages. The key insight: "the older you get, the more you live like a baby again" — front-opening designs work for infants too, and adults in the hospital need the same. Age-inclusive design isn't a senior sub-brand; it's building functionality into the mainstream product line. A typical scene: an IV drip after surgery, breast pads after breast-cancer surgery, nursing bras for new mothers, and fleece or light-down vests that keep seniors warm. The original line: "Even if I end up bedridden, I'd love to wear Uniqlo's fully opening underwear" — the nurse's letter that pushed the product into existence. The related concept: it's the opposite of the "dark-red floral mom-dress" stereotype; fleece vests became standard in Japanese nursing homes, yet young people buy them for winter too. And culture moves: retired couple BangBang511 share daily outfits on Instagram and draw 800,000 followers; the magazine "Elegant Her" sold over 50,000 copies in three days, and cover model Anna Tsuji's silver hair at 70 became a benchmark that normalized natural gray for readers. The older we get, the more we're like babies again. What works for babies works for elders. Build the function into the main line. Don't segregate seniors — integrate the features.

blocks.label: Food: Long-Term Care Insurance and the UDF Food Ecosystem
blocks.text: Now food and the care system. The mechanism: legislated in 1997, it turned elder care from a family matter into mutual aid through social insurance. The core idea is "supporting and promoting seniors' independent lives" — keeping them at home as long as possible. The key insight: by 2025, about 18.4 million households have heads over 65, and 37 percent live alone without children; "elder caring for elder" means family care capacity keeps falling, making insurance plus home services a hard necessity. A typical scene: up to 200,000 yen in subsidies for home modifications, and wheelchairs rented through the insurance at about one-tenth of market price — 202 yen a month. The data: home-service users grew 2.1 times from 2000 to 2022, while institutional care grew only 0.53 times. Then the UDF food system: Japan's Care Food Council classifies food by hardness and viscosity into four levels — easy to chew, crushable with teeth, crushable with the tongue, and no chewing needed. In 2016 they added three color codes — blue for nutritional supplements, red for swallowing difficulties, yellow for chewing difficulties. Related concept: using eggs as an example — tamagoyaki falls under "easy to chew," while chawanmushi is close to "no chewing needed," helping consumers judge for themselves. Keep elders at home as long as possible. Home first, institutions as a last resort. Food is graded by how easy it is to chew. From "easy to chew" down to "no chewing at all."

blocks.label: Housing: Panasonic's H&Life and Aging-in-Place Renovation
blocks.text: Next, housing. The mechanism: researching senior needs since 1990, the H&Life brand spans appliances, assistive devices, care services, and senior housing. Its landline phones add voice and flashing reminders, scam-call warning recordings, temperature and humidity sensors, and disaster alerts. The key insight: grab bars aren't installed casually — position, angle, and material need an on-site assessment by a professional planner, and they're often hidden in the cabinetry's tones to reduce psychological cues. Slip-proof bathrooms, sit-down showers, and electrically adjustable care beds are the renovation priorities. The boundary: high-end nursing homes cost 200,000 to 500,000 yen a month, far beyond a typical pension — 150,000 to 250,000 for employees, about 70,000 for the self-employed — reaching only a few; Panasonic works downward to community care centers and home renovations. And the neighborhood layer: convenience stores like 7-Eleven sign guardian agreements — meal and medicine delivery, tracking for those who wander, and stopping ATM scam transfers — building a 30-minute elder-care circle. Then Tomo's own experience: after surgery, the first time he got out of bed he nearly fainted on the way to the toilet; with an IV and tubes, even eating and undressing were hard. "It's not just any grab bar that lets me sit up — position, angle, and material make a world of difference." His words: "When you're recovering and living ordinary days again, you can't imagine how powerless frailty can make you." blocks.label: Getting Around: Mobility, the Shopping-Vulnerable, and Structural Dead Ends
blocks.text: Then getting around. The mechanism: about 8.5 million people — 3.8 million over 65 — live more than 500 meters from a fresh-food store with no car, per 2010 data. Country stores close, bus lines die — 14,000 kilometers of routes were cut from 2007 to 2016 — gas stations dwindle, and in the housing blocks, elders climb stairs with no elevator while the supermarket downstairs has shut. The key insight: "when elders say staying home is comfortable, is it really easier at home, or is going out just too hard?" Being housebound — leaving home less than once a week — causes both muscle and cognitive decline, which in turn demands more care. Even with barrier-free facilities up to standard — a 94 percent step-elimination rate — depopulation leaves 60 percent of bus operations in the red: the technology is ahead, but it can't cover most people. One closure triggers the next. A chain reaction of shut shops and dead buses. It's not comfort — it's exhaustion. Going out became harder than staying in.

blocks.label: Data and the China-Japan Comparison
blocks.text: Finally, the big picture. Why it matters: businesses often treat elders as a distant, special group, offering only medical care or dark-red floral mom-dresses; Skechers' shift to older customers worked only because the shoes were genuinely light enough. The boundary: the silver economy is legitimate, but if you only chase quick money without solving real pain points, the market will eventually drop you. The key line: "Old age isn't an opposite — it's everyone's natural life stage. It could be your parents, and it will be your future self." How to apply it: meet real users before developing products — ZOZO's offline sign-ups, nursing-home pop-up stores, magazine phone orders — push age-inclusive design to all ages, and refuse the age-shaming that stinks of marketing discrimination. title_en: E220 | In Conversation with Nie Huihua: Everyone Says the End of the Universe Is the Civil Service Exam — But What's the System Really Like?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: E220 | In Conversation with Nie Huihua: Everyone Says the End of the Universe Is the Civil Service Exam — But What's the System Really Like?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Renmin University professor Nie Huihua joins the tavern with his new book The Operating Logic of Grassroots China. As civil service exam applicants overtake graduate-school applicants for the first time, he dismantles three big misconceptions about the system, how to judge whether you're suited for it, how to pick a post, and the local-debt dilemma. The core conclusion: taking the exam is fine, but don't expect an iron rice bowl. Choose the city first, then the department — and put the invisible realities on the table before you register.

blocks.label: Behind the Civil Service Craze: How Much Do We Really Know?
blocks.text: The core mechanism: in 2026, applicants for the national civil service exam overtook graduate-school exam takers for the first time; if you add provincial exams — roughly twice the national count — the total pool is about three times the size of the postgraduate exam. The Hurun Rich List also shifted its tycoon sources, from study-abroad agencies and test-prep institutions to the founder of Offcn Education. The key insight: exam technique tips are everywhere online; what's truly scarce is how a grassroots civil servant's day actually goes, which personality traits fit, and how city, department, and position differences shape your life — questions no exam technique can answer. A typical scene: a relative's kid is preparing for the civil service exam; before registering, they should learn the operating logic of the system rather than just grinding practice questions. As the episode put it: when more and more people choose the same direction, how much do we actually know about that road? Related concept: unlike the 'pass-the-exam success stories,' which teach you how to get in, this book teaches what you face after you're in. Nie Huihua starts from historical works like Soulstealers: most people don't hold power, but the moment they get a chance to share in or observe how power runs, they never miss it. The viral Bilibili series 'How Much Power Does a County Magistrate Have?' proves the public's intense curiosity about how power works. blocks.label: The Three Biggest Misconceptions
blocks.text: The first misconception, the reason: 90% of grassroots civil servants top out at division-chief level, and 99% at deputy bureau level. College graduates typically reach deputy division level, but anything beyond is extremely hard. The fix: before registering, ask yourself — if your classmate becomes a section chief in three years and you're his subordinate, can you accept that calmly? If not, don't take the exam. How serious? Fatal — if you can't accept it, you'll suffer long-term, because leaders use the 'cold shoulder' instead of firing. As Nie Huihua put it: 'Entering the civil service means you'll get promoted' is the biggest misconception. The second misconception, the reason: researching mining accidents and official governance, Nie found that prefecture mayors and county party secretaries are far more likely to be arrested than miners are to die in a disaster. During the Dongguan officialdom earthquake, the city party committee had one member arrested every few days. The fix: don't treat 'not seeking great wealth, only safety' as a default guarantee — the risk is real. The fix: don't treat 'not seeking great wealth, only safety' as a default guarantee — the risk is real. Nine in ten grassroots civil servants peak at division chief. Most careers flatline at the division level. They can't fire you, so they freeze you out. The punishment is the cold shoulder, not the axe.

blocks.label: Are You Cut Out to Be a Civil Servant?
blocks.text: The core mechanism: you don't need extraordinary creativity or top-notch smarts, but you do need high emotional intelligence: sharp eyes, quick ears, a tight mouth, diligent legs, a keen nose for office politics, and good speaking skills. Most people can't manage all of it, which is why most people aren't suited. The key insight: inside the system, you can't use school logic — venting to your professor is fine at school, but complaining about your boss in a government office can end your career. A leader can't fire you, but they can put you in the freezer, and once your age slips past the window, promotion gets far harder. A typical scene: a county party secretary with an uncooperative subordinate can't fire him; he can only promote those willing to work and freeze out those who won't. As the episode put it: 'If you don't take on important tasks, no leader likes you, and your age window slips away — how could you possibly get promoted?' The organization department is extremely strict about age, while ability, virtue, and character are relatively 'soft' criteria. Structural quotas — a leadership team must include a post-80s member, a woman, an ethnic minority — create special fast tracks, but also fiercer competition. As the episode put it: 'What's the hardest of all hard levers? Age — it's the least fakeable.' blocks.label: The Operating Logic of Grassroots China
blocks.text: The core mechanism: China's system is hierarchical — the higher you go, the more important formal institutions become, approaching a complete contract; the lower you go, the more important informal institutions become, approaching an incomplete contract. Personal connections are crucial at the grassroots. The key insight: resources follow power, and power is embedded in hierarchy. Price isn't the deciding factor for resource allocation in every setting. A typical scene: in a prefecture-level city of two hundred thousand people, the people who matter might number just a few hundred, and the local print-shop owner can recognize most faces in the photos — the network of personal connections is extremely dense. As the episode put it: 'Winners go where the resources flow; resources follow power; and power is embedded in hierarchy.' Related concept: it's a completely different game from first-tier city rules — county-town logic plays by another set of rules. Historically, in a Qing dynasty county, only the magistrate was an official; everyone else was self-hired. The fiscal system left no legal legitimate income for the magistrate, who had to self-fund, repay debts, and bear unlimited joint liability. What kept it running were informal institutions — gentry, clerks, and their networks. blocks.label: Credential Inflation and the Vanishing Era Dividend
blocks.text: The core mechanism: studying and earning credentials is a way to send a signal that distinguishes you in an information-incomplete world — but when the whole society demands a PhD to be a civil servant, the signal is overshot. Grassroots work doesn't need theoretical thinking; it needs execution. The key insight: a Tsinghua-Peking PhD working at a street office is a misallocation of resources, but the root cause is that career paths are too narrow and everything is tied to exams, driving credential inflation and internal competition. The boundary: in ministry research departments there's still professional value; in pure execution roles, it's severely overqualified. As the episode put it: 'Finish a PhD, then go for the next degree — it could go on endlessly; from society's perspective, it's truly a waste of resources.' Yubai pointed out that young people were thrown into higher education by linear thinking, still believing 'getting the license equals getting the reward' — but in 2007, 4 million undergrads were in short supply, versus over 10 million today; the game has changed. Nie Huihua admits he can't even find a 'dream' convincing enough for young people — but every era has its competition; only the form of competition changes. As the episode put it: 'In an era when the era dividend is fading, how do you live a good life? That's genuinely a hard question.' Once you settle in a city, it's extremely hard to leave; a good city with a mediocre department still lets you switch departments; a bad city loses the whole game. The key insight: avoid the 100-plus shrinking cities with declining populations and economies. Organization departments and discipline inspection commissions offer fast promotions, but heavy workloads and high risk; even a great position in an obscure backwater gets you frozen out. A typical scene: spatial dividends are more uneven than time dividends — the hardware innovation ecosystem of Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei versus a shrinking county town shows a gap far bigger than any era difference. Practical order: city (development potential) → department (promotion/pressure trade-off) → position (avoid marginalization). blocks.label: The Future of Work and Nie's Four Pieces of Advice
blocks.text: When productivity, robots, and AI are developed enough, maybe only 10% of people working could feed the whole society. Manufacturing employment will inevitably shrink; government procurement spending on AI has already approached 14%. Employment will gradually stop being the core question — the key becomes 'do you know how to have fun' — arts, emotional value, entertainment. title_en: Ideal L9 Livis Launch Review: Without an Instant 'Wow' Moment, Can Emotional Value Be a Selling Point?
