blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Four auto-industry guests on the Baba Wu podcast take apart the launch of the Ideal L9 Livis. The Apple-style recorded launch fell flat, and only the 50,000-yuan price cut lit up the comment feed. In an age of homogenized flagships, the L9 Livis fights for emotional value with a 'luxury without shouting' design language and consistent interior-exterior styling. But the 'embodied-intelligence flagship' ships only about 10% of its architecture, lacks the instant visual hit of an 'Ice-Crystal-Sand' paint job, and 70% of test-drive buyers are existing owners coming back to repurchase.

blocks.label: The Launch: A Form and a Message That Stalled
blocks.text: The launch is where the L9 Livis stumbled. Ideal stuck with a fully online, pre-recorded event, refusing the theater effect of a live show — a sharp contrast with the passionate on-stage launches from Xiaomi, Huawei, and NIO. The insight: any car feels more thrilling live, while watching on a laptop keeps you cool and rational — a structural communication disadvantage, not a product problem. Sun Shaojun streamed two launches side by side: when Richard Yu spoke, the comments exploded; when the feed cut to Ideal, they went quiet, until a 50,000-yuan cut from 559,800 ignited them again. Even Apple flies media to the venue for atmosphere; Ideal skipped that step too. And by 2026, every flagship has active suspension and 800-volt — 70 points versus 75 makes no difference. The mechanism: Ideal stuck with a fully online, pre-recorded launch, refusing the theater effect of a live event — a sharp contrast with the passionate on-stage launches from Xiaomi, Huawei, and NIO. Typical case: the host Sun Shaojun streamed two launches side by side — when Richard Yu spoke, the comments exploded; the moment the feed cut to Ideal, they went silent, until a 50,000-yuan cut from 559,800 ignited them again. As the host recalls: 'The moment Richard Yu spoke, everyone was thrilled... the instant it cut to Ideal, the comments went quiet... only when the price was announced — down 50,000 from 559,800 — did everyone get excited.' Related point: even Apple, which also does recorded launches, still flies media to the venue to build atmosphere — Ideal skipped even that step. By 2026 there are too many flagships — active suspension, 800-volt architecture, and fridge-and-TV features are everywhere, so '70 points versus 75 points makes no difference to me.' The L series exploded back then because 'only you had it,' but now everyone has everything, and the sense of boredom has deepened visibly. The recorded launch fell flat. Without a live audience, the energy never came through. Live, everything feels thrilling; on a screen, you stay rational. The on-site buzz is something a stream can't transmit. blocks.text: On the product itself, the guests give the L9 Livis real credit. title_en: EP01 Conversation with Liu Zhenyun | When Words Fail Me, I Stay Silent

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: EP01 Conversation with Liu Zhenyun | When Words Fail Me, I Stay Silent

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: In this conversation, writer Liu Zhenyun talks about his novel 'The Salty Joke'. He explains how he builds the character Du Taibai through nothing more than his three daily meals, and goes on to explore many-sided lives, the traps of the internet, and a philosophy of silence. Literature, he argues, must capture what philosophy cannot explain — the irregular, the disorderly. When truth is still lacing up its shoes, lies have already run around the world; and when words fail you, silence itself becomes an act. A literary master on why keeping quiet can be the most eloquent thing you do.

blocks.label: Writing a Character Through Three Meals a Day: The Philosophy of Literature
blocks.text: To write the character Du Taibai, Liu Zhenyun lets his meals do the talking. Du gathers a dozen ingredients for his mixed-grain porridge, agonizes over whether to fill his dumplings with a mixed or a plain vegetable filling, and switches his plans mid-way to buy mutton instead. It looks like writing about food; in reality it is writing about a man's habit of living seriously. The author cannot describe 'what kind of person Du is' in rational language — that would be the author's invention. The reader has to read it out of the details for themselves, and that is what literature is. When Du hits a dead end, he stops caring about food; when the storm passes and he reopens his restaurant, his seriousness returns. Eating is the attitude that guards the bottom line of living. The core mechanism: Du Taibai gathers a dozen kinds of ingredients for his mixed-grain porridge, agonizes over whether to mix two fillings for his dumplings, and changes his mind to buy mutton halfway to the butcher — it seems to be about eating, but it is really about his habit of living seriously and his worldview. The key insight: the author cannot describe 'what kind of person Du Taibai is' in rational language — that would become the author's invention; literature happens when readers discover it themselves through the details of three meals a day. A typical scene: when Du Taibai falls into trouble, he stops caring about food; once the storm passes and he reopens his restaurant, his seriousness about food returns — eating is an attitude that guards the bottom line of living. In the author's own words: it looks like writing about three meals a day, but actually it is tied to the character… the pleasure comes from this kind of thinking about how the food is structured. A related idea: this echoes Proust's madeleine cake in 'In Search of Lost Time', where a small cake triggers memory, and Proust's philosophy of stretching time. Philosophy uses reason to explain the world; literature writes exactly what philosophy cannot explain — the things without rules. Ask Kant to analyze Du Taibai's meals and you enter a completely different system of language; literature hides its reason the deepest. It looks like writing about food, but it's really writing about a man. The meals are just the surface — the person is the real subject. Readers have to discover it for themselves — that's what literature is. The meaning shouldn't be handed to readers; they have to earn it.

blocks.label: Many-Sided Lives: What Supports You Beyond Side A
blocks.text: Everyone has more than Side A, the one you show on the street. There are Sides B, C, D, E, and F — often unknown to others, sometimes ignored even by yourself, yet they are what hold Side A up. Liu's cousin, a farmer called Newton, is obsessed with higher mathematics and physics, and that joy supports his dull life of labor. Du Taibai was also called Newton as a child — the same spiritual lineage. Online, young people are white-collar workers by day, then make museum merchandise on weekends or write 'Mom, get off work early' on a convenience store blackboard. Flat characters with only one side are not the scope of literature. Every peasant and every ordinary person is different — so many unknown sides deserve respect and display, and that is a major engine for writing. The core mechanism: everyone has more than Side A — the one walking the street; there are Sides B, C, D, E, and F, which are often unknown to others, sometimes ignored even by yourself, yet they support Side A. The key insight: his cousin Newton is a farmer but is obsessed with higher mathematics and physics — that joy supports his dull working life; Du Taibai was also called Newton as a child, the same spiritual lineage. A typical scene: young people online are white-collar workers by day, then make museum creative merchandise on weekends or write 'Mom, get off work early' on a convenience store blackboard — using Side B to handle the anxiety with no place to land. In the author's own words: his joy supports him… a job without joy, even a life without joy, but a person always has one joyful fulcrum hidden behind. A related idea: 'love yourself as an old self' resonates with the line in the book, 'everyone walking the street has worked hard.' Flat, one-sided characters are not the scope of literature. Every farmer and every little person is different — life holds so many unknown sides worth respecting and showing, and this is an important engine for writing. Everyone has a side nobody ever sees. There's a hidden layer to every person — even to yourself. That hidden joy is what holds his ordinary life together. Side B is doing the heavy lifting for Side A.

blocks.label: A Writer's Evolution: How to Stay Young
blocks.text: A writer evolves in stages. In the first stage, the author has something to say — he becomes his own megaphone, as in 'Ground Covered with Chicken Feathers'. In the second, the people in the book have something to say — the author turns listener, as in 'I Am Not Madame Bovary' and 'One Sentence Is Worth Ten Thousand'. In the third, he turns to a universe and tells everyone, 'you've all worked hard' — like Du Fu moving from 'I will climb to the summit' to 'the country broken, rivers and mountains remain' to 'how could I get ten thousand mansions to shelter the poor'. The danger is a writer stuck forever in stage one. Life keeps moving; if your understanding stops, you age. His readers for 'The Salty Joke' are mostly in their twenties and thirties, and their comments are strikingly fresh — 'under the water floats all our life.' The younger your writing, the longer you last as a writer. Stage one: the author has something to say — he is his own megaphone (the 'Ground Covered with Chicken Feathers' period). Stage two: the people in the book have something to say — the author becomes a listener ('I Am Not Madame Bovary' and 'One Sentence Is Worth Ten Thousand'). blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Hong Huang talks with Fudan University's Spanish culture expert Cheng Yiyang, starting from Loewe's 180th-anniversary archive exhibition and weaving through the artisans' collective founding in 1846, Moorish culture, the Franco era, and Jonathan Anderson's contemporary design — revealing how this Spanish luxury house has kept its vitality through drastic social change by staying 'craft at the core, playfulness intact.'

blocks.label: Origins: Why a Collective of Artisans, Not a Family Brand?
blocks.text: In 1846, Spain was still shifting from agriculture to industry; artisan craftsmen had not yet formed monopolistic family dynasties, so they pooled resources in a mutual-aid collective — much like the shepherd associations that still operate today. Loewe's founding year predates most European luxury houses; it belongs to the 'pre-capitalist economy' era. Because Spain's economy developed more slowly than Britain's and France's, it kept more of its collective-collaboration traditions. The setting: Madrid was the court and royal consumption center, central Spain's pastoral regions supplied leather, and southern Cordoba's Moorish craft traveled north — forming a four-in-one breeding ground of materials, technique, aesthetics, and purchasing power. As the guest said, these craftsmen hadn't yet formed any single family that could monopolize the trade... they needed a mutual-aid collective to do something together. Unlike Barcelona's rising capitalism, Madrid was an aristocratic and royal consumption hub — that decided the brand's location logic. In 1872 the German Enrique Loewe Roessberg joined the workshop and named it after himself; 'Loewe' means 'lion' in German, so the little red lion became the brand mark. Spain was ruled in turn by Romans, Visigoths, and Muslims — a deeply mixed nation that is naturally not exclusionary. It started as a cooperative of craftsmen, not a family firm. A nation shaped by many rulers is naturally open. Centuries of mixing made Spain allergic to exclusion.

blocks.text: During Muslim rule, Cordoba became Europe's largest city in the tenth century, and the leather industry was largely inherited from the Moors; Granada's Alhambra is the most-visited monument in all of Spain. A huge share of Spanish vocabulary comes from ancient Arabic. Spain's cultural precision stops north of the Pyrenees — the southern Moorish tradition makes it strikingly different from northern Europe, and that difference shows directly in Loewe's color choices and curved lines. As the guest said, Spain's entire leather industry, to a degree, was inherited from the Moors. blocks.text: In 1905 Loewe earned the Spanish royal household's official supplier certification. Although the monarchy has gone through ups and downs — the Republic, the Civil War, Franco, democratization — it still carries prestige in people's minds. Spain's 'old money' culture values surnames: know a person's paternal and maternal family names and you can judge their family's standing in the trade. As a surname brand plus royal recognition, Loewe equals a quality guarantee. As the guest said, once you know the father's and mother's family names... if the family is prominent in the trade, people trust it. Spain also has a long archival tradition — the Church, the royal court, the courts, and colonial institutions all filed records systematically. Loewe's 180th-anniversary exhibition is the brand extension of this archival culture. blocks.text: Why it was hard: after the 1936–1939 Civil War, Catholic conservatives took power — women's dress was restricted, and divorce and abortion were banned. The core conclusion: it doesn't feel very 'foreign,' but the value for money is excellent. What's truly worth it isn't checking off sights, but talking with locals and opening the kids' eyes. blocks.label: Part 1: Choosing Your Route and Budget
blocks.text: Here's the core framework: a 6-7 day trip means one day in Kuala Lumpur in West Malaysia, a two-hour flight to East Malaysia like flying from Shanghai to Xinjiang, and then four to five days in Kota Kinabalu or Semporna. Kuala Lumpur has plenty of Chinese speakers and solid infrastructure, but it feels less like being abroad; East Malaysia is all about the sea and rainforest. The key distinction: Kota Kinabalu, the capital of Sabah, has better accommodation and an easier pace; Semporna is more pristine but demands roughing it. The activities are essentially the same — snorkeling, island hopping, and sea views. A typical choice: pick Kota Kinabalu if you're traveling with a middle-schooler and want an easy beach trip; pick Semporna if you're a diving fanatic who can accept basic lodging. As the episode put it, the more exhausting the journey, the simpler the island days — just playing on the beach, snapping photos, snorkeling to see fish, and having a meal. To clarify, island hopping isn't diving into water — you charter a boat and hit two to four islands in a day, with each stop being beach, snorkeling, and lunch. The budget: flights from Nanjing to Kuala Lumpur round-trip were about 3,000 yuan per person during the Spring Festival, plus a 600-yuan-a-night rental for six nights, roughly 12,000 to 13,000 yuan; food ran about 1,000 yuan a day for six days; group tours for snorkeling and the mangrove forest added around 3,000. Off-season, round-trip Hangzhou–Kota Kinabalu tickets can be as low as 1,300 yuan. blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: On Yuexia Outdoor, gear reviewer Boss Crab and outdoor consumer Miya break down how men and women buy outdoor gear differently: spec chasers versus experience-seekers, the military-techwear style, a five-day hiking setup on a 10,000-yuan budget, and how to choose hard shells, down jackets, shoes, socks, and backpacks — plus overlooked women's needs like sports bras. The real conclusion: what determines your experience isn't gender, but the scenario, your experience level, and how the gear actually feels on your body.

blocks.label: Buying Psychology: Stereotypes and the Real Motives
blocks.text: Let's open with buying psychology. Miya thinks men buy outdoor gear to look capable and professional — military-style labels like the 'military Arc' sell an idealized self-image. Boss Crab pushes back: men care just as much about looks, only with different taste — techwear and military style are men's emotional value. The key insight: spec chasers aren't mindlessly piling on features — men use rational dimensions like materials, data, and value to filter before buying. Women rely more on trying things on and how they feel over the long run, which is why women's clothing return rates are extremely high. A typical scene: a man checks the Coolmax moisture-wicking fiber percentage before ordering; a woman buys five or six quick-dry shirts, tries them on, and keeps only the most comfortable one. As the hosts put it, girls spend all their money on clothes while boys spend all theirs on gear — but Boss Crab says gear is like a toy to him, kept on the nightstand to play with. In short: specs are men's looks-filter, while looks are women's experience-projection device. And really, an Arc'teryx hard shell for seven or eight thousand yuan is useless when you squeeze onto the subway every day, but the higher the specs, the more men love it — driven by the psychological need to look impressive. blocks.text: Now, spending priorities on a ten-thousand-yuan budget for a five-day hike. A premium pair of wool socks, say 150 yuan, sharply cuts friction and blisters — a bigger experience upgrade than an expensive hard shell. blocks.text: Let's go deep on categories. First down jackets. Two jackets both rated 100 grams of fill and 800 fill power can differ hugely in real warmth — the key is cluster size, quilting style, box versus sewn-through, and how much feather fiber is mixed in. Sewn-through quilting squeezes the down at the edges so it can't loft. And goose down versus duck down: goose down has larger clusters and less smell than duck down. Gray duck down and white duck down keep you equally warm — they only differ in how they look. European brands shifting to gray duck down and transparent shells is an environmental choice. Typical uses: city outdoor wear, resting at camp, and as a mid-layer. blocks.label: Overlooked Needs and the Debate
blocks.text: Finally, the overlooked needs. You wear top-tier quick-dry and down on the outside, but underneath is a sports bra that soaks and never dries — support, wicking, and chafe-resistance all improvised. A trail-running pack can rub the skin off your armpits. Women aren't the main consumer base for outdoor gear, so this need has been ignored for years. As Miya puts it: we can put people on Mars, but we still can't make a decent sports bra. Why does this happen? Recommendations on platforms like Xiaohongshu often ignore real usage scenarios, so people end up with piles of gear that doesn't fit them. The fix, as Boss Crab stresses, is to find it by using it — early on you'll definitely buy plenty that doesn't fit, and that's a necessary stage. Visit physical stores and see things in person. Watch out though — it wastes money and time, but it won't create a safety risk. blocks.text: Teacher Zhang, a high-school geography teacher and science popularizer, joins the Mountain Synergy podcast to answer practical questions for hikers: glaciers, why lakes are blue, contour lines, campsite selection, the Aotai route, the Hengduan Mountains, fjord misconceptions, reading altitude from vegetation, finding water, and sea-of-clouds and lightning. The soul of geography is practice — reading the landscape beats just checking it off your list.

blocks.label: Glaciers: The Core Fascination of Field Geography
blocks.text: The mechanism is simple: it needs to be cold enough, and year after year the snow gets compacted into ice — it's not water freezing directly. Low-altitude, rounded mountains were mostly carved gently by water, while sharp high-altitude ridges are the violent product of glaciers sliding down and grinding against rock. Seeing a glacier usually means the trail also passes forest, grassland, and desert — a full sequence of landscapes. China's glaciers mostly sit above 4,000 meters. Maritime glaciers in western Sichuan grow fast and are covered in debris and hard to reach; continental glaciers like Qudenima have less moisture and stay cleaner. Ice towers form when a glacier's lower half moves at uneven speeds and cracks, and the tops melt faster; because the bottom grinding against the ground also speeds melting, glaciers usually melt from the base first. blocks.text: Contour lines that are packed close together mean a steep slope; multiple lines merging into one mean a cliff; lines curving toward higher ground mark a valley, and curving toward lower ground mark a ridge. blocks.label: Camping & Safety: A Geographic Decision Framework
blocks.text: Stay away from the base of steep cliffs: at high altitude, water seeping into rock cracks freezes at night and pries the rock apart, so rockfall risk is far higher at night than it feels in the daytime. Stay away from valley bottoms: they collect water, so flood risk is high. Stay away from livestock trails: if the grass is trampled bare, cows and sheep regularly walk there, and there are real cases of tents being stomped to pieces by cattle. And be careful with ridgelines: wind speeds are high, and on the Aotai line, north and south air masses meet, making the weather flip violently. blocks.text: Glacier flour reflects blue, karst carbonate areas like Jiuzhaigou reflect blue-green light, low-altitude lakes show the color of their algae, and sediment also tints the water. Jiuzhaigou's water is crystal clear yet colored, because carbonates reflect blue-green light; the difference between milky blue, sapphire blue, and green comes from different mineral combos. In Xinjiang, the shady slope has more trees than the sunny one — because strong sunlight means heavy evaporation and less water, which flips the intuition that trees love sun. The Hengduan Mountains are a series of north-south ranges marking the boundary between the Sichuan Basin and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. On the Erlang Mountain tunnel, the east side is wet with broadleaf forest, while the west side is so dry it even has cacti, in dry-hot valleys like Luding. Gao Ligong Mountain, at the southern end, is a plant gene pool where low latitude plus huge vertical drops let tropical plants and high-altitude cold-wet species coexist. title_en: The Photo That Changed a Magnum Photographer's Life 29 — Peter Marlow: Let the Picture Happen Naturally

blocks.label: 英文标题

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Photo Reason episode 29 decodes a single frame by British Magnum photographer Peter Marlow: a hot-spring self-portrait that embodies "letting the picture happen naturally." From his war-reporting days, through the Concorde project, Kaliningrad, and his 42 English cathedrals, the episode explores creative confidence, project completeness, and the discipline that made his late work so calm — summed up in his own philosophy: "be true to yourself, get up early, and don't try too hard."

blocks.label: This Episode's Photo: Two Feet in the Hot Spring
blocks.text: Let's start with the photo. The mechanism: one morning in 2000, his Japanese fixer Kadowaki Kazuto dragged Marlow out of bed, and the two walked naked into a river hot spring. The frame is minimal: a pair of feet sticking out of the water, reflections, misted mountains and trees behind — a world away from his early war images. The key insight: Marlow said his career had entered a new phase — pictures don't have to be driven by events. Photography and authorship come down to confidence; you can be less invasive, let situations unfold on their own, and find images in ordinary transitional moments. A typical scene: in this situation, a news-style shot would have been "wrong," so he chose to become part of the frame himself — lying still in the water and photographing his own feet. In his own words: "Ultimately I try to let photographs happen naturally, because I'm now confident enough that they will happen. What could be simpler than that?" The original note: heat and meaning existed in the same place at once; photographing it in a journalistic way seemed wrong, so he expressed the experience by becoming part of the photograph. And the source of that confidence: years of experience, a relaxed natural state, and the standing and achievements in photography together built it — "whatever I shoot is fine." The same subject, shot by an amateur versus a master, lands with completely different weight. blocks.label: Life Path and Creative Shift
blocks.text: Now the life path. The mechanism: his father, John Marlow, engineered the Concorde's engines, and his mother was a precision-engineering draughtswoman. That German-style, engineering middle-class home instilled his rigorous control of perspective and geometric lines, running through his work from early to late. The key insight: he had his first Kodak at five and built a darkroom in the basement at eight — an early-established obsession. After a psychology degree from Manchester, he skipped further study, used a friend's wedding portfolio to land a cruise-ship photographer job, and once he'd earned the fare, applied to the SIGMA agency in Paris. A typical scene: front-line assignments in Northern Ireland, Lebanon, Angola, and the Philippines brought physical fear — and sparked a deep questioning of photojournalism's brutal competition for fame and prizes. The related concept: set against Don McCullin's benchmark of war photography, Marlow admitted "I could never be Don McCullin" — and deliberately walked a different road. He became a full member in 1986 and, in 1987, co-founded Magnum's London office with Chris Steele-Perkins. He served as president twice; Martin Parr said it's "hard to overstate Marlow's historical contribution to Magnum's development." And the turning point: in Liverpool, "Looking Out to Sea" documented urban decay under Thatcher, the homeless, and the survival instincts of every kind of person — a key turn from war zones to domestic social documentary. In 1978, acclaimed director Shin Sang-ok and beloved actress Choi Eun-hee vanished one after another — both kidnapped by Kim Jong-il to make films in North Korea. After eight years of captivity, they staged an escape drama in Vienna, one specifically written and performed for the "General" himself, and finally burst into the US embassy to be rescued. The escape leaned on a secretly recorded tape, a taxi dash, and cash bribes — a real-life thriller that still echoes through Korea's abduction cases.

The key insight: fame and income were wildly out of step — already a top Korean star, she was too poor to pay the heating bill. That explains why she later fell for the lure of "making a film in Hong Kong to raise money." A typical scene: under an authoritarian regime, artists are both the country's face and the victims of censorship and moral scrutiny. The original line: "By then Choi Eun-hee was already a very famous actress in Korea, but she earned very little — the family was so poor they couldn't even pay the heating bill." The reason: in late 1977, a man called Wang Dong-il, claiming to run a Hong Kong film company, repeatedly invited Choi Eun-hee to Hong Kong as a director and drama-school manager; Lee Hyang-hee — whose husband ran a pro-Pyongyang trading business — handled the reception. Already divorced, Shin Sang-ok still questioned it: "Hong Kong has so many directors — why does he keep coming after you?" The takeaway: watch out for overseas offers that promise easy money out of nowhere, and check whether the contact's background touches sensitive cross-border trade with North Korea. Severity: fatal. Choi Eun-hee was sedated and taken to North Korea, and in February, Shin Sang-ok was held at knifepoint on Repulse Bay and dragged onto a boat. The guest's account: Choi Eun-hee believed Shin Sang-ok was trying to "suppress" her and insisted on going. She checked into the Palma Hotel on January 11; by the 14th she had disappeared, and her luggage sat there for over ten days. The mechanism: Kim Jong-il was obsessed with film since childhood, hoarding about 15,000 foreign films privately, publishing "On the Art of Cinema" in 1973, and taking over North Korea's film system. He needed a full team that understood commercial movies, the star system, and international distribution. The key insight: Shin Sang-ok had studio-system experience, Choi Eun-hee was a star and director, and the two were married — "the perfect prey." Kidnapping also served to train spies — teaching language and foreign customs — and to create political bargaining chips. The tape, passed to Korea through a Japanese film critic, became the backbone of their public reappearance in 1984. The original line: "We brought the two of you here separately... Miss Choi was the bait." How to apply it: under extreme pressure, exploit the other side's psychological lapse — treating guests with respect meant no body search — and use an everyday object, the recorder, to fix key statements in evidence. title_en: 002. What's Life Like Speaking Five Languages?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: 002. What's Life Like Speaking Five Languages?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Two polyglots, Ruixue Cloe and Yvonne Du, talk about what a five-language life feels like: self-teaching English through celebrity fandom, Italian sparked by Lady Gaga, and French revived by love. Their core takeaways: any language is learnable, an accent is a badge of the road you've traveled, and every new language is a wider world you get to walk around in.

blocks.label: 1. The Fundamentals of Language Learning
blocks.text: The fundamentals: language is different from math or physics — no matter how hard a language is, Arabic, Latin, Polish, there's a whole community of native speakers using it every day. Humans are born with a language-learning system because we're social animals, and communication is a must-have skill in almost every industry. The key insight: language talent shows up in the sensitivity of your ears and tongue — the ability to accurately catch and replicate pronunciation. A strict Wenzhou Chinese teacher drilled front-versus-back nasal sounds, and kids who could imitate precisely usually had higher language aptitude. The typical scene: before traveling or settling in a new country, learn basic local phrases — street signs, thank you, let's go — otherwise you'll feel like sitting on pins and needles, without a sense of security. As they put it, "No matter how hard a language is — Arabic, Latin, Polish — there are people using it in the world. As long as you find a learning style that fits you and give yourself enough time, you can master any language." What sets this apart from rote grammar drilling: language learning is essentially repetition plus meaning, similar to learning music. And if someone questions your accent, you can say: "If I have an accent, it means I'm speaking my second language — it means I don't just speak one." Your accent records the roads you've walked, the teachers who taught you, and the cities where you've lived. An accent is a medal, not a mark of shame. Every accent is a map of the speaker's journey.

blocks.label: 2. Two Very Different Self-Learning Paths
blocks.text: Ruixue scored 144 out of 150 in high-school English yet felt terrible at it — the real breakthrough came from fandom. Chasing the K-pop group TVXQ, she taught herself English and Korean romanization just to sing along to the lyrics. When she campaigned to be English class representative, a line — "English is in my soul, in my heart" — won the teacher over, and her self-identity shifted from that moment. Her method: copy lines from English movies and memorize song lyrics; at a more advanced stage, she watched with no subtitles at all, forcing her brain to interpret plot and gestures while not fully understanding, then checked words only after replaying ten times. As she says, "The less you understand, the more immersed you get in reading the story — your brain works really hard to decode it, and slowly you just get it." To apply it: pick a show or song you genuinely love, start with dual subtitles, move to listening only, and write down the words that keep appearing even though you don't understand them, then look them up. Yvonne's path was different: at twelve, in Vienna, she began systematic German study while learning American English from MTV; she deliberately avoided a German-accented English and binge-watched American shows. Italian was her university major plus a Milan cross-cultural master's, and she's done Chinese-Italian interpreting. Her three reasons for Italian: the differentiation of a less-common language, the spark of Lady Gaga not speaking Italian, and a longing for Italian culture. blocks.label: 3. Memory Types & Language Talent
blocks.text: People generally fall into three memory types: visual, auditory, and textual. Yvonne photographs a page into her mind like a camera; Ruixue remembers through repeated listening. If you can't remember a language, you're probably using the wrong channel. The common traits of language-talented people: they like talking and reading aloud, they enjoy hearing their own voice, they sing anywhere and everywhere — and people with good pronunciation often have strong musicality, because the same brain region controls both. The boundary: imperfect pronunciation doesn't mean no talent — talent may live in math, drawing, or other fields. Language is a visible gift you can hear the moment you open your mouth, which makes it relatively fair. As one guest says, "Tell me something a hundred times and I may still forget it, but show me once and I'll remember it for sure." Why accents come out wrong: many foreign phonemes don't exist in your mother tongue — like Mandarin's x or German's uvular r — and if your mouth muscles lazily use native habits, you get Chinglish or German-flavored English. The fix: deliberately adjust your lips, tongue, teeth, and airflow. But don't over-worry: "Just speak whatever you want, we don't judge." blocks.label: 4. Multilingual Personalities & Cultural Switching
blocks.text: Her personality shifts with each language: in Mandarin she's sensible and refined; in Chongqing dialect she sits street-side with legs crossed and insults are a hundred times funnier; in English her voice gets higher and she's more outgoing; in Italian she becomes a sexy, bold girl. Every language has a different resonance point, so her posture shifts with the words. As she says, "If you can't speak this language, you'll never reach this part of me." The mechanism of learning transfer: after Italian, French comes much easier — the grammar is roughly similar and the words are close, you just change the pronunciation. Italian is "spell it as you say it," like a straightforward older sister; French adds little tails and hats, prizing formal beauty. The key insight: words like pasta and hostel trace back to the same Latin roots, and each language keeps adding its own personality. Yvonne's French carries an Italian accent because her teacher was Italian — accents are the map of where you've been. It echoes the sci-fi premise of Arrival, where a linguist learns an alien way of thinking. And a romantic coda: after meeting a French boy, the French vocabulary she'd studied three or four years earlier suddenly came flooding back. Random words he taught her — like saule for willow — burned in thanks to situational memory. As a French proverb says, "in parlar una lingua, con una lingua" — learning a language with your tongue is the best way. I'm a different person in Italian than in Mandarin. The second language pays off for the third. Learning transfer makes each new language a bit faster. Nothing you learned is ever wasted. blocks.label: 5. Debate: Motivation & Boundaries in Language Learning
blocks.text: The reason most people don't speak: fear of being laughed at. Ruixue was mocked as a child for her rural Chongqing accent by kids from the main urban area; she gritted her teeth and learned the city accent within a few months. The fix: don't rush results — the process is the journey, and anyone brave enough to speak deserves respect. Severity: critical — shame is the biggest barrier for most language learners. The guests agree: "Even if we made a fool of ourselves, said things wrong every day, and were actually laughed at, we kept speaking — that's how we got here." Why it matters: translation apps can't replace direct human communication; every language has untranslatable words — like side hustle or satisfy — so learning a language is like installing a new operating system in your brain. The boundary: you don't need fluency in every language — understanding the culture's way of thinking and basic communication is already enough to bring a sense of security and a global mindset. blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: In one sentence: Elly, with zero internship background, prepared for three months and landed offers from JD and Qunar, then swept special offers from ByteDance, Shopee, Meituan, Didi, and over a dozen other top companies. The core methodology: keep a fast-iterating keyword library for your resume, dig into every line to anticipate follow-up questions, and build a custom interview question bank per company with efficient review. Job hunting is like the college entrance exam — nail the fundamentals and 80% of the offers are within reach.

blocks.label: Fundamentals: Prepare Like You're Studying for the Gaokao
blocks.text: The core framework: job hunting is like the gaokao — 80% of the baseline score comes from fundamentals. The process: know yourself, define a direction, polish your resume, do mock interviews, review your mistakes, and then pick offers on your own terms. The key insight: first figure out what direction you want, then build experience with intent. Effort without direction is a scattergun; preparation with direction hits the target precisely. The typical case: a product applicant with zero or little internship experience prepares systematically for three months and lands a big-tech offer — Elly herself went from zero internships to JD and Qunar, then over a dozen special offers. As the original episode put it, if you nail these fundamentals, you have a shot at 80% of the offers out there. The contrast: unlike blasting your resume everywhere, it's not casting a wide net — it's polishing for a specific target and then applying precisely. blocks.label: The Keyword Mindset: A Building-Block Method for Resumes
blocks.text: Keywords serve two purposes: first, they match your target direction; second, when interviewers have no time to read your resume closely, keywords become their entry point and a summary of your experience. The key insight: one internship can map to multiple keywords — data analysis, user research, user-journey optimization. Put different keywords on the same experience and it fits different job descriptions. A typical scene: switching from strategy PM to user PM doesn't require rewriting your resume — just pull the user research and user operations keywords out of your bank and rearrange them. As the episode put it, one experience can carry different keywords, so just attach multiple keywords to a single experience. The workflow: list your experience details, extract your own keywords, download the target company's JD and extract its keywords, match them both ways, then rewrite your resume accordingly. The reason: interviewers read dozens of resumes a day and have no time for word-by-word reading. Resumes without keywords drown in the screening stage. blocks.label: Deep-Digging Your Resume: Micro Detail, Macro Attribution
blocks.text: The core mechanism: your resume says what you did and the results, but the interview is about why you did it, how it turned out, and where the metrics fall short. You should plan that story while writing the resume. The key insight: ask yourself three questions — does this metric truly represent success? Why was it the only metric available at the time? How would you improve it now? As the episode noted, Google Analytics tracks which channels the traffic comes from and how conversion rates look; Mixpanel matters more for seeing how users navigate the product — because their metric dimensions differ. In related terms: Google Analytics focuses on traffic, channels, and conversion; Mixpanel on user-behavior paths — your tool choice reveals which analysis dimension you think in. As an intern, don't just list trivial tasks — think about: what was the team's OKR? What was my role? What did I contribute to the OKR? And why did the project succeed or fail? A startup case: the job-seeking community project won an award but actually failed — user numbers spiked during spring and autumn recruiting but couldn't hold; old users left as soon as they got offers and couldn't be retained; the time, labor, and experience costs were too high for the business value. When interviewers ask why he didn't continue a success, macro attribution is the best answer. title_en: Quanji Hotel: A Ladle of Eastern Aesthetics for Worldwide Decency

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Quanji Hotel: A Ladle of Eastern Aesthetics for Worldwide Decency

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Huisi and Jackie break down Quanji Hotel from two ends — market logic and cultural aesthetics. In 2010 it targeted the 300-500 yuan business-travel gap, serving road warriors with 'arranged darkness' lighting, warm wood textures, and Eastern minimalism. Compared with Atour's peak-end experience spikes, Quanji runs a low-variance, steady route that drew rational consumers back after the pandemic. Founder Ji Qi's 'three no's' principle and national-hotel strategy turn the white-porridge-style Eastern aesthetic into a switch for cultural self-construction.

blocks.label: User Insight: Who Stays at Quanji, and What Do They Fear?
blocks.text: The core mechanism: Quanji's target users are workers sent out by their departments and digital nomads — they head out early to inspect projects and come back at night to revise PPTs; they need efficient recharging, not sightseeing experiences. The key insight: in 2010, corporate travel reimbursement standards spread to 300 to 500 yuan a night. Four-star hotels exceeded the limit, and budget hotels offered only a bed with no workspace — a huge gap opened in the middle, and Quanji positioned itself precisely there. A typical scene: the reimbursement system caps at 300 yuan, and with no low-price hotel in the city, you end up staying in a neighboring city and spending 1,000 yuan on a cab — an absurd but all-too-real office-worker routine. As the episode put it, the people staying at Quanji aren't big bosses; they're workers sent by their departments, waking early to inspect projects and returning to their rooms at night to open the laptop and edit things. Unlike Atour's enthusiastic-host positioning, Quanji's users lean practical — they fear fuss, and they want stability. When traveling or on business, you're often in a state that's neither the vacation class nor the working class — appearing in a strange city while still needing to stay efficient and decent. The atmosphere needs to be neutral, neither too homey nor too corporate, and Eastern minimalist white space happens to provide exactly that sense of order. blocks.label: Spatial Aesthetics: Arranged Darkness, Warm Wood, and the Lighting System
blocks.text: The core mechanism: Quanji doesn't use the hotel industry's standard lighting templates. It customizes a layered soft-light scheme — darkness builds a gentle order, and light retreats after its work is done, without the domineering power of traditional top lights and grand chandeliers. Compared with Tadao Ando's Church of Light, where light leaks through a slit as the spiritual center, Quanji systematizes light into a replicable soothing experience rather than an artistic experiment. A typical scene: multiple bedside switches control different zones of brightness — dim but never dark, most noticeable during long evenings on business trips. As the episode put it, rather than arranging light, they're arranging darkness; the light has that feeling of completing its work without taking credit. And the materials matter too: cold marble and hard tile trigger a sense of hierarchy and authority, so Quanji uses wood extensively to deliver warmth rather than luxury, letting travelers drop their guard. blocks.label: 'Eastern Aesthetics': A Term in Trouble and the White-Porridge Strategy
blocks.text: Here's a subtle point: in the global context, East has long retreated from othering Orientalism — in Western usage, East means the Middle East, not East Asia; saying Orientals implies I am the observer and they are the observed. But in everyday Chinese usage, Eastern aesthetics still conveys its mood without friction — a deliberately vague, practical term rooted in local context. As the episode put it, the East isn't a style; it hints at a way of being watched… who would call themselves Oriental? The core mechanism: Quanji extracts elements from deep, complex culture that can adapt to industrialization and markets — wood tones, bamboo and linen, tea sets — low-cost, standardizable symbols that build a Chinese-character-culture temperament rather than heavy national style. The key insight: calling Quanji Chinese style or national style would be too heavy, making tradition too thick; to foreigners, its visual experience reads equally as Japanese, Korean, or Chinese — like a bowl of white porridge, easy to accept, eaten in every household. blocks.text: The core mechanism: the aroma evokes time-layered memories — the Proust effect — tying you to home, festivals, and temples; the tea set carries the act of brewing, evoking behavioral memories of order — a slow, restrained rhythm. The key insight: we may no longer brew tea or burn incense, but the deep philosophy tied to those rituals still lives in modern life; Quanji puts indicator lights on these invisible circuits to trigger a sense of recognition. The boundary: for users allergic to fragrance or from completely different cultural backgrounds, the symbol-trigger effect drops off sharply. As the episode put it, sometimes we haven't really lost tradition — we've lost the visible form of tradition. How to apply it: when designing brand spaces, prioritize smell and movement triggers over hanging a Chinese painting — they activate cultural subconsciousness more effectively. title_en: 17. Why Does Everyone Think They're a Victim?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: 17. Why Does Everyone Think They're a Victim?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Starting from internet flame wars, Shiyu analyzes how victimhood culture evolved from honor culture and dignity culture, revealing the psychological machinery of the 'self-mo' era, the virtuous victim, and competitive suffering. He explores how to find empathy and personal growth between acknowledging trauma and staying wary of the victimhood narrative — where seeing pain can either arm you or armor you.

blocks.label: Where Victimhood Culture Comes From
blocks.text: Sociologists like Bradley Campbell argue that the moral logic of handling conflict has undergone three transformations, and we're living in the third, increasingly popular stage. The moral meaning has now outweighed honor and dignity themselves — 'victim' has become the identity label with the most moral capital. Online, fights no longer argue about who's more right, but about who's been more harmed, who's worse off. Victimhood culture keeps honor culture's sensitivity to being insulted, and inherits dignity culture's reliance on a third party's fair judgment. The character 'mo' comes from fan-fiction circles, meaning making a character fragile and pitiable to win affection; evolved into 'self-mo,' it points to the grievance of 'not being treated fairly' in social interactions — needing to be understood, cherished, and seen. As Shiyu says, if he got beaten up, he'd want people to see his black-and-blue bruises, to cherish him and gently understand him. The core mechanism: sociologists like Bradley Campbell propose that the moral logic of handling conflict has gone through three transformations, and we are now in the third, increasingly popular stage. The key insight: the moral meaning has become more important than honor and dignity themselves — 'victim' has become the identity label carrying the most moral capital. A typical scene: online fights no longer argue about who's more right, but about who has been more harmed and who's worse off. 'Victimhood culture both preserves honor culture's sensitivity to being insulted and inherits dignity culture's reliance on a third party's impartial judgment.' 'Mo' comes from fan-fiction circles, meaning making a character fragile and pitiable to gain affection. As it evolved into 'self-mo,' it points to the grievance of 'not being treated fairly' in social interactions — needing to be understood, cherished, and seen. 'If I got beaten up, I would actually want everyone to see my black-and-blue bruises, to cherish me and understand me gently.' Fights now decide who's more hurt, not who's right. Suffering has become the argument. Victimhood became a currency of moral standing. Being the victim is now a status symbol.

blocks.label: The Trauma Consensus Online
blocks.text: In real life you know the other person's history and life experience, so communication has a basis of consensus. Online, the two sides are blank slates to each other — the only consensus either can offer is often the trauma they share. Trauma becomes the corpus for mutual understanding, and the cheapest way to confirm each other — 'you've been hurt like this too, we see each other.' When you realize an online opponent may be explaining themselves through a trauma narrative rather than pure logical attack, the argument reads differently. When we long for genuine communication, the dialogue is built on trauma consensus like 'we were both treated this way by our families of origin.' The victim identity expresses 'who I am' and 'what I long for' at the lowest cost and fastest speed, and lets similar people gather and comfort each other. Distinguish 'seeking understanding' from 'fighting for the moral high ground' — the former may bring growth, the latter often sinks into a suffering-comparison loop. What it's about: in real life you know the other person's history and life experience, so communication has a basis of consensus; online, the two sides are blank to each other, and the only consensus either can offer is often the shared trauma. The key insight: trauma becomes the corpus for mutual understanding and the lowest-cost mutual confirmation — 'you've been hurt this way too; we see each other.' How to use it: realize that in an online argument, the other side may be explaining themselves through a trauma narrative, not pure logical attack. 'When we crave genuine communication, the dialogue is built on trauma consensus — like "we were both treated this way by our families of origin."' The reason: the victim identity expresses 'who I am' and 'what I long for' at the lowest cost and fastest speed, and lets like-minded people gather and comfort each other. The solution: distinguish 'seeking understanding' from 'fighting for the moral high ground' — the former may bring growth; the latter often sinks into a loop of comparing suffering. Shared pain became the cheapest bond. Trauma is the one thing strangers online have in common. There's a line between seeking understanding and seeking the moral crown. One heals, the other escalates.

blocks.label: The Virtuous Victim and Competitive Suffering
blocks.text: Virtuous victimhood: it's not enough to suffer — you must also be a 'good person.' That's why the 'beautiful, strong, and tragic' archetype hooks us: beauty and strength prove you deserve help. Supporting them is essentially compensating for your own wish to be treated fairly. Competitively, when accused of harming someone, the first reaction is rarely an apology — it's claiming 'I'm the real victim' or 'I've suffered more than you.' Related concepts include moral dualism of doer versus sufferer, moral zero-sum games, and the dissolution of collective guilt. Claiming competitive victimhood reduces the guilt of 'I harmed someone,' reclaims the moral high ground, and cancels others' moral claims — 'because I'm also a victim, I don't owe you anything.' The boundary: real harm to structurally disadvantaged groups is not in scope here; the critique targets the 'reverse-victim' performance by privileged groups in public opinion and mutual suffering-comparison in relationships. 'Being morally clean, being a good person, owing no one anything — this mental state outweighs almost every other safety attribute.' Virtuous victimhood: it's not enough to be pitiable — you also have to be a 'good person.' That's why the 'beautiful, strong, and tragic' archetype hooks us: beauty and strength prove you deserve help. Supporting such figures is essentially compensating for your own wish to be treated fairly. Competitiveness: when accused of harming others, the first reaction is rarely an apology — it's declaring 'I'm the real victim' or 'I've suffered more than you.' Related concepts: moral dualism (the doer versus the sufferer), moral zero-sum games, and the dissolution of collective guilt. Claiming competitive victimhood reduces the guilt of 'I harmed someone,' reclaims the moral high ground, and cancels others' moral claims — 'because I'm also a victim, I don't owe you anything.' The boundary: acknowledging real harm to structurally disadvantaged groups is not included here; the critique targets the 'reverse-victim' performances of privileged groups in public opinion, and mutual suffering-comparison within relationships. 'Being morally clean, being a good person, owing no one anything — this psychological state matters more than almost every other safety attribute.' Only beautiful-and-broken characters grip us. Suffering alone isn't enough — you need to be a good person too. Claim victim status first, apologize never. The reflex is to one-up the suffering.

blocks.label: The Rift Between Social Structure and Explanatory Frameworks
blocks.text: Two dominant schools today offer incompatible explanations of suffering. The first attributes all pain to external structure — 'I'm a structural victim.' The second privatizes all suffering — 'everything happens for my good; you are responsible for yourself.' That both run equally hot reflects a shared need: whatever the framework, we urgently need our suffering seen and clearly explained, or we can't keep living. The popularity of victim narratives isn't just an individual psychological phenomenon — it's driven by an incentive structure in which society grants the victim identity the highest moral authority. Books like The Forbidden Garden of Fang Siqi write about structural victimhood not to keep women in a weak position, but because a civilized society must prioritize the sensitivity and visibility of harm among those still vulnerable. The standard isn't 'does it change reality immediately,' but 'after seeing the pain clearly, can it give you the strength to keep moving forward.' For the structurally vulnerable, offer visibility and help; for yourself, ask — is this expression the beginning of defense, or the completion of understanding? The core mechanism: two dominant schools today give incompatible explanations of suffering — the first attributes all pain to external structure, 'I'm a structural victim'; the second privatizes all suffering, 'everything happens for my good, you are responsible for yourself.' The key insight: that both are equally fervent reflects a shared need — whatever the framework, we urgently need our suffering seen and clearly explained, or we cannot keep living. 'The rise of victimhood narratives isn't just an individual psychological phenomenon — it's driven by an era's incentive structure that grants the victim identity the highest moral authority.' Books like The Forbidden Garden of Fang Siqi write about structural victimhood not to keep women in the weaker position, but because a civilized society must prioritize the sensitivity and visibility of harm among those who remain vulnerable. The standard: the question isn't 'does it change reality immediately,' but 'after seeing the pain clearly, does it give you the strength to keep moving forward.' How to apply it: for the structurally vulnerable, offer visibility and help; for yourself, ask — is this expression the beginning of defense, or the completion of understanding? Pain is either blamed on society or on yourself. Two maps of suffering, same desperate need to be seen. Is this defense or understanding? Am I arming myself or finally seeing myself?

blocks.label: Defense, Agency, and the Way Out
blocks.text: Being overly sensitive to what others say and habitually answering with 'I'm more victimized' is, at root, the incomplete state of an individuality or agency that hasn't been established — a stress response in an unsafe environment. Admiring the strong and comparing suffering aren't contradictions — both demand to be seen and acknowledged through an identity, whether the strong one or the virtuous victim, rather than about real strength. Notice whether you're 'controlling' the relationship in defense, or 'understanding' yourself in growth. Related concepts: Jungian individuation, agency, control versus understanding, expression completed versus desire satisfied. If telling your trauma is only to extract compensation from outside to fill a vast insecurity, it's a deformed defense — it won't get the real acknowledgment you want. The boundary: for those still inside structural harm, being seen is the precondition; this practice applies to contexts where you already have some sense of safety and can reflect on yourself. What it's about: being overly sensitive to others' expressions and habitually responding with 'I'm more victimized' is, at its root, the incomplete state of an individuality or agency not yet established — a stress response in an unsafe environment. The key insight: admiring the strong and comparing suffering are not contradictions — both seek to be seen and acknowledged through an identity, whether as the strong one or the virtuous victim, rather than being about real strength. How to use it: notice whether you are 'controlling' the relationship in defense, or 'understanding' yourself in growth. title_en: E225 | SaaS Lost Hundreds of Billions: How AI Is Reforming Organizations?

blocks.label: 英文标题

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Anthropic Cowork's 11 enterprise plugins triggered a 'SaaS doomsday': global software stocks evaporated hundreds of billions of dollars. BaiRong Cloud Technology CEO Zhang Chaofeng — who commands 200,000 silicon-based employees with just 1,000 carbon-based ones — explains why the per-seat subscription model is loosening, how SaaS, BaaS, and RaaS business models are evolving, and how traditional enterprises can use agents to transform their organizations rather than simply being replaced.

blocks.label: SaaS Doomsday: The Per-Seat Model Cracks
blocks.text: The core mechanism: Anthropic released 11 function plugins on its Cowork platform — covering legal, finance, sales, and data analysis — calling out nearly every profitable line of traditional SaaS, one by one. Within a week, global software stocks evaporated hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. The key insight: this isn't just a stock adjustment — it's a declaration that the trillion-dollar empire built over the past 15 years on selling seats per head is starting to crack. When a single AI plugin can do the work of an entire department, what's the point of a seat? A typical scene: enterprises no longer want to pay for a software seat; they want to buy a partner that truly solves their problems — whether that partner is carbon-based or silicon-based. As the episode put it, enterprises don't want to pay for a software seat; what they want to buy is a partner that can genuinely help them solve problems. In related terms: OpenClaw targets individuals, while Anthropic's plugins target the enterprise level — the latter directly threatens the existing B-end SaaS market. Zhang Chaofeng said bluntly: in China, not just SaaS but software as a product industry never really existed, and its output value may be only 4% of America's. Before ChatGPT launched in 2021, investors once demanded he switch to the American-defined SaaS model, and he fired back on the spot: China skipped SaaS entirely and jumped straight to charging by transaction results. blocks.label: Three Moats for SaaS Survival
blocks.text: First moat, data: when data settles in a specific domain, general large models like OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Google Gemini can't produce agents of the same quality, because they lack your data. The key insight: even the big players can't do it — they don't have your data. This is the strongest barrier. The boundary: it only works for vertical SaaS with irreplaceable industry data; generic tool-type SaaS has no such advantage. Second moat, complex processes: traditional software has accumulated complex enough workflows — like a 20-step ERP process. Agents are probabilistic models; each step has a 1-2% error rate, and after 20 steps multiply, the error rate becomes unacceptable. The key insight: this gives traditional ERP and SaaS companies a roughly 3-year redemption zone to complete their self-revolution — but at today's AI speed, 3 years may already be too long. blocks.text: Every technology shift has the same problem: digital cameras weren't invented by the new kings, and the wireless communication revolution wasn't built by Huawei — Kodak and Nokia had the technology early on but were afraid to use it. There are two reasons. First, the tech company itself: the previous generation's on-premise model charged once plus 15-20% maintenance fees; switching to SaaS means low early revenue and uncertain renewals, and the bigger the existing base, the harder it is to commit to change — just like Google dare not touch its search revenue. Second, the client: the people championing the old king are old people inside their own organizations, and they're harsh on new things — if it breaks and works worse than before, that locks the transformation down in reverse. As the episode put it, by the time everyone accepts the new paradigm, the new king's technology is already mature. Then when the old king wants to transform, some parts may genuinely be beyond catching up. The key insight: the org chart isn't necessarily silicon at the bottom and carbon on top — it may be an interleaved mesh. The top layer may still be carbon, but the middle layer could see silicon managing carbon. A typical scene: a junior frontline carbon employee can command 10 to 100 silicon employees from day one; and in a chat, you can no longer tell whether the other side is carbon or silicon — ChatGPT passed the Turing test long ago. Especially in China, where SaaS can't deliver end-to-end results and enterprises are weak on willingness to pay, RaaS delivers a position or a result directly, and the value can be quantified. blocks.text: The June 18 morning edition of the 'Morning Coffee' podcast: Yum China pays 1.2 billion dollars to own the Pizza Hut brand in China outright; Sam's Club China replaces both its chairman and chief purchasing officer after a regulatory talk while speeding up expansion into lower-tier cities; ByteDance's AI pivots from the consumer-facing Doubao to enterprise services; SpaceX acquires the coding tool Cursor for 60 billion dollars in stock; and a World Cup special on how soccer overtook baseball to become America's third-favorite sport.

blocks.label: Retail & Consumer: Pizza Hut China and the Sam's Club Shuffle
blocks.text: The mechanism: Yum sold its global Pizza Hut business for 2.7 billion dollars, and Yum China paid 1.2 billion dollars to buy the brand ownership for mainland China — moving from franchisee to brand owner, no longer paying franchise fees. The key insight: Pizza Hut in the U.S. has seen sales fall two years in a row and plans to close 250 stores; in China, it covers more than 1,100 cities with 4,000-plus outlets — hot and cold markets on either side of the Pacific. Yum China's CEO says brand ownership brings more flexibility, and the franchise fees saved can be poured into localized operations. As the company put it, Pizza Hut is doing much better in China, covering more than 1,100 cities with over 4,000 stores. It echoes the KFC model, where the local operator gradually takes the lead in the brand. Meanwhile, on June 17, Walmart China Investment replaced its chairman with Liu Peng, who once led the Sam's Club format, and the chief purchasing officer resigned the same day for personal reasons. The local operator now holds the brand, not just the stores. One market is cooling, the other is boiling. The U.S. shrinks while China expands — two opposite stories.

blocks.label: Tech Briefs: AI Monetization, Mergers, and a Reality Check
blocks.text: LatePost reports: Doubao has over 200 million daily active users, yet daily revenue is under 1 million yuan, mostly from e-commerce commissions, while computing costs run tens of millions a day. The video model Seedance takes the B2B route, with annualized revenue around 2 billion dollars, enough to offset Doubao's compute costs. Anthropic shows that AI coding can make huge infrastructure spending pay off, pushing its valuation toward a trillion dollars. But Seedance growth is slowing, Kuaishou's Kling is decelerating too, and AI video generation still needs better model performance. Just four days after its listing, SpaceX bought the AI coding tool Cursor with 60 billion dollars in stock — Cursor was founded in 2022 with around 2.6 billion dollars in enterprise revenue, though its market share fell from 41 to 26 percent, with Anthropic taking roughly half. Analysts say the listing gave SpaceX a highly valued stock, letting it close big acquisitions with a stock premium. blocks.label: World Cup Special: Why Soccer Keeps Winning America Over
blocks.text: Gallup data: from 1937 to 2004, fewer than 2 percent of Americans named soccer their favorite sport. A recent Economist survey shows more than 10 percent now do, edging past baseball to rank third behind American football and basketball. A Johns Hopkins professor argues that American football, baseball, and basketball are firmly entrenched; Americans favor high-scoring sports and sports invented at home, while soccer has few goals and even draws, so it stayed marginalized for a long time. But the mechanism has changed: the 2024 Copa América final drew more than 12 million U.S. viewers, a record, over half of them Latino, and 40 percent of the nearly 10 million viewers of the Euro final were Latino. According to Pew Research, Latinos are one of the fastest-growing groups in America, nearly doubling in population over 20-plus years to about a fifth of the country. For many Latino families, soccer isn't just entertainment — it's the bond that holds community and family life together. title_en: Ep. 96 | The Mountain God Blesses Everyone Who Carries Their Trash Out

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Ep. 96 | The Mountain God Blesses Everyone Who Carries Their Trash Out

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Mujiang, a programmer, founded the volunteer group "Shou Hu Zi Ran" (Hands Protecting Nature). Over five years and more than a hundred mountain-cleanup events, volunteers hauled out about 12 tons of trash. This episode breaks down why people litter outdoors — from the broken-window effect and self-heating hotpot hotspots to the hidden traps of "cleanup fees" — and ends with the seven Leave No Trace principles and the small, practical waste-reduction steps anyone can take on their next hike.

blocks.label: Shou Hu Zi Ran: From Picking Up Trash to a Hundred-Person Volunteer Group
blocks.text: The group was founded in October 2020 by Mujiang, a programmer from Yunnan. On weekends, volunteers head into the mountains to pick up trash along the whole route, gather it at the end, carry it down, and drop it at the village recycling station, where the city's waste system takes over. The key insight: picking up trash yourself has an extremely low barrier — a pair of gloves and a bag — but running it as an organization brings a second set of problems: trademark registration, a legal entity, and sustainable funding. Charity and organizational survival are two different challenges. By the numbers: over a hundred events, roughly 12 tons of trash — about one person's decades of household waste — more than thirty team leads, over seven thousand volunteers in the community, and each event capped at fifty people. As he says, "We've run over a hundred events so far and picked up about 12 tons of trash… more than thirty team leads, around seven thousand volunteers." Conceptually it complements Leave No Trace: Shou Hu Zi Ran does the cleanup afterward, while LNT focuses on prevention and minimal impact beforehand. Mujiang writes code by day and squeezes time for mountain cleanups in his spare hours. In 2018, on Hebei's Xiaowutai, he first carried two bags of trash down on a whim; in 2019, on Gongga in western Sichuan, he saw self-heating meals and disposable raincoats on high-altitude trails — "out-of-awareness trash" — and realized the problem was systemic. In 2020 he organized it. The volunteering is easy; the sustainability is the hard part. Carry it out and let the city system deal with it. Everything comes down to one rule: pack it out.

blocks.label: Where the Trash Comes From: Who Litters, What, and Where
blocks.text: First, the self-heating hotpot. It's bulky, full of soup and oil, and hard to carry back down — and it pollutes heavily if left behind. Casual hikers, unaware of lightweight cooking options, think hotpots are the only option outdoors. The fix: for day hikes, keep trail food as simple as possible — sandwiches, rice balls, bread, sausages — and de-package it at home into reusable containers. Severity: fatal, ranking in the top three of what they clean up: water bottles, then food bags, then hotpot boxes. As the guest puts it, "Don't bring self-heating hotpots hiking… they're bulky, and they produce lots of soup and oil, so first of all you'll struggle to carry them back down." Second, the broken-window effect: any piece of human trash, even "biodegradable" stuff, sends later visitors the signal that "it's okay to drop things here," so one spot spreads into a whole area — visual pollution plus copied behavior. The key point: at home you wouldn't spit sunflower seeds on the floor, so don't do it outdoors either. Discuss whether something is civilized first, and whether it degrades second. A hotpot is a nightmare to haul back down. You'll never want to carry that greasy pot out again. One piece of trash invites the next. Litter begets litter — that's the broken-window effect. If you wouldn't do it in your living room, don't do it in the wild. The same manners apply — just with better scenery.

blocks.label: The Hidden Costs of Wilderness Trash
blocks.text: Here's a trap: after outdoor activities exploded in popularity, villagers along popular trails started charging "cleanup fees." But they lack the capacity and knowledge to actually deal with the waste, so the common results are burning, burying, or hiding it in bushes. The fix: carry out the trash you generate and bring it back to the city's proper processing system — that's the cheapest and most reliable option. Severity: critical, because it creates the wrong expectation that "I paid, so I can litter." As the guest recalls, "I was shocked to find the trash had all been buried — they just made it invisible… and you think the problem is solved." On Hong Kong's MacLehose Trail, wild boars smelling food trash approach campsites; in Hebei campsites, cattle drawn by food once caused a scary incident with a herd rushing at a tent. Dumping oily, spicy soup kills vegetation and changes animal foraging habits — like the black birds on Beilingshan that show up every Sunday right on time for the abandoned camp waste. The boundary: inland low-elevation trails have fewer wild animals, but the risk of changing animal behavior exists just the same in dense camping zones. blocks.label: Leave No Trace & Pre-Trip Preparation
blocks.text: Leave No Trace started in the United States as an outdoor lifestyle: when you're in nature, minimize your impact — not just trash, but damage to the ground, disturbance to plants and animals, and the effect on other visitors, like blasting music out loud. The key insight: absolute zero trace isn't possible, but good pre-trip preparation avoids most avoidable impacts. The hardest principle for ordinary people: taking the time to prepare well. The training path: a casual intro takes ten to thirty minutes; the professional version is a two-day-one-night field practice covering campsite selection, waste handling, hanging food, and walking on different terrain. Shou Hu Zi Ran is also promoting LNT instructor training — and waste handling is just one part; where you camp and how you handle fire, like no fires in fire season or using a fire pan, matter just as much. On water: use a hydration bladder or soft flask — an empty bag doesn't get thrown away — and if you bring bottled water, tear off the labels at home first. On food: sandwiches and rice balls go in containers, de-packaged at home, and avoid foods with troublesome peels — skip the watermelon, and pick cucumber, tomato, or apple instead. Skip the foods that leave peels behind. Choose snacks that go wrapper-free and peel-free.

blocks.label: The Real Struggle of Running the Organization
blocks.text: Why it's hard: hauling ten-plus kilos of trash down the mountain feels like manual labor, and the next time you come, the trail is full of trash again — you start to doubt whether volunteer appeals make any difference at all. Mujiang's answer: after the emotion fades, he still "can't stand it" when he sees trash. The solution has to run on multiple tracks — better regulations, public awareness, and volunteer cleanup — without expecting any single fix to work overnight. Severity: moderate — it affects long-term participation, but it doesn't negate the value of the action. As online feedback puts it: "At first it felt great, but later no matter how much I picked up there was always more — it even felt empty and hopeless." title_en: Ep184 Shenzhen Survival Manual: A Flood of Fresh Ways to Make Money Rushed Into My Head

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Ep184 Shenzhen Survival Manual: A Flood of Fresh Ways to Make Money Rushed Into My Head

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Host Mao Dong brings Ning Jiayu, Xiao Kuai, Da Xiong, Feng Ge, and a live audience together for a Shenzhen edition of the podcast Basically Harmless. Together they bust the stereotype that "everyone in Shenzhen is just chasing money," walking through the city's real texture: the handshake buildings of urban villages, plastic-bag baths at Lotus Hill bathhouses, the "leading talent" residency program, and Huaqiangbei beauty brands going overseas. The portrait that emerges is of a migrant city where, despite crushing housing prices, people still believe there's a chance.

blocks.label: 1. City Identity & Population Structure
blocks.text: Shenzhen has almost no "native" narrative — identity is layered by when you moved in and what the residency policy says: pre-special-zone villagers, third-generation builders' descendants, tax-paying leading talents, and ordinary workers. The key insight: "Once you arrive, you're a Shenzhener" is a policy slogan — your actual experience depends on your hukou, your property, and your industry. The typical situation: deciding whether to apply for residency, choosing between an urban village or the far suburbs for rent, and whether starting a business here is worth betting on Shenzhen's policies. Feng Ge calls himself a "leading talent who got paid to become a Shenzhener": a company paying several million in tax can earn an official title plus yearly subsidies. Da Xiong came from Chaoshan with his parents at age three, so he considers himself a local — just not a native. It's the opposite of Beijing and Shanghai, where "failing to get residency turns you artsy" — Shenzhen's residency still feels reachable, so people are willing to grind harder. Mao Dong himself came in 2014 because a partner was starting a business here; had he gone to Beijing, he says he might have been just "a directionless artsy youth." Back then Shenzhen was cheaper to start a business in than Shanghai and had fewer artsy kids than Beijing — "only Shenzhen had this power to force talent into action." Everything turned smooth once they moved from a remote Longhua-Buji office to the Science and Technology Park. title_en: S8E3 How Does a Girl Grow Up? The Summer I Learned What Love Was

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: S8E3 How Does a Girl Grow Up? The Summer I Learned What Love Was

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Three hosts read Claire Keegan's short story 'Foster' together: in rural Ireland in 1981, a deeply sensitive nine-year-old girl, fostered for the summer, is treated with gentleness for the first time. Through a held hand, a shared secret, and the word 'Daddy,' they talk about where blood ends and family begins, the 'slack' real caregiving requires, and how the short story uses tension rather than drama to capture the daily struggles of overlooked people.

blocks.label: Part One: A Summer Foster Placement
blocks.text: The setup: in rural Ireland in 1981, a nameless nine-year-old girl is sent by her father to be fostered for several months with the Kinsellas, a couple who are relatives. Told in the first person, she observes that summer's care, labor, and shifting emotions, and at the parting she runs after Kinsella, hugs him, and calls him Daddy. The key insight: the story looks ordinary on the surface, but the contrast between her birth family and the foster family lets readers infer how she was treated before. Keegan has written five books totaling only about 140,000 words, yet she packs enormous feeling into very short spaces. If you want to understand how a highly sensitive child gets raised — or how foster care and family trauma work — start with this roughly seven-thousand-word story. As one host says, 'this is a story about how to raise a highly sensitive child.' It echoes the question from the film Shoplifters: does blood make you family? The story is short yet incredibly rich, like a karst cave where every step reveals a new view.
