The story is short yet incredibly rich, like a karst cave where every step reveals a new view. Each reader finds a different facet: some see the clockwork-precise cause and effect, others fall for its poetic moments — like the sky outside the car window split into neat squares by the wires. The setup: a girl is sent to stay with relatives for the summer. Here's the premise: she's fostered by a couple who are distant relatives. It's tiny in length but huge in feeling. A short story that packs a whole emotional world into a few pages.

blocks.label: Part Two: You're Born with Relatives, but Not Necessarily a Family
blocks.text: The setup: the girl's birth father tells the Kinsellas, 'she will eat but you can work her' — he treats her as a pair of hands. A few days later, Mrs. Kinsella says, 'all you need is minding' — all you need is to be cared for and kept in mind. The key insight: the slack in parenting isn't really about money — it's whether there's room in your life to care about how someone feels. In urban families living in poverty, parents may not love less; they simply have no energy left to mind. So when you judge a relationship, don't ask whether people are blood-related; ask whether they share a life, take care of each other, and build a daily rhythm together. As the hosts say, 'you're born with relatives, but you're not born with a family. A family is something you have to build.' And when Kinsella takes the girl's hand, she realizes at once that her father never held her hand before. Inside, she wishes he would let go — sudden gentleness feels uncomfortable and unsettling, not a relief of 'so this is what love is.' Being genuinely cared for was brand new to her. It's not that they don't love — they have no margin left. The love is there, but the energy to show it isn't.

blocks.label: Part Three: Is One Summer of Being Loved Enough?
blocks.text: The setup: at the parting, the girl runs out and throws herself into Kinsella's arms, just as her birth father walks up. She calls him Daddy — Kinsella reminds her that he is Kinsella — and it's the first time this sensitive girl has ever taken the initiative to express love. The key insight: by plot, it's a bad ending — she goes back to her birth family; but by growth, it's a good ending — she now knows what love is and how to express it, and that learning can never be taken back, like learning to ride a bike. This ending is a classic case for asking whether a short period of high-quality company can change the course of a life. As one host puts it, 'if you weren't properly loved as a child, do you really have the capacity to build new relationships and good love?' It echoes the line 'you have to see a dragon to believe in unicorns' — what the Kinsellas open up is her imagination of love, not a single standard answer. The hosts also debate: one camp believes children grow into themselves no matter what; the other believes even a small misstep can hurt a sensitive child, so parents end up being overly careful. It's a sad ending in plot, but a hopeful one in growth. By the story it's a loss; by the child it's a win. Once you learn what love feels like, you can't unlearn it. That lesson can never be taken back from her.

blocks.label: Part Four: The Restraint and Tension of the Short Story
blocks.text: On craft: Keegan says Foster was born from a single image — a child's handprint on still water. The short story compresses time, squeezing a whole summer into a few dozen pages, and finds its rhythm between stillness and flow: a held hand is a spotlighted instant, while day-after-day chores are a static, repeating motion. The key insight: Keegan doesn't write drama — she writes tension. The event has already happened, the conflict is over; she writes the moment a man buys petrol, has a smoke, and doesn't want to go home. So when your story feels not dramatic enough, pivot to inner tension and the daily lives of overlooked people. As she puts it, 'if tension sees drama at the party, tension leaves.' This connects to Frank O'Connor's 'The Lonely Voice' — the short story depicts submerged population groups, like the extra child whose hand her father never held. An office worker climbs the equivalent of Everest every year just going up and down stairs; finding the drama in that paperwork Everest is harder than writing about explorers, and it's exactly what draws Lao Yuan to Keegan's work. blocks.text: The setup: a summer foster placement becomes the first time the girl is treated gently. You're born with relatives, but a family is something you have to build. The lesson of being loved can never be taken back — like learning to ride a bike. Keegan writes tension, not drama — the conflict is over before the story even begins.

title_en: S8E2 After Graduation: The Distance Between Us and Society

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: S8E2 After Graduation: The Distance Between Us and Society

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: A graduation-season special: Xixi, Xiao Jiao, and Lao Yuan, three veteran graduates, start from their own graduation memories, work through listener letters, and talk about crushed passion, the grading game of socialization, and their rules for life after school — asking how to live with the distance between yourself and society once you graduate.

blocks.label: Graduation Memories: Haste and Celebration Side by Side
blocks.text: The starting point: graduation is never a single emotion — it's a mix of relief, loneliness, confusion, or happiness. Xixi graduated from her master's during the pandemic, picking up her diploma at the school gate like exchanging intelligence, then spotting a stunning sunset on Beijing's empty streets and laughing out loud in the car — finally, no more studying! Xiao Jiao's PhD defense advisor vanished before the defense, the committee had to be reassembled at the last minute, and she graduated in a state of total suspension. Lao Yuan graduated from undergrad in a plaid skirt, drinking with friends until six in the morning, excitement and confusion side by side. So when your graduation feels not perfect enough, remember that haste and uncertainty are the norm for most people — a composed graduation is the lucky minority. One foot has already stepped forward, but the last step's problems are still unsolved. It contrasts with a listener letter saying 'graduated and unemployed, but oddly calm' — there is no standard answer to how you should feel. Related idea: it contrasts with a listener letter saying 'graduated and unemployed, but oddly calm' — there is no standard answer to how you should feel. Xixi mentions teaching freshmen who already ask how to plan a career — and she, in her thirties, still doesn't know. Ten years ago students sneered at career-development classes; now the anxiety has clearly moved earlier. Graduation is a cocktail of emotions, not one feeling. It's relief, loneliness, and confusion all at once. A picture-perfect graduation is the exception, not the rule. Most graduations are messy and rushed — and that's normal.

blocks.label: Passion and Love: A Luxury or a Compass?
blocks.text: The setup: she chose her path by passion, got into the best school in the field, then found in an internship that she couldn't feel passion for the work itself — but switching fields means starting from zero. The key insight: this confusion means you're still searching — your standards haven't blurred, and that's actually a good thing. Chasing passion is itself a luxury; many people face the numbness of 'A is fine, B is also fine.' So when you're already in an ideal position, you don't have to switch immediately — explore other possibilities while doing what you do now. As the hosts say, having this confusion is actually a good thing, because it means you're still searching. Xixi pursues excellence and keeps looking for a place where she can fully realize her potential. Lao Yuan's standard is simpler: passion equals physical and mental health plus not being exhausted — because of his migraines, when he overdoes it, he collapses, so he refuses to burn himself out. Because of his migraines, when he overdoes it he collapses, so his standard is simply not burning himself out. Not feeling passion doesn't mean you're failing. Struggling with passion just means you're still searching. Nothing really excites me — A is fine, B is fine too. I've gone numb to choosing between options.

blocks.label: Socialization: The Grading Game and Its Academic Roots
blocks.text: In film school, Lao Yuan learned from crew dinners that turning the cup upside down after drinking means sincerity. When he did it in front of his master's advisor and classmates, the whole room went pupils quaking — social skills have completely different applicability in different settings. As he jokes, if someone says you're very social, that's definitely an insult. The concept: in Parsons' structural functionalism, socialization is a mechanism of social reproduction — like a cultural download of learning how adults are supposed to behave. The key insight: who decides the norms? Marginalized groups don't have this grammar. The same behavior can be absurd in a different cultural setting — the flipped cup, the rules about the seat of honor. And the boundary: in academia, socialization is not a compliment; carrying on bad culture, the drinking-table rituals, the ranked seating, is not the same as maturity. As the hosts ask, by learning all this, aren't we really just perpetuating some pretty bad culture? The same move that's golden at a crew dinner is absurd at a defense. Mastering the rituals isn't the same as growing up. Following bad culture isn't maturity — it's just conformity.

blocks.label: Moving Forward and Separating Feelings from Action
blocks.text: Xixi proposes a way to open up life: instead of do what you love, it's whatever you've chosen to do, find a way to love it. Just as the body needs moderate discomfort to grow, so does the mind. In practice, for introverts, treat necessary socializing as a job to get done — don't pour too much feeling into it, and lower the psychological threshold. Meanwhile, a friend told Lao Yuan on a walk, 'you still need to look forward and do new things' — it shook him, because he and many of his friends never look forward; they stay parked at a certain stage. But he also notes that artists need to stay somewhere and keep digging deeper — it's ordinary people who look forward. As he puts it, people who look forward are ordinary people; artists are people who stay in one place — and he's not an artist. There's also the move of replacing 'do I want to?' with 'should I do it?' When a project-manager role demanded socializing, she treated it as work, separating feelings from action — and it went well, with positive feedback. Treat socializing like a task on your to-do list. See it as work — do it well without overinvesting emotion.

blocks.label: Three Rules for Life After Graduation
blocks.text: Why it matters: Lao Yuan once suffered endless meaningless pain in screenwriting for the sake of perseverance — until he broke down with no warning at all. Virtues must come in pairs: perseverance with joy or health, kindness with boundaries, courage with wisdom, endurance with self-love. The boundary: even when short-term pain buys a long-term right direction, joy still has to stay as your baseline calibration. So in practice, whenever you try to convince yourself with 'just persevere,' ask: does this make me happy? Is it healthy for me? Xiao Jiao adds a second rule: going to a bigger world when you're young — big cities, different industries — reveals that society runs on many rule sets, so you're never forced into a closed little society's binary choice of join or don't join. And it doesn't have to mean going abroad; the path from a small city to a provincial capital to a big city counts too. title_en: Cameras, Millimeter-Wave, LiDAR, UWB — What Actually Drives Smart Perception?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Cameras, Millimeter-Wave, LiDAR, UWB — What Actually Drives Smart Perception?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: The host breaks down the five sensors behind new-energy smart driving in plain language — ultrasonic radar, UWB, cameras, millimeter-wave radar, and LiDAR — starting from the Li L9 ditching its twelve ultrasonic sensors for UWB. Each sensor's principle, pros and cons, and fusion strategy is explained, so buyers can't be fooled by salespeople. The episode covers why ultrasonic radars lost their place, how UWB nails precise near-field positioning, why a camera that understands beats a camera that only sees, how 3D and 4D millimeter-wave radar differ, and why expensive LiDAR is still indispensable. The takeaway: no sensor or stack is perfect, so the real competition is fusing sensors well and letting algorithms grasp space.

blocks.label: Ultrasonic Radar: The Veteran Replaced by UWB
blocks.text: Let's start with ultrasonic radar. It sends out ultrasonic waves like a bat and judges distance from the echo timing, which works great for close-range, low-speed stuff — reversing, parallel parking, creeping along a wall. It's cheap, stable, and mature, so it used to be standard on every trim. But it can only tell you that there's an obstacle and roughly how far away it is. In the eyes of an ultrasonic radar, a pillar, a trash can, a cat, and a plastic bag are basically the same thing — all just obstacles. That's why it's being replaced by UWB near-field sensing; the Li L9 dropped all twelve of its ultrasonic sensors at once. It only measures distance, can't grasp spatial meaning, gets fooled by rain and thin objects, and can't keep up with what advanced driving needs. The mechanism: it sends out ultrasonic waves like a bat and works out distance from the echo timing — great for close-range, low-speed detection within a few meters, like reversing, parallel parking, and creeping along a wall. The insight: it's cheap — the front-install cost is nearly negligible — plus stable and mature, so it used to be standard on every trim. But it can only tell you 'there's an obstacle here and it's this far away'; it can't tell a pillar from a plastic bag. Typical uses: basic reversing alerts, low-speed obstacle avoidance, and front and rear parking assist. As the show puts it: 'In the eyes of an ultrasonic radar, a pillar, a trash can, a cat, and a plastic bag are basically the same thing — they're all just obstacles.' Related concept: it's being replaced by UWB near-field sensing — the Li L9 dropped all twelve of its ultrasonic sensors at once. Why: first, it only measures distance and can't grasp spatial meaning; second, it's easily confused by rain, snow, standing water, slopes, and thin obstacles — there's a famous case of a car hitting a thin pole; third, it can't keep up with what advanced autonomous driving needs for spatial positioning. It used to come standard on every model. It was standard equipment across the whole lineup. To it, they're basically all the same. It can't tell them apart — they're all just obstacles. It can't keep up with what ADAS needs. It falls short of the spatial positioning new systems require.

blocks.label: UWB: The New Star of Precise Near-Field Positioning
blocks.text: Now UWB. It uses ultra-wideband radio signals for meter-level ranging accuracy, almost immune to temperature and humidity. It can recognize road signs, branches, and pets or toys under 20 centimeters, outputting distance and direction at once. In plain words, it's a really precise near-field positioning technology. Bluetooth knows someone is coming; UWB knows there's a person standing at the left front door, 1.2 meters or 1.1 meters away, moving toward the rear. It evolved from the BMW-led UWB digital key into part of the car's near-field sensing. During auto parking, the camera handles what we see, while UWB handles exact distance. But it solves positional relationships, not world modeling — great for hands-free entry and curb parking, useless at a distance. Ultra-wideband radio signals deliver meter-level ranging accuracy, almost unaffected by temperature and humidity. It can recognize road signs, branches, and pets or kids' toys under 20 centimeters, outputting distance and direction at the same time. In plain words, it's just a really precise near-field positioning technology. As the show puts it: 'Bluetooth knows someone is coming. UWB knows there's a person standing at the left front door, whether it's 1.2 meters or 1.1 meters away, and that they're moving toward the rear.' The mechanism: it evolved from the BMW-led UWB digital key for hands-free locking and unlocking into part of the car's near-field sensing. During auto parking, the camera handles 'what we see' while UWB handles 'exact distance.' The insight: UWB solves positional relationships, not world modeling. It's great for hands-free entry, low-speed obstacle avoidance, and parking tight against a curb — but it's useless at a distance. Typical uses: hands-free unlock, auto parking, remote valet parking, and squeezing through narrow lanes. As the show says: 'UWB solves positional relationships, not world modeling — at best, it covers your near-field sensing needs.' In plain words, it's precise positioning. Put simply, it just tells you exactly where things are. The car unlocks as you walk up. It's hands-free — no touching the phone. At best, it handles near-field needs. It can't do much beyond close range.

blocks.label: Cameras: Understanding Beats Resolution
blocks.text: Cameras are the sensor closest to the human eye. Musk says people drive with their eyes, so cars should too — that's Tesla's vision-only approach. Chinese automakers mostly don't dare go vision-only, keeping LiDAR fusion instead. But cameras struggle with backlight, heavy rain, snow, fog, glare, and low light — human eyes can barely see at night, let alone a camera. Still, what makes cameras great isn't seeing clearly, it's understanding what they see. Fusing with LiDAR covers the bad-weather gap, and pairing with UWB delivers ranging while parking. Musk strictly controls costs and rejected LiDAR's price; after the 2021 white-truck crash, Tesla went fully vision-only around 2023. But under China's complex road conditions, LiDAR won't be abandoned anytime soon. The mechanism: it's the sensor closest to the human eye. Musk argues that people drive with their eyes, so cars should too — that's Tesla's vision-only approach. Most Chinese automakers don't dare go vision-only and still keep LiDAR fusion. The insight: cameras struggle with backlight, heavy rain and snow, fog and glare, and low light — human eyes can barely see at night, let alone a camera. Typical uses: lane recognition, traffic-sign reading, pedestrian detection, and visual mapping for parking. As the show puts it: 'What makes cameras great isn't seeing clearly — it's understanding what they see.' title_en: No.25 It Was Never Just Football: A Century of Love-Hate Between Spain and Argentina

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: No.25 It Was Never Just Football: A Century of Love-Hate Between Spain and Argentina

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: From the May Revolution of 1810 to the 2026 World Cup final, Spain and Argentina have played out a century of love and hate: colonial independence, reverse migration, the Perón-Franco wheat diplomacy, the green-pitch exchanges of Di Stéfano, Maradona, and Messi, and the YPF nationalization and the diplomatic storms of the Milei era. The recurring tension is between the sting of economic plunder on one side and the genuine joy of sport on the other — two countries that can never quite be at peace, and never quite apart.

blocks.label: The Road to Independence: From Admiration to Superiority
blocks.text: Let's go back to 1810. On May 25, Buenos Aires set up its own ruling junta, pledging loyalty to the imprisoned legitimate king, Ferdinand the Seventh — a political move that legally pushed out the Spanish viceroy. Argentina didn't declare independence right away; it used the 'loyalty to the king' excuse to gain legitimacy, and only on July 9, 1816 did the Congress of Tucumán formally sever the bond with Spain. This is the classic Latin American strategy: formal loyalty, actual self-rule. As the sources explain, they declared they would not obey the French-backed puppet government of Spain, and that the junta was established out of loyalty to the previous legitimate Spanish king. Unlike the Thirteen Colonies' cry of 'no taxation without representation,' Argentina's independence was more about a power vacuum left by the collapse of the mother country itself. Meanwhile the Spanish viceroy Sobremonte fled to Córdoba with the treasury in tow, while the citizens of Buenos Aires, led by merchant guild leader Martín de Alzaga, repelled the British troops twice. They pledged loyalty in form, but ruled themselves in fact. The loyalty was a legal fiction — the real goal was self-rule. The mother country collapsed, leaving a power vacuum. Spain's implosion opened a window for independence.

blocks.label: Migration and Football: The Birth of La Nuestra
blocks.text: Football came with the migrants. After Spain's crushing defeat in the 1898 Spanish-American War, the disaster of the generation of 98, huge numbers of farmers from Galicia and the Canary Islands migrated to Argentina. By the 1910 centennial, one in ten people in Argentina had been born in Spain. This flow of people dissolved the geographic distance between the two countries and created a community where each lives inside the other; Argentines even lumped all Spaniards together as 'Gallego,' with an affectionate teasing tone. And it continues today: after the 2001 crisis, hundreds of thousands of young Argentines used their grandparents' Spanish passports to migrate in reverse — a second-generation return wave. The football connection goes back to 1928: seventeen players crossed the Atlantic on an ocean liner for 22 days, and in Galicia and Madrid they beat Celta, Atlético Madrid, and Real Madrid in a row. After scoring, player Garmelo Boso gave an exaggerated bow to King Alfonso the Thirteenth — a South American commoner's contempt for European royalty. That's how Argentine football remade itself from the hard-nosed English style into La Nuestra, our style, blending tango rhythm, street feints, and delicate dribbling. Spanish media called Boca an acrobatic troupe on the pitch, and today's tiki-taka has one of its earliest roots in Argentina. blocks.label: The Perón-Franco Era: Wheat in Exchange for Dignity
blocks.text: After World War Two, Spain was isolated by the United Nations and fell into the 'Years of Hunger,' Años del Hambre. Argentina provided 350 million pesos a year in revolving credit from 1948 to 1951, one point seven five billion over four years, earmarked to buy Argentine wheat, beef, and leather — saving the Franco regime from collapsing into famine. Argentina also fought hard against UN sanctions on Spain, acting as Franco's most steadfast geopolitical safe harbor. The official line was warm: 'We are compatriots; blood is thicker than water. We must give back to our brother nation.' But the 1947 'Rainbow Tour' only looked like the peak of the political honeymoon — behind the scenes, the two first ladies were full of class and psychological conflict. So understand Peronism as a political chameleon: it holds both far-left elements like workers' welfare and nationalization, and far-right elements like military rule and anti-communism, so it can't be simply equated with Francoism. blocks.label: Mutual Conquest on the Pitch
blocks.text: Then came mutual conquest on the pitch. In 1953, Di Stéfano moved from River Plate to Real Madrid, helping break Barcelona's myth and launching five straight European Cup titles. Franco's government used Real Madrid's European victories as a showroom to break diplomatic isolation and display a new Spain. It perfectly matched the two countries' supply and demand: Argentine wheat filled Spanish stomachs, while Spain absorbed Argentina's top sports talent into its national brand. Di Stéfano eventually naturalized as Spanish and played for the national team. Compare that with Messi: Di Stéfano chose Spain, while Messi flatly refused — a mirror of two kinds of Argentine attitudes toward the former colonial power. In between came the greats of the eighties: Kempes, champion of the 1978 World Cup, played for Valencia at the time. In 1982, Maradona joined Barcelona — the spell was imperfect, marred by hepatitis, a broken leg, and clashes with the board — but he kept displaying his extraordinary skill later at Sevilla. And picture this scene: while Spanish financiers signed capital-acquisition deals in Buenos Aires, ordinary fans cheered the Argentine king of football at the stadium every weekend — economic plunder and genuine sporting joy struck a compensatory balance in the collective subconscious. Argentina's finest crossed the ocean to play for Spain. The best Argentine talent ended up in Spanish colors. Plunder on the balance sheet, joy on the pitch — they cancel out. The financial sting got soothed by weekend glory.

blocks.label: Capital Game: The Second Conquest and the YPF Storm
blocks.text: The second conquest came through capital. In 1989, hyperinflation hit Argentina, and the Menem government privatized core state companies: YPF, telecom, electricity, railways. Spanish firms, armed with the advantage of a shared language and culture, went on a buying spree. Understand how this expansion, which nearly bought up the whole lifeline of Argentina's economy, stirred geopolitical populist resentment: it modernized services on one hand, while on the other, profits from strategic resources flowed back to the old colonial power. And that proved fatal — it laid the groundwork for the 2012 YPF nationalization crisis. The scale was shocking: Repsol swallowed YPF, Argentina's state oil company and the most sacred business in national sentiment, for 14.855 billion dollars; Telefónica monopolized southern communications; Endesa controlled the electricity supply. Then came the storm. After the 2010 discovery of the Vaca Muerta super-giant shale field in Patagonia, with reserves of about 22.8 billion barrels of oil equivalent, President Cristina Fernández took to national television on April 16, 2012, accusing Repsol of chasing short-term dividends and underinvesting in exploration — then forcibly seized 51 percent of the shares in a nationalization. Spain's Rajoy government denounced it as an outright plunder of Western capital and recalled its ambassador. Argentina finally settled with a five-billion-dollar ten-year bond, but other shareholders won 16.1 billion dollars in US courts — a settlement that still shackles Argentina's finances today. blocks.label: Messi: The Perfect Product of a Century of Entanglement
blocks.text: And finally, Messi — the perfect product of a century of entanglement. Because of a growth hormone deficiency, and because Argentine clubs couldn't cover the monthly treatment bill, Messi crossed the ocean with his father to Barcelona. The timing aligns almost perfectly with Argentina's 2001 financial collapse and the middle-class reverse migration — Messi was essentially one of those hundreds of thousands of Argentines who flowed to Spain looking for dignity. Spain's federation repeatedly lobbied him to join the Spanish national team and play alongside Xavi, and was flatly turned down every time. In 2004, the Argentine federation hastily arranged a friendly against Paraguay to permanently lock down his Argentine nationality. As the episode puts it: his future may be in Barcelona, but his soul and his jersey will always belong to Argentina. He carries the Argentine gene: at his core, the barrio spirit of the Rosario streets — unpredictable shifts of balance, exquisite dribbling in impossibly tight spaces, to a height that approaches art. title_en: E116: Is the 66,600-Yuan 'Fly-Anywhere' Product Worth It?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Three hosts from Hudao (Cutlass) deeply dissect Hainan Airlines' 66666 Shunxing Card and the 6666 fly-anywhere pass: the former deposits 66,600 yuan for a year with a full refund plus 3,333 points worth roughly 8 flight tickets; the latter costs 199 yuan per flight but is limited to early-morning and late-night departures. They also share the SOP for handling fraudulent overseas credit-card charges and the trick for signing corporate-rate hotel deals.

blocks.label: Comparing Hainan Airlines' Two 'Fly-Anywhere' Products
blocks.text: The first product: pay 6,606 yuan once for the entitlement, then 199 yuan per flight, limited to early-morning and late-night departures, and it blocks school holidays and hot routes. The per-trip cost is rock bottom — great for 'special-forces' style travelers and people who can wake up early or stay up late to grab tickets; hot routes like Shenzhen to Hulunbuir sell out in seconds. A typical case: Shenzhen to Hulunbuir is already an early flight anyway, so 199 yuan is a steal; Cutlass flew 14 trips, and one round trip to Hohhot already paid for the whole pass. As they quoted, a 660-yuan ticket costs just 199 if you can grab it, but there's a time restriction. Compared with the Shunxing Card: the 660 pass books at most three tickets at once (three segments), and changes and refunds cost extra, while the Shunxing Card books unlimited tickets and refunds free seven days ahead. And the Shunxing Card itself: deposit 66,666 yuan with Hainan Airlines for a year, fully refunded at maturity (no interest). In return you get 3,333 points, worth roughly eight economy-class tickets on any route nationwide — including full-fare tickets, summer, and Spring Festival — each equivalent to 379 yuan. title_en: 2026 Summer Camera Roundup: Are These New Cameras Just AI Chum?

blocks.text: 2026 Summer Camera Roundup: Are These New Cameras Just AI Chum?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Hosts Hailu and Jingya round up the 2026 summer camera releases: Fujifilm's 40th-anniversary disposables, Sony's RX10 V and FX5, Panasonic's LUMIX L10, and the rumored Nikon fixed-lens camera. Their core take: in a camera-market winter, the "bridge camera" has become every maker's only lifeline, and new releases look less like innovation and more like feeding the AI — just to stay in the conversation. The only thing actually worth buying, they argue, is the pay-per-shot disposable film experience.

blocks.label: Fujifilm: The Profit-Margin King and a Textbook in Pay-Per-Use
blocks.text: Let's open with Fujifilm. The mechanism: for the 40th anniversary, Fujifilm released the Active (waterproof, 4,480 yen) and the Black & White (4,300 yen, C-41 processed) — essentially an Ilford XP2 reskin with a 50 percent markup. The key insight: the price is pegged to a single manicure or haircut, a hundred or two yuan, so the decision cost is tiny — you never have to calculate how many times a year you'd need to shoot to break even. A typical scene: beach water play, hiking, one-time shooters in girls' group photos — shoot it, and it's gone, no secondhand market. As the hosts put it: "It's about the same price as a manicure trip... people accept pay-per-use very easily." Related concept: unlike film purists who buy rolls and process them, the target users are the "light experience" crowd — not photographers at all. And the campaign, "Unretouched moments hit differently": actor Yoshizawa Ryo shoots a sunset on a hillside, and days later his phone pushes the photos back for a rewatch. It perfectly matches the disposable-film aesthetic of "real, un-PS'd." blocks.text: Next, Sony. The mechanism: a one-inch stacked CMOS — the same sensor as the 2019 RX100 VII — with a 24-600mm f/2.4-4 Zeiss zoom and a non-interchangeable lens. Official price: 15,199 yuan, 3,000 more than the fourth generation in 2017. The key insight: a bridge camera sits between a pro DSLR and a point-and-shoot — for people who want to shoot everything but never change lenses. RX naming: RX1 is full-frame, RX10 mid, RX100 small — the bigger the number, the smaller the sensor. A typical scene: camera-friendly theaters and concerts, birdwatching — though the P1000 is cheaper with more reach — and "frame-chaser" audience members whose phone zooms just aren't enough. As the hosts note: "For people who really chase the frame, one inch seems a bit thin." Compared with Nikon's P1000: that one runs 7,000 to 8,000 yuan with 125x zoom but a smaller sensor; Sony focuses and images better but costs twice as much. blocks.label: Panasonic L10: A Bridge Ambition That Left Its Cheap Self Behind
blocks.text: Now Panasonic. Why: the LX100 II ran 5,000 to 6,000 yuan, while the L10 launches in China at 10,998 — 8,998 at launch — and the body grew from a pocket camera to something aimed straight at Fujifilm's X100 line. The call: if you value a zoom bridge and want a low-key flex, it's worth a look; but the X100VI sits at the same price with a Leica-lens halo and comes out cheaper for what you get. Watch out: the feel in store is solid and dealers will bargain with discounts and freebies, but online channel pricing can actually be higher. title_en: Suntory Oolong's 30-Year Chinese Visual Love Affair: A Dreamland and Women's Growth

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Suntory Oolong's 30-Year Chinese Visual Love Affair: A Dreamland and Women's Growth

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: From 1984 to 2011, every Suntory oolong tea commercial was shot in China, used Chinese models, and told Chinese stories — yet was shown only to Japanese audiences. The program walks through six phases: the Chinese-style illustration period of 1984-1987, the tea-ism and Chinese symbols period of 1987-1990, the peach-blossom paradise period after Ueda Yoshihiko joined in 1991-1994, Chinese women going global in 1995-2005, the sisters' daily life period of 2006-2009, and the Chinese celebrity period of 2010-2011. The core theme: how one Japanese brand shaped a generation of Japanese impressions of China, through Ueda's photography philosophy of 'distance' and the brand spirit of always looking up to something.

blocks.label: Product Positioning: Why Oolong Plus China?
blocks.text: Technically, semi-fermented oolong is the hardest tea to make — you have to stop fermentation exactly halfway. In ancient China it was tribute-grade. Green tea is unfermented, black tea is fully fermented, and even the Japanese never mastered the semi-fermentation in between. From the market side, the whole world knows Fujian makes the best oolong — the rock teas of Wuyishan and Tieguanyin from Anxi are already internationally recognized. So Suntory's origin strategy was naturally tied to China. And the product route was to treat premium tea drinks the way you'd treat whisky: in 1984, nobody in Japan was used to buying bottled tea on the street, so Suntory made it a drink with an overseas label and a sense of premium. China was the obvious home for the brand's story.

blocks.label: Phase 1 (1984-1987): The Chinese-Style 'Grand Gentleman' Illustrations
blocks.text: Art director Kasai Isao originally wanted to shoot on location in China, but from 1984 to 1985 Japanese crews couldn't get entry permits. So he settled for the next best thing: a Qing dynasty official, the 'grand gentleman,' as the protagonist, set against Chinese landscape paintings treated with modern composition. Four years of iteration followed: year one, the gentleman alone; year two, he gains a wife; year three, a family of three; year four, a son-in-law joins to make four — they even studied China's one-child policy on purpose. The image came from Meiji-era posters, a Japanese vision of ancient China straight out of imagination. Since location shoots were impossible, they pivoted to illustration. The family kept growing year after year. Each year added another family member.

blocks.label: Phase 2 (1987-1990): Tea-ism and Chinese Symbols
blocks.text: After getting the permit in 1987, the team rushed into China. They filmed tea-picking women workers in Fujian and scenes of sorting and roasting in the factory — a very direct product-traceability approach. 'Tea-ism': at the time, China was also showing the world its socialist green mountains and rivers and its young women workers happily laboring. It was a two-way cultural display. Then came the 1990 turning point: Kasai grew tired of documentary-style filmmaking, assembled a triangle team — himself, copywriter Ando Takashi, and photographer Ueda Yoshihiko — and began hunting for cultural Chinese symbols, shooting training scenes at an opera theater. blocks.label: Phase 3 (1991-1994): The Peach-Blossom Period — Ueda's Visual Revolution
blocks.text: Why Kasai chose Ueda: he valued the sense of distance in Ueda's photographs — not the traditional advertising look of crisp, reachable lighting, but a feeling of information arriving through an atmosphere from every direction. The language strategy matched: Chinese dialogue and Chinese songs throughout, with no Japanese subtitles — only the last five to ten seconds announce the brand name and slogan in Japanese. This can't-understand-it-but-it's-beautiful distance was itself part of the brand strategy. All the models came from dance academies — natural-faced, tall, slender young women, bigger-built than the average Japanese woman. blocks.label: Phase 4 (1995-2005): Chinese Women Going Global

blocks.label: Phase 5 (2005-2009): A Pivot Under Political Shadows
blocks.text: In 2005, anti-Japan protests broke out in many Chinese cities amid rising tensions after the Koizumi government took office, so Suntory's team couldn't shoot in China and had to fill the ads with old empty footage plus visual effects. The 2006-2009 sisters series then shifted the focus to everyday life — chatting at the dinner table, cooking in the kitchen, ballet practice, mother and daughter having tea. The style shifted from grand, magnificent Chinese landscapes to warm, everyday family scenes — but Chinese elements ran through everything. blocks.label: Phase 6 (2010-2011): The Celebrity Era and the End
blocks.text: Zhang Zhen in 2010, Fan Bingbing in 2010-2011 — Chinese celebrities, cheongsams, Chinese food plus oolong. But the visual style had moved close to the standard playbook of contemporary Japanese food ads: every gesture and emotion of the star in close-up, with the sweeping far-away scenery gone. blocks.label: Walmart's Fresh Choice Remodel: It's the Assortment, Not the Renovation
blocks.text: Walmart didn't just renovate the store — it rebuilt the assortment. The third floor is nearly eighty percent stocked with its own brand, Fresh Choice. The aisle layout is designed like a snake: all the familiar big brands line both sides, while the middle keeps you walking past Fresh Choice the whole way. Shoppers are physically surrounded by the private label. Yet the store looks old and plain. What changed wasn't the lighting or the decor, but the product mix and the price tags. The key insight: what changed wasn't decor or lighting but the assortment itself — the physical layout soaks shoppers in the private label while keeping big brands as anchors of trust. Fresh Choice prices the same packs 10 to 15 percent lower than Hema and Sam's Club, and covers both single-serving mini packs and family bundles with smaller packs inside. What shoppers build with these retailers is essentially a 'trust contract' — you barely hesitate when buying a category you need, while the retailer keeps rotating suppliers to stay fresh. The aisle layout funnels you straight through the private-label shelves. The store layout steers you past their own-brand section no matter which way you go. blocks.label: Private Labels: OEM Repackaging or a Brand Revolution?
blocks.text: There are three paths to private labels. First, born-native brands like Uniqlo and Muji, which control design and the whole process. blocks.text: China's market is big and fast, and each region grows its own model. Serving Shenzhen and serving Jinan are completely different games. title_en: Trekking Tanian Taweng: From a Mountain-Closure Mix-Up to a Tour Operator Survival Guide

title_en: Why Tesla Picked 'Second-Tier' Battery Maker Sunwoda

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Why Tesla Picked 'Second-Tier' Battery Maker Sunwoda

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Three-Dao breaks down why Sunwoda became Tesla's fifth global battery supplier. From a new cooperation model where Sunwoda supplies only battery cells rather than finished modules, to the twin strategies of supply-chain diversification and de-empowering suppliers, he reveals how Tesla — facing falling revenue and halved gross margins — used a 'cheap and compliant' second-tier player to chip away at CATL's pricing power. He also maps the global battery landscape, where Chinese makers now hold a 70% share, and what that means for the balance of power in the industry.

blocks.label: Part 1: Tesla's Battery Chessboard
blocks.text: Let's look at Tesla's battery chessboard. Sunwoda produces LFP battery cells at its Yiwu factory in Zhejiang and ships them to Tesla's Shanghai gigafactory, where Tesla does the module and pack assembly, thermal management, BMS, and final packaging itself — like BMW shipping CATL cells to its Shenyang plant. The shift is from buying finished packs to buying raw cells, which gives Tesla more control over cost, performance, and supply-chain leverage. Models exported to Europe already use Sunwoda cells, while CATL still supplies 40 to 50 percent of Tesla's global procurement. The two reasons are simple: first, cheap — Sunwoda's 9.77 percent gross margin is less than half of CATL's 23.84 percent; second, compliant — second-tier players accept lower conditions, station teams on-site, and even hand over technology. The mechanism: Sunwoda produces LFP battery cells at its Yiwu factory in Zhejiang and ships them to Tesla's Shanghai gigafactory, where Tesla does the module and pack assembly, thermal management, BMS, and final packaging itself — a model similar to how BMW ships CATL cells to its Shenyang plant for assembly. The insight: Tesla is shifting from buying finished battery packs to buying raw cells, which gives it more control over cost, performance, and supply-chain leverage. Suppliers used to sell finished products; now they sell raw material. Typical case: models like the Model Y exported to Europe use Sunwoda cells, while CATL still supplies most of the LFP batteries at home and abroad — 40% to 50% of Tesla's global procurement. As the host puts it: 'Sunwoda's current cooperation with Tesla is that it only supplies the most basic LFP cells — note, cells, not batteries.' Related concepts: this is a completely different depth of cooperation from CATL's 'direct module supply to the car line,' and a step toward the ultimate ideal of Tesla's in-house 4680 battery — 'growing your own vegetables and cooking your own meals.' Three-Dao boils it down to two reasons. First, cheap: Sunwoda runs a small-margin, high-volume model, with a power-battery gross margin around 9.77% — less than half of CATL's 23.84%. Second, compliant: second-tier players negotiate from a weaker position, so they accept lower conditions, station teams on-site, let the carmaker control core processes, and even give up technology. Tesla is shifting from finished packs to raw cells. Instead of buying the sandwich, Tesla now buys the ingredients. Second-tier suppliers negotiate from a weaker position. Smaller players have to be more accommodating. They run on small margins and high volume. It's a low-margin, high-volume play.

blocks.label: Part 2: Tesla's Results Force a Cost Crackdown
blocks.text: Tesla's results are forcing the cost crackdown. The Model Y was the best-selling single model in the world, gas cars included, but revenue fell 3 percent for the first time ever, net profit plunged 46 percent, and deliveries fell two years in a row. Auto gross margin was halved from about 30 percent to 15.4 percent, and China market share slipped from 6 percent to 4.9 percent. With Optimus and Robotaxi burning cash, the car business is the cash cow. And battery cost is over 30 percent of the vehicle — so the first cut has to be there. Meanwhile CATL is printing money: 423.7 billion yuan in revenue, a 39.2 percent global share for nine straight years, and a battery margin higher than Tesla's whole-car margin. That's the pricing power Tesla wants to crack. The mechanism: the Model Y was the best-selling single model worldwide, gas cars included — yet revenue fell 3%, its first drop ever, net profit plunged 46% year over year to 3.794 billion dollars, and deliveries fell for two straight years to 1.636 million vehicles. The insight: auto gross margin was halved from about 30% in 2021 to 15.4% excluding carbon credits; China market share fell from 6% to 4.9%, and price cuts can't bring back the peak. Optimus and Robotaxi keep burning cash, so the car business is the cash cow that funds everything. Typical case: cutting unprofitable Model S and X — models with symbolic status, from falcon-wing doors to China's first celebrity owners — and turning fully to cost minimization. As the host says: 'Battery cost is about 30% of the whole car's cost — probably more than 30%.' Related concept: battery cost at over 30% of the vehicle is the first cut for cost reduction; bringing in Sunwoda is the inevitable choice under margin pressure. CATL's 2025 results: revenue of 423.7 billion yuan, up 17%; net profit of 72.2 billion, up 42%; a global share of 39.2%, first for nine straight years, with installed capacity about 2.4 times BYD's. Its power-battery gross margin of 23.84% runs 5 to 15 percentage points above peers — higher than Tesla's whole-car margin. Margins were halved. Profits were cut in half. The car business is the cash cow. Cars are what fund the moonshot projects. Battery is the first cost to cut. The easiest savings sit in the battery.

blocks.label: Part 3: The Global Battery Market Reshuffles
blocks.text: The global battery market is reshuffling. Installations hit 1,187 gigawatt-hours in 2025, up 31.7 percent, and six of the top ten makers are Chinese, together holding 70.4 percent — up from 60.4 percent in 2022. Gotion grew 82.5 percent, the fastest of all. Meanwhile the Japanese-Korean trio fell to a combined 15.3 percent, and Samsung SDI was the only maker in negative growth. Chinese makers are also building plants in Europe, so Japan and Korea can't even run away. The reasons are clear: they missed China's boom, the West is cooling — US EV sales fell 2 percent in 2025 — they bet on premium NMC while LFP blew past 50 percent penetration, and they depend too much on single customers like Tesla's Model Y. The mechanism: global EV battery installations hit 1,187 GWh in 2025, up 31.7%. Six of the top ten are Chinese — CATL, BYD, CALB, Gotion, EVE Energy, and Svolt — together holding 70.4% of the market, up from 60.4% in 2022. The insight: Chinese makers grew 30% to 80%, outpacing the market, with Gotion the fastest at 82.5%. The Japanese-Korean trio of LG, SK, and Samsung fell to a combined 15.3%, down 3.4 points, and Samsung SDI was the only one in negative growth at minus 6.9%. Typical case: domestic EVs can't use Japanese or Korean cells — for reasons of sentiment, value, and supply-chain completeness — so Japan and Korea can only go to Europe and America, where Chinese makers are building plants to grab share anyway. As the host says: 'Six of the top ten in the global battery market are Chinese makers... together crossing 70.4% market share.' Related facts: CATL holds nearly 40% of the European market with its Germany plant at full capacity, while Sunwoda is pushing localization at its Hungary factory. Why they're falling: first, they miss out on China's EV boom; second, electrification is cooling in the West — US EV sales fell 2% in 2025, the first drop in a decade; third, they bet on the premium NMC route, losing the mid-and-low end once LFP passed 50% penetration in 2024; fourth, they depend too much on single customers — Panasonic and LG lean heavily on Tesla's Model Y. Chinese makers are outpacing the global market. They're growing faster than the overall market. They missed out on China's EV boom. The China windfall never reached them. Relying on one customer is fragile. Too many eggs in one basket.

title_en: Vol.331 Thinking, Fast and Slow: Why Does My Brain Keep Fooling Me?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Vol.331 Thinking, Fast and Slow: Why Does My Brain Keep Fooling Me?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Three hosts from the Wenhua Youxian podcast revisit Daniel Kahneman's Nobel-winning classic. System One, the fast intuition, handles 95% of daily decisions; System Two, the slow reasoner, is inherently lazy and mostly just rubber-stamps. From anchoring and loss aversion to the peak-end rule, they show how the brain fails in systematic, predictable ways — and how awareness plus a checklist of questions can push back against irrationality.

blocks.label: Part One: The Two-System Framework
blocks.text: System One is the unconscious fast thinking that runs on its own, great at intuitive association and emotional reaction, handling 95 to 96 percent of daily decisions. System Two is the effortful, energy-burning slow logic that handles complex calculations, but it's lazy by nature and mostly just rubber-stamps System One's conclusions. So the deliberation you think you're doing has, 95 percent of the time, already been done by System One — System Two only confirms it afterwards. Listening to a podcast runs on System One; the moment someone asks you what 17 times 24 is, System Two wakes up. Dayi joked that System Two's laziness is like a mountain of a father: it doesn't move. blocks.text: We don't evaluate gains and losses by their absolute amount, but by change relative to a reference point. blocks.label: Social Distance and How We Perceive Body Odor
blocks.text: Let's start with the basics: only body odor within social distance, about half a meter to one and a half, becomes a problem. Something you smell riding past in the distance has nothing to do with you. And among all body odors, bad breath is the most damaging within social distance. Underarm smell barely travels unless it's extremely strong, but smelly feet can cut right through a cubicle wall. Think of the typical scenes: the subway, the office, waiting rooms, and close relationships. As the hosts say, bad breath is actually the biggest nuisance for people, while underarm odor, unless extremely strong, doesn't affect that many people. Interestingly, pandemic-era mask wearing made people more sensitive to their own body odor. Lili spent a Monday morning at the hospital, and nearly everyone had bad breath — it crushed her appetite and her goodwill toward the world. People wearing masks gave off no smell at all, and she wished she hadn't given up that barrier after the pandemic. blocks.text: Next, the biology. Eccrine glands, all over the body and on the soles, secrete odorless sweat. And here's a neat indicator: sweaty ears mean developed apocrine glands, which correlates with the likelihood of underarm odor. blocks.label: Everyday Habits That Make Odor Worse
blocks.text: Now, the everyday habits that quietly make it worse. The cause is simple: you shower clean but put on worn clothes, synthetic fibers don't breathe, sheets dry in the shade, and rooms are poorly ventilated — odors ferment and pile up on the fabric. blocks.label: The Scientific Odor-Reduction Checklist
blocks.text: So here's the scientific odor-reduction checklist. One: thoroughly wash the apocrine-rich areas — underarms, ear canals, perineum — with body wash, not just a rinse of water. Their shared conclusion: pure rational consumption doesn't exist — the end of rationality is individuality. The same big project-type expense flows to completely different places — for Eric a Disney cruise, for Shixin desert hardship and rock climbing, for Haoyue game recharges and tech gear. title_en: When I Stopped Letting Work Define Me: 5 Ordinary People Rebuild Their Sense of Worth

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: When I Stopped Letting Work Define Me: 5 Ordinary People Rebuild Their Sense of Worth

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Host Yubai collected listener stories: beyond work and income, what holds up your sense of worth? Five ordinary people — screenwriter Xiaoyang, state-owned-enterprise employee 313, debt survivor Xiaomao, big-tech worker Gaifan, and restaurateur Lao Li — each rebuild a self no longer defined by their job title, through companionship, care, honesty, hobbies, and a deliberate choice. Facing burnout, animal rescue, financial crisis, job-hunting anxiety, and a fork in the road, their stories form a quiet argument that value lives in who we are when no one is grading us.

blocks.label: Story 1: Xiaoyang the Screenwriter — From Workaholic to Father
blocks.text: The first story is Xiaoyang the screenwriter. He left a small Henan town where writing paid the bills, and entered the TV industry in 2017 after seeing his partner's comfortable life — complete with 36-yuan cat food cans. From ghostwriter to credited writer, his worth was chained to writing a great script and sitting at the head table. But last year, burnout plus becoming a new parent plus his mother's worsening illness pushed him to cut back on projects and move the eight-member family — four cats and a dog — back to Xinxiang. His daughter's first roll-over showed him how hard life works for a single moment. As he puts it: in the end, no problem really got solved — but they're still here for each other. The mechanism: Xiaoyang left a small Henan town where writing helped pay the bills, and entered the TV industry in 2017 after seeing his partner's comfortable life — complete with 36-yuan cat food cans. From ghostwriter to credited screenwriter, his sense of worth stayed chained to 'writing a great script, becoming a big name, sitting at the head table.' The insight: last year, burnout plus becoming a new parent and his mother's worsening illness pushed him to cut back on projects and move the eight-member family — four cats and a dog — from Shanghai back to Xinxiang. His daughter's first roll-over showed him that 'life works so hard for a single roll,' dissolving the self-exploitation of the idea that parenthood must fit into a 'complete life.' Typical moment: when creative passion fades and family needs you, pull 'who I am' out of the industry's judgment and point it at family time that can't be repeated. 'In the end, it's like no problem really got solved — but we're still here for each other.' Related concept: a screenwriter's income splits into 'humiliation pay, criticism pay, and creation pay' — versus the audience's assumption that writers hold the creative power of 'the script is the foundation.' The three parts of the paycheck: humiliation pay for balancing everyone's opinions, criticism pay for the backlash every broadcast brings, and pay for serious creation. A screenwriter is an 'emotional masseur' — late-stage revisions often drift far from the original intent, but keeping everyone calm comes first. His sense of worth was chained to his career. He tied his identity to being a big-name writer. We didn't solve anything, but we showed up for each other. Sometimes presence matters more than progress. His pay splits three ways — humiliation, criticism, and creation. Part of the fee is basically for absorbing abuse.

blocks.label: Story 2: 313 — 'I Am a Good Person'
blocks.text: The second story is 313, a construction SOE employee. For seven years, the startup-phase team was united on goals and reviewing upward. Then management changed, and new superiors who don't understand the business used their authority to push people down — the harder you work, the more you take on, and the more likely you are to be sacrificed. This made her ask: if doing more just gets you blamed, what's the point of being conscientious? Her worth became simple — 'I am a good person.' She adopts stray dogs, rescues injured cats, and the little white dog became the matchmaker that brought her a partner. Because in a bureaucratic SOE, relationships can outweigh the work itself: when it goes well, it's the leader's ability; when it goes wrong, it's frontline execution. The mechanism: seven years at a construction SOE, with a startup-period team united on goals and reviewing upward. Last year the management changed; new superiors who don't understand the business started using their authority to push people down, and those who work hard take on more responsibility only to be sacrificed. The insight: 313 always knew work was only part of her life's value, but this incident made her ask 'if doing more just gets you blamed, what's the point of being conscientious?' Her sense of worth became simply: 'I am a good person' — she adopts stray dogs, rescues injured cats, and she and her partner built a home for six cats and dogs. Typical story: the pets needed more space, so she rushed to a bigger rental, then bought a home. The little white dog was the 'matchmaker's red thread' that brought in a partner who vibes with her. 'Apart from that, my biggest value is being a good person.' In an economic downturn inside a bureaucratic SOE, relationships can outweigh the work itself. If a thing goes well, it's the leader's ability; if it goes wrong, it's the frontline's execution that failed. 'Should people who do their work conscientiously be treated like this?' Do more, get blamed more. You can't win: hard work gets punished, silence gets praised. What's the point of being conscientious? Why bother being diligent when it backfires? The dog became the matchmaker. That little white dog led her to her partner.

blocks.label: Story 3: Xiaomao — Twice Into Online Debt, and Learning to Tell the Truth
blocks.text: The third story is Xiaomao, twice into online debt. She did well in school in a small county town, but her divorced parents kept pulling her into money disputes, and she desperately wanted to be independent and respectable. The loan apps ran a smooth combo: a few hundred yuan in installments looks payable, then you borrow to repay, until it reached nearly 300,000 yuan. She couldn't face the full statement. The first time, her father refused to help; she confessed to her mother and they pulled the bills together. The second time, she only came clean after her credit was drained and the chain broke. The real turning point: admitting 'I can't solve this alone.' Yubai asks listeners not to rush to judgment — the question is why she kept sinking in, and how she finally started asking for help. The mechanism: she did well in school in a small county town, but her divorced parents kept pulling her into money disputes, and she desperately wanted to be independent and respectable. The loan apps run a 'smooth combo': a few hundred yuan in installments looks payable, then you borrow to repay, and twice it added up to nearly 300,000 yuan. She couldn't face the full statement, dreaming that 'a 15,000-yuan job would cover it.' The insight: the first time she asked her father for help and was refused; she confessed to her mother and they pulled the bills together. The second time, she only came clean after her credit was drained and the borrow-to-repay chain broke. Admitting 'I can't solve this alone' is where escaping the trap actually begins. Typical moment: on repayment day the credit runs out and no platform will lend another yuan — you're forced to face reality. Pitfalls to avoid: borrowing to repay, refusing to total the accounts, and using spending to keep up the 'smart and respectable' persona. How to act: confess to someone you trust — her cousin first, then her mother; list every platform's bill and every expense; and make a monthly plan to save and repay. Yubai asks listeners not to rush to judgment — the story worth hearing isn't just how much she owed, but why she kept sinking into the same trap the same way, and how she finally started admitting she needed other people's help. Borrowing to repay the old debt. He was robbing Peter to pay Paul. She couldn't face the full statement. She avoided adding up the real number. Admitting you need help is the first step. Saying 'I can't do this alone' is where it starts.

blocks.label: Story 4: Gaifan — Job-Hunting Anxiety and a West Lake Sunset
blocks.text: The fourth story is Gaifan, a 2024 liberal-arts graduate. Pandemic-era online classes left her with almost no internships, so her entire worth was tied to finding a job. She landed a big-tech offer — but work stress wrecked her health, and she had surgery alone. Still groggy from anesthesia, she sat on a bench by West Lake on a weekday evening and watched the sunset: mandarin ducks in pairs, wild ducks, squirrels, an old man singing. 'So a weekday evening can be this beautiful too.' She realized she'd gained a good job but lost a lot along the way. Her family had hidden her grandmother's terminal cancer out of concern for her; she found out only when she rushed home. Her grandmother, still traveling Europe at over 80, made her see life's fragility — and the urgency of being present. The mechanism: a 2024 liberal-arts graduate whose pandemic-era online classes left her with almost no internships, so all her worth was tied to landing a job. After getting a big-tech offer, work stress wrecked her health and she had surgery alone. The insight: still groggy from the anesthesia, she sat on a bench by West Lake on a weekday evening and watched the sunset — pairs of mandarin ducks, wild ducks, squirrels, an old man singing. 'So a weekday evening can be this beautiful too.' She realized she'd gained a good job but lost a lot along the way. Typical story: hobbies — sports, drawing, photography, travel, podcasts — got squeezed to the edge by job hunting and work; and her grandmother's late-stage illness was kept from her, which she only discovered when she rushed home. How to act: bring back piano practice, sports, and photography; accept that 'work is not the only urgent and important thing.' Her family hid her grandmother's terminal cancer out of concern for her state; when she rushed home and finished practicing piano, her mother broke down and told her. Her grandmother, still traveling Europe at over 80, made her see life's fragility and the urgency of being present. 'It felt like fate was playing a very, very cruel joke on me.' All her worth was tied to landing a job. Her self-esteem rode entirely on one offer. A weekday evening can be beautiful too. Beauty doesn't clock out on workdays. She gained a job but lost a lot along the way. The offer came at a price she didn't notice.

blocks.label: Story 5: Lao Li — The First Choice He Made Himself
blocks.text: The fifth story is Lao Li, and it's about his first deliberate choice. Born in 1997, he studied in America because his mother decided, majored in linguistics because his counselor chose it, and stayed in Shanghai because an ex lived there. From 3,000 yuan a month in a small county to his first 200,000 and then a million in revenue, he rested half a day a week and numbed the stress with alcohol. In April 2025, he ended his Shanghai restaurant career. Using Naval's three decisions — city, career, partner — plus Munger-style inversion: if you don't know what you want, first remove what you don't. Shanghai wasn't the answer, but he didn't know where the answer was, so he took the first step: back to Chengdu. As he says, he'd never once listened fully to his heart and acted on it. The mechanism: born in 1997, he studied in the US — his mother decided on studying abroad, and his counselor picked the school and the linguistics major — then worked in Shanghai restaurants because an ex lived there. From a 3,000-yuan monthly salary in a small county to his first 200,000 and then a million in revenue, he rested half a day a week and numbed the stress with alcohol. The insight: in April 2025 he ended his Shanghai restaurant career, using Naval Ravikant's 'three decisions' — city, career, and partner — plus Munger-style inversion: if you don't know what you want, first remove what you don't. Shanghai wasn't the answer, but neither did he know where the answer was, so he took the first step of leaving for Chengdu. Typical moment: the relationship ended, the work ended, every reason to stay in Shanghai disappeared — and for the first time he 'gave himself to the flow of life.' 'Never once in my life did I listen fully to my heart, give myself an answer, and act on it.' A typical day: a 9 a.m. meeting with finance, procurement, the head chef, and the owner rotating in; prep by 10:30; service from 11:30 to 2 p.m.; then from 2 p.m. on, planning pop-up events and designing menus, often working until 11 p.m., with half a day off each week. 'What determines most of the quality of most people's lives comes down to just three decisions: where you live, what you do, and who you're with.' His life was decided by other people. Every major turn was chosen for him. If you don't know what you want, rule out what you don't. Inversion: subtract instead of add. Three decisions shape most of life's quality. Where you live, what you do, who you're with.

blocks.label: Practice · 练习
blocks.text: Nothing got solved, but we were here for each other — and that was enough. Borrowing to repay the old loans is a trap with no exit. The job offer came at a price she didn't notice until it was too late. When you don't know what you want, start by ruling out what you don't.

blocks.label: Pitfalls · 常见错误
blocks.text: My biggest value is being a good person. He was borrowing to repay the old loans — robbing Peter to pay Paul. She gained a good job, but it came at a price she didn't notice. Never once did I listen fully to my heart and act on it.

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Xia Zheng, founder of Yinian Caomu and a former VP at Affu essential oils, sits down with hosts CK and Iris to take apart China's tea market through nine questions: a trillion-yuan scale that stays extremely fragmented, why Lipton lost China, the real relationship between unsweetened tea and freshly made tea drinks, the Pu'er financialization scam, and how a loose-leaf tea brand carves its own path in the bad-money-drives-out-good environment of Douyin — through flavor naming and high consumer involvement.

blocks.label: Industry Basics: Big But Not Strong
blocks.text: Let's start with the industry basics. The loose-leaf tea market was about 350 billion yuan in 2024, yet it barely appears in brokerage reports — only a handful of public companies like Lancang Ancient Tea and Bama, and Chali is still on the edge of delisting. The key insight: the claim that 70,000 tea companies can't match Lipton dates to 2001, when China's tea output was over 30 billion yuan versus Lipton's global 30-plus billion. Even today, China's top ten loose-leaf brands still trail Lipton globally — but mainly because Chinese brands only play domestically while Lipton plays worldwide, much like Chinese box office versus Hollywood's global box office. A typical scene: when evaluating tea investments, don't just look at GMV — look at brand concentration, supply-chain integration, and consumer trust cost. As the guests say, this industry has no small size — it's actually huge — but it has almost no presence. Compared with coffee, the pattern is coffee at home equals tea abroad; China's bigger opportunity for tea may lie overseas, where it once made up a third of export trade. The cause is structural: around 10 million tea farmers plus a million tea enterprises means an extremely low entry barrier. The household responsibility system left production expansion uncontrolled — blueberries and Shine Muscat grapes are the cautionary tales. Division of labor is weak; a farmer who grows, processes, and sells it all himself is still trusted. blocks.label: Tea's Four-Layer Structure and the Brand Opportunity

China's brand opportunity sits in the flavor and culture layers, not the functional one. As Xia Zheng says, let's put the food-value attribute aside — flavor has nothing to rationalize; it is experience, pure experience. The core mechanism: the closer a lightly processed agricultural product is to its origin, the harder it is to brand — think German home-brewed beer or coffee beans from a Brazilian friend. Europe grows no tea, which is why Lipton could become a global brand. With over a million tea enterprises in China, buying channels are so numerous they smother brands. title_en: Why Is Everyone Raving About XPeng's Gen-2 VLA?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Why Is Everyone Raving About XPeng's Gen-2 VLA?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: This episode takes three deep cuts at XPeng's second-generation VLA world model: the generational leap from VLA 1.0 'understanding what you see' to 2.0 'insight'; a comparison of four tech routes from Huawei, Nvidia, Li Auto, and Yuanrong Qixing; and how interpretability rebuilds public trust in autonomous driving. The core argument: sensing isn't understanding, and action isn't reasoning — the real question is whether the car can predict intent and explain itself in human language.

blocks.label: What Is VLA? From 'Seeing' to 'Understanding' to 'Insight'
blocks.text: The core mechanism: a Vision-Language-Action model — it first 'sees' the road, uses 'language' to describe and understand it, then 'executes' the driving action, fusing perception, reasoning, and decision-making into one. The key insight: nearly every on-device end-to-end autonomous driving campaign slaps on a VLA label, but the depth of implementation varies wildly. Cars with lidar use fused perception; cars without lidar go pure vision — at the core, everything is vision-based. A typical scene: complex intersection games, unmarked roads, construction detours — open scenarios with no standard answer, 'semi-open questions.' As the episode put it: sensing doesn't equal understanding — just seeing something doesn't mean you understand it; and action doesn't equal reasoning — a pure reflex is a hard shot, not thinking. Related concept: end-to-end doesn't equal VLA; VLA is an advanced form of end-to-end with an added language reasoning layer. The three stages: stage one, rule hard-coding — like memorizing a dictionary; if the question isn't in the bank, the car freezes. title_en: Ep.007 Growth Is Loosening the 'Self' I Thought I Knew, Feat. Yang Tianzhen

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Ep.007 Growth Is Loosening the 'Self' I Thought I Knew, Feat. Yang Tianzhen

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Shao Yibo talks with Yang Tianzhen. "Being yourself" is far harder than just being willful — the core question is figuring out who the "self" actually is. The shell, or social persona, can be put on and taken off like armor; the true self only shows in limited spaces. The pursuit of "truth" is the source of all one's energy, and growth is a five-stage journey of loosening rigid self-concepts, driven by crisis or by vision.

blocks.label: What Is the "Self"?
blocks.text: Let's start with the question itself. The mechanism: "being yourself" is made of "being" and "yourself." "Being" means aligning knowledge with action; "yourself" is the awareness you notice in meditation, the thoughts you dare not speak in real life — which layer is the true self? The key insight: the self is a dynamic concept that gets overturned and rebuilt many times. What you once believed was your "true thought" may only be a phrasing — beneath it could be moral judgment or fear. A typical scene: when you discover "I actually care what people think" or "I actually want intimacy," that's not failure — it's the beginning of loosening something rigid. The original line: "Figuring out the definition of yourself might be the first step to being yourself. But the self is a dynamic thing." The related concept: the difference from "willfulness," "persona," and "social image" — willfulness is escape; being yourself is expression after awareness. And Yang Tianzhen's own shift: she used to think she was valuable only when sharing career tips; later she realized her greatest value is simply "living well" — loving herself from the heart, unafraid of controversy, and sharing the process of exploration. Criticism doesn't move her, and praise doesn't either. The mechanism: "being yourself" is made of "being" and "yourself." Criticism doesn't move her, and praise doesn't either. Being yourself is harder than it sounds. It's not about being willful — it's about knowing who you are. Loosen the grip of old beliefs about yourself. Unfreeze the identity you built.

blocks.label: The Shell, the True Self, and the "Flower Key"
blocks.text: Next, the shell. The mechanism: the shell we build from childhood lets us meet the expectations of parents, teachers, and social settings — it helps us survive and avoid hurt. But the shell also limits feeling — Shao Yibo once lived behind an "emotionless" shell, blind to the scenery and unable to understand his daughter's tears. The key insight: the shell never fully dissolves, and it doesn't have to. The goal is not to mistake the shell for yourself — treat it like armor you can put on and take off. The true self holds unlimited love, courage, and compassion. A typical scene: put on the shell in hostile environments to protect yourself; take it off in safe spaces to reconnect with the true self. The original line: "We shouldn't be putty — we should be a fixed skeleton that can wear many pretty outfits." Yang Tianzhen uses the Flower Fairy's magic key as an analogy: playing different roles in different settings isn't hypocrisy — the true self needs protection and only shows in limited spaces, before limited people. And the reason: the shell is fragile and needs constant upkeep; cruel blows either shatter it or make it thicken and harden, cutting you off from the true self for 20 to 50 years. blocks.label: The Pursuit of "Truth"
blocks.text: Now the pursuit of truth. "Truth" isn't a subjective definition, nor a camera's objective shot — it's what people privately know to be the case between them. Relationships must face the truth; everything fake isn't worth investing in and will shatter anyway. The boundary: truth is only known to those involved and those who shared the experience; the way you deliver it can be practiced — Yang Tianzhen once learned how to say "the ship is sinking" more responsibly. Her own words: "There's something pulling me through life, and it may be the source of all my energy — it's your pursuit of truth." How to apply it: stop performing as someone else in intimate relationships; the truth may not land as expected, but the price of pretending is total exhaustion. The mechanism: Yang Tianzhen once feared "melting love" — the self dissolving without boundaries — and showed aggression and "I don't need it." Deep down she feared not getting it and not knowing how to handle it, wrapping it in the persona that "love wastes your life." The key insight: admitting "I also deeply want this melting love" takes enormous courage — admitting it to yourself, and even more, admitting it in public. blocks.text: Then the five stages. Yang Tianzhen adds: breaking rigid beliefs is risky — the sense of safety vanishes, confidence wobbles, and some people retreat while others push further forward. The reason: 90 percent of the drive comes from the crisis of "can't accept the status quo"; only 10 percent is vision-driven, and that's hard to sustain. The solution: start with small changes to get a taste of payoff and freedom, then drive bigger changes; accept that new anxiety will surface along the way — Shao Yibo admits his anxiety lasted half a year. Severity: negligible — no crisis doesn't mean you can't start; curiosity is also a doorway in. blocks.text: Finally, relationships. Then the airplane oxygen-mask principle: in an emergency, take care of yourself first, then others if you have anything left. Protecting only yourself is selfish, but protecting yourself first is guarding your energy. As one line puts it: "Small daily kindnesses — kindness with genuine intent. When the intention differs, the whole act differs." Now she sees that accepting someone's kindness matters more than eating the meal you had in mind. A good relationship aims for "you're happy, and so am I" — not "only I'm happy." blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: In one sentence: Yao Shunyu — a physics PhD who came to AI midway, working on Claude 3.7/4.5 and Gemini 3 training — spent nearly four hours telling it straight that the industry has entered a 'collectivist era': once model capabilities flatten out, the bet is on defining the problem; reliability beats genius; shells can't escape the model's gravity; and pre-training is far from done.

blocks.label: Industry Landscape: From Chasing Capability to Betting on Definitions
blocks.text: A year ago, everyone worried about whether they could catch OpenAI. Now none of the three — OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google — worries about falling behind. The harder thing is figuring out what to build, and that's a bet that requires human insight. On paper, the models have become highly similar: on benchmarks like SWE-bench, the gaps are mostly within one or two points of noise. But real usage still differs: Claude excels at agentic and tool-calling work, Codex is catching up in pure coding, and Gemini shines in reasoning and everyday scenarios. So when choosing a model, don't just read the leaderboard — test it against your actual use case. In the end, the most important trait in this industry isn't a big brain; it's being reliable. The era of individual heroism is over — we're all surfers now, and the wave is the real story. A year ago, everyone worried about whether they could catch up with OpenAI. We're all surfers now, and the real story is the wave, not the surfer. The benchmark gaps are basically noise. The leaderboard differences are within the margin of error. Reliability beats brilliance. Give me dependable over dazzling any day.

blocks.text: Scaling laws still hold, and pre-training is far from saturated. The bottleneck has shifted from raw compute to data quality, problem definition, and training details — many model differences come from engineering details you'd never imagine, like GitHub data being naturally higher quality. One way to see it: pre-training is also a form of reinforcement learning — train with finite context, then use it as if the context were infinite. This doesn't apply to small teams that have stopped scaling, but for leading labs it's still the main battlefield. GitHub gives you naturally high-quality, verifiable data; code can be automatically checked by compiling and testing, which closes an RL loop; and agents writing code make the product simpler — around 90 percent of Google's internal code is now generated by models. blocks.text: Zhang Xiaoyu, founder of Youzhiyouxing, returns to the podcast after five years in hiding.
