title_en: Smart Glasses: A Buying & Disillusionment Guide — with Zhang Yan, Xu Ran, Dongdong Qiang & Beiming Cheng Haisheng

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Smart Glasses: A Buying & Disillusionment Guide — with Zhang Yan, Xu Ran, Dongdong Qiang & Beiming Cheng Haisheng

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Four guests — an edge-computing engineer, a heavy power user, and media people — take a sharp, unsparing look at smart glasses, AR, VR, and XR. They dismantle the fake demand, the 'Douzhir economy' where everyone takes a sip but few order another, and the trap of end-to-end family-bucket strategies. Then the show slides into a philosophical abyss about AI cyber-immortality and the value of the human body. It all ends with one brutally practical piece of advice: have your kids learn massage.

blocks.label: Part 1: The Concepts — What Actually Differs Between AR, VR, and XR
blocks.text: Here are the definitions: VR is fully wrapped, eyes-covered immersion; AR overlays information on the real world; XR is the mixed reality in between. But the market reality is that surviving products look more like 'headphones hung on your nose' than the all-day AR interface from sci-fi films. The technical categories are clean, but user perception is blurry. Lightweight products like Thunderbird take the audio-plus-light-display route; the Vision Pro goes for high-end VR with passthrough, but you're exhausted in half an hour, you can't take it on the street, and there's almost no 3D content. VR suits fixed-scene gaming like flight simulators or skiing; AR's ideal scene is navigation and information overlay, but the cameras and displays aren't there yet; audio glasses suit commuting with podcasts. 'In the end, everyone making VR glasses is doing it for a jar of vinegar… after half an hour, your head feels squeezed.' See-through was built as a window to the outside world for VR — they call it making a whole dumpling feast for a single jar of vinegar. And Zhang Yan's company does edge computing that turns 2D videos into 3D in real time — but with glasses stock running low and demo units loaned out, hardware supply chains are still the bottleneck. The core mechanism: VR is fully wrapped, eyes-covered immersion; AR overlays information onto the real world; XR is the mixed reality in between. But the market reality is that surviving products often look more like 'headphones hanging off your nose' than the all-day AR interface from sci-fi. The key insight: the technical categories are clear, but user perception is blurry. Lightweight products like Thunderbird take the audio-plus-light-display route; the Vision Pro takes the high-end VR plus passthrough route, but you're exhausted after half an hour, you can't take it out on the street, and there's very little 3D content. In the author's own words: 'In the end, everyone making VR glasses is doing it for a jar of vinegar… after half an hour, your head feels squeezed.' A related idea: See Through was built as a channel to the outside world for VR — the guests call it 'making a whole dumpling feast for a jar of vinegar': the core need is immersion, and passthrough is just a patch. Zhang Yan's company does edge computing, and its core capability is turning traditional 2D videos (like Tom and Jerry) into dual-eye 3D in real time. Converting theaters to 3D used to be a huge project; now a small box can do it — but with glasses stock running low and demo units loaned out, hardware supply chains are still the bottleneck. They're making a whole dumpling feast for a jar of vinegar. All that engineering for a tiny niche of a need. These products are basically headphones hanging off your nose. It's less a glasses story and more an audio story.

blocks.label: Part 2: The Transition Trap — Why Not to Buy Right Now
blocks.text: Many AI gadgets live in a transition phase, the 'tell AI to do it for you' stage. It's like the Jiyue car that removed every physical button — cool on paper, but when you need to turn off the air conditioning or adjust the volume, you have to dig through menus, and the experience becomes anti-human. So wait until the final form is clear: either a pure audio glasses (clear demand), or AR display with a mature ecosystem (at least three to five years). Don't pay full price for a 'maybe in the future.' It's risky — you'll probably buy it and let it gather dust, but it's not fatal. As one guest says: 'You didn't remove the physical buttons for the sake of removing them; you removed them because it really can drive itself. If autonomous driving were done well, removing them would be fine — but the in-between state is neither done well nor kept, and that's what's so uncomfortable.' Zhang Yan uses Beijing's fermented Douzhir to describe the market: everyone is curious enough for one sip, but very few drink it daily. Capital loves a sexy full-stack story of display plus computing plus AI; display makers can't raise money without computing, so they're forced to burn cash on what they're bad at. The reason: many AI hardware products are stuck in the transition stage of 'having AI do things for you' — like the Jiyue car that removed all physical buttons: the product concept is cool, but when you need to turn off the AC or adjust the volume, you have to dig through menus, and the experience becomes anti-human. title_en: Vol.65 How Long Does It Take to Lose 1kg of Fat? How Do You Actually Lose Fat?

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Vol.65 How Long Does It Take to Lose 1kg of Fat? How Do You Actually Lose Fat?

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Elijah, a world champion kettlebell athlete and strength coach, breaks down fat loss through biochemistry: 84 percent of fat leaves the body as carbon dioxide; the 7,700-calorie formula is wildly imprecise once metabolic adaptation, glycogen water, and measurement error kick in; the scale is a high-noise signal; exercise matters more for preserving muscle than for burning calories; and the framework that actually works is a small deficit plus high protein, strength training, sleep, and periodization.

blocks.label: Where Does Fat Go? Breathing Is the Main Exit
blocks.text: The mechanism: about 87 percent of body fat is triglycerides. When the body needs energy, adrenaline and glucagon trigger lipolysis, and free fatty acids enter the mitochondria for aerobic oxidation, producing ATP, water, and carbon dioxide. The CO2 leaves through your lungs; the water leaves through urine and sweat. The key insight: a 2014 BMJ study asked more than 150 doctors where fat goes when you lose it, and 98 percent got it wrong — the most common answer being 'it turns into energy.' The right answer: you breathe it out as CO2. To oxidize more fat, you want a low-insulin environment plus enough mitochondrial oxidizing capacity from aerobic training and preserved muscle. As Elijah says, you literally breathe your fat out — this is not a metaphor, it's a literal chemical reaction. One gram of pure fat oxidizes to about nine kilocalories, and one kilogram of fat tissue contains roughly 870 grams of triglycerides — about 7,830 kilocalories, close to the classic 7,700. But as a practical tool, the human body is not a calorie calculator. The mechanism: about 87 percent of body fat is triglycerides. The body isn't a simple calorie spreadsheet. You can't just do the math — the body doesn't follow the formula.

blocks.label: Metabolic Adaptation: Your Body Is Smarter Than You
blocks.text: The setup: fourteen reality-show contestants dieted extremely and trained hard, losing 58 kilograms on average. Six years later almost all of them regained the weight, and their resting metabolism was still about 500 kilocalories a day lower than people of the same weight who never dieted — the body remembers the starvation history and keeps saving energy. Adaptation has three layers. First, resting metabolism drops beyond what the weight loss itself explains. Second, NEAT, non-exercise activity thermogenesis, collapses, which can cancel out more than half of your calorie deficit. Third, leptin falls and ghrelin rises, and that appetite surge can't be fought with willpower alone. Every aggressive diet lowers your metabolic floor a little more, so when you stop dieting, the body thinks it's entered a calorie surplus. The fix: a small deficit of about 300 kilocalories a day avoids triggering big adaptation, and periodized maintenance phases let the hormone system reset. After a run you lie down even more, and your appetite grows with exercise too. The more you diet, the more your body goes into power-saving mode. Crash dieting just trains your metabolism to spend less. No amount of willpower beats a ghrelin surge. Appetite hormones will outlast your discipline every time.

blocks.label: The Scale, Exercise, and the Last 5 Kilograms
blocks.text: The mechanism: a single reading is swayed by glycogen and water — each gram of glycogen binds three to four grams of water, adding one to two kilograms on your body — plus sodium-driven water retention of half to one and a half kilograms, menstrual cycles that can add one to three kilograms in the luteal phase, and the weight of the food and drinks you just consumed. None of it is fat. The key insight: a weekly average of fasted morning weigh-ins, plus waist and thigh measurements and how your clothes fit, beats any single daily number. Lifters may see the scale hold still while their waist shrinks, because muscle weighs more than fat. And here's the math: a 70-kilogram adult running at 10 kilometers per hour burns about 700 kilocalories, theoretically one kilogram of fat in eleven days. But metabolic adaptation, NEAT compensation, and post-exercise appetite eat most of that gap, and a single ordinary delivery meal takes one to two hours of moderate exercise to cancel out. Exercise's real value is preserving muscle, improving insulin sensitivity, and optimizing hormones — strength training is the most underrated fat-loss tool. blocks.text: Principle one: a small, sustained deficit beats aggressive dieting — 300 kilocalories a day, 500 at most, so you don't trigger a large metabolic adaptation. Principle three: sleep and stress — with too little sleep, cortisol rises, ghrelin rises, and leptin falls, and in matched interventions, the group with good sleep lost more fat and kept more muscle. Principle four: periodize and accept plateaus — fat loss is not linear, so after a stretch, a two-to-four-week maintenance phase near energy balance lets hormones reset before the next block. And the boundary: for non-competitive goals, prioritize sustainability; if fat loss is seriously hurting your social life, work, or quality of life, it's time to ask whether it's even necessary. title_en: Matt Damon on The Odyssey: Why Coming Home Is Harder Than Winning

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Matt Damon on The Odyssey: Why Coming Home Is Harder Than Winning

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: After the Beijing premiere of The Odyssey, host Ruixue sits down with Matt Damon for a face-to-face chat about the Homeric epic — the Trojan horse, twenty years adrift on the way home — and the real question at its heart: not how to win, but what you carry and who you answer to once you've won. Matt's answer: 35 is the age when you try to win, 55 is when you start coming home. Coming home is harder than winning, desire is a form of suffering, and peace and clarity have to be earned with the years.

blocks.label: The Odyssey: An Epic Pointed at 'After the Victory'
blocks.text: Homer's epic, The Odyssey, is one of the most important works in Western literature — basically Europe's answer to Journey to the West or The Investiture of the Gods. Odysseus, king of Ithaca, is the sharpest commander in the Greek alliance, so crafty he's been called the Greek Zhuge Liang. When Troy wouldn't fall, he took the city with the Trojan horse and won a glorious victory. But once the war was won, he set out for home — cursed, attacked by monsters, lured by sirens, battered by one disaster after another — drifting for twenty full years. So the movie and the epic aren't really about taking the city; they're about the road home after you've won. Most stories deliberately skip that 'after' — this one deliberately stops and stays there. Ruixue puts it simply: most stories tell us how hard it is to win, but The Odyssey focuses on what happens after the victory. It's the key to the whole interview — the chain of win, carry, and come home starts right here. Asked why coming home is harder than winning, Matt doesn't talk about heroes — he pulls the question back to ordinary people: after you win, what do you carry, what do you shoulder, and how accountable are you for the decisions you made? blocks.label: The Core Question: Why Coming Home Is Harder Than Winning
blocks.text: Winning only requires that you have the ability to get it done. Coming home demands that you face the consequences of your win — what did you trade for it? What did you sacrifice? Who are you accountable to for the choices you made? Matt says this question has existed since the day the epic was written, because it has no standard answer — only an answer that shifts with whatever stage of life you're in. A useful habit: after every milestone — a promotion, an award, a product launch — run your own little accountability check: what did this win cost me? That's the motif The Odyssey and Oppenheimer share. The fix: before you announce any victory, answer three questions — what did I sacrifice for it? Who am I accountable to for the decisions I made? Who do I want to be after I win?

title_en: From Cheers to Central Perk: The Third Place in American TV

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: From Cheers to Central Perk: The Third Place in American TV

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: From the little Boston bar of Cheers in 1982 to the orange sofa of Central Perk in 1994 — in twelve years, America's 'third place' moved from bar to coffeehouse, and from escaping life to talking about it. Reality shaped TV, and TV shaped reality right back.

blocks.label: Cold Open: Why Start with American Sitcoms
blocks.text: While sorting through material, the host spotted an obituary: legendary sitcom director James Burrows had passed away peacefully in his sleep at eighty-five. Fifty-plus years in the business, more than a thousand episodes directed, eleven Emmys — his credits run from Friends and Cheers to The Big Bang Theory, 2 Broke Girls, Will & Grace, and Frasier. It basically covers every coffeehouse image from our youth. So why does a director's passing open a coffee podcast? Because American sitcoms built our whole imagination of what a cafe should look like — the orange sofa, the grande latte that never runs out, the owner forever wiping cups behind the counter. Here's the opening question: how much of your mental image of a cafe comes from overseas TV shows? Are these pictures reality shaping TV — or TV shaping reality? As the host put it, 'legendary sitcom director James Burrows passed away peacefully in his sleep,' and 'from here, we set out from American sitcoms.' That's the opening hook for season two's metamorphosis of coffee and culture — America turned coffee into an orange sofa on the screen. blocks.label: Cheers: The Prototype of the Third Place
blocks.text: Cheers aired on NBC in 1982 — a Boston bar show with a minimal set: dark wood, brick walls, a plain bar. Nothing fancy, not fashionable, but very warm. The regulars come from every walk of life — a bartender, a waitress, a mailman, a psychiatrist — and they all share one thing: their jobs are lousy and their home lives are unhappy, but at least they have a place to go back to. Now, Cheers is a bar, not a cafe; it's beer, not latte. But that doesn't matter. What matters is the function of the space: a place you can return to over and over, with a regular seat and familiar faces. Sometimes you want to go where everybody knows your name. That line hits precisely because it captures the core function of a third place — it's not that everyone loves you, or that everyone needs you, just that everybody knows your name. Being seen, being remembered, being accepted — that's enough. Cheers was the first to define America's imagination of the third place; it's just that, back then, that space was a bar. And here's a quick test for whether a place is your third place: does anyone there know your name? blocks.label: Central Perk: The Myth of the Orange Sofa
blocks.text: Friends premiered in 1994, with six young New Yorkers gathering at the fictional Central Perk. The name fuses Central Park with 'Perk' — a slangy shortening of percolator, that drip-pot of French origin, which means both brewing coffee and perking you up. The pun already hints that coffee isn't just a drink — it's something that lifts you. Central Perk was designed as a third place from day one. And it almost didn't happen: the studio thought a cafe was too artsy, too New York, and suggested a diner instead. But the creators insisted — they wanted a place that belongs to no one's home and no one's office, a pure third place. Fans did the math: across all 236 episodes, the six friends drink a total of 1,154 cups of coffee — nearly five cups an episode. But they're not really drinking coffee; they're using it as background music. Most of the time they just hold a cup and chat, argue, and fall in love. The coffee is a prop — but that prop defines the whole vibe of the space. Friends premiered in 1994, with six young New Yorkers gathering at the fictional Central Perk. blocks.label: Four Coffeehouses, Four Answers to the Same Question
blocks.text: Frasier is the Cheers spin-off that premiered in 1993. Psychiatrist Frasier leaves Boston for Seattle, and he still needs a place that's neither work nor home — so we get Nervosa, the neurotic cafe. Central Perk is a hangout for young people; Nervosa is the third place of middle-class intellectuals. Two extremely particular, extremely neurotic brothers discuss wine, classical music, and psychology there — plus their elderly father's strange behavior. The season-one finale, 'My Coffee with Niles,' is basically a stage play: Frasier and his brother Niles never leave the cafe for the whole episode. Interrupted by all kinds of people, they keep circling a deceptively simple question — are you happy? And there's the four-cups running gag: Frasier starts tormenting the waitress the moment he orders, and the coffee gets remade four times — the first isn't decaf, the second doesn't have non-fat milk, and the third has cinnamon powder in it. Near the end everyone leaves, and the waitress brings the final cup: now, are you happy? Two psychiatrists in expensive suits spend the whole episode asking, are you happy? And yet to the very end it's all about life's confusions — the answer never actually arrives. The coffee and the staff that keep reappearing become the only audience for the brothers' entire afternoon. And Frasier's answer to the last cup: yes, in the greatest of choices, I am. blocks.label: Twelve Years: Why the Third Place Moved from Bar to Coffeehouse
blocks.text: Reason one: coffee culture happened to take off in the nineties. Peet's opened in Berkeley in 1966, Starbucks opened in Seattle in 1971, and by the nineties Starbucks was expanding hard across the US. Coffee was no longer just a pick-me-up — it was becoming a fashionable lifestyle. Reason two: young people shifted from alcohol to caffeine. Health awareness was rising, and caffeine fits the daytime far better than alcohol — so more and more young people chose the cafe. Reason three — the one you can't overlook: women's presence in public space changed. The bar culture of Cheers was still essentially a male space; even with female characters, the bar belonged to men. But the cafe was neutral from day one — regardless of gender, you could sit alone in a cafe, zone out, read, or strike up a chat without anyone thinking it strange. So from this angle, going to a cafe is a universal shift of public space. Map the three reasons to three levels: supply — coffee's expansion; demand — the health pivot; structure — gender neutrality. And here's the emotional core: in Cheers, people go to the bar to escape — escape work, family, their own problems, sit at the counter with a drink, complain about this and that, or think of nothing at all. In Central Perk, people go to the cafe to talk — talk about work, love, life choices, sit on the orange sofa and discuss whatever comes to mind. blocks.label: Third-Place Theory: Neutral Ground and Company That Asks for Nothing
blocks.text: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg keeps stressing the neutrality of the third place in The Great Good Place: a third place stands on neutral ground, where everyone exists in a state of social equality. Anyone can come and go; anyone can speak or stay silent. The person can be anyone — or no one at all. On this neutral ground, we don't have to play any social role — not some company's employee or boss, not someone's spouse, not someone's kid's parent. I'm just me, and you're just you: someone having a coffee or a drink, sitting there, with nothing to prove. Toru Watanabe says something similar when Midori asks him whether he likes being alone — that push-pull of craving connection while fearing hurt was exactly the host's state of mind in her early twenties. And a third place is just right for avoiding that disappointment — you don't need to get anything from anyone; you just sit there, next to a bunch of people sitting the same way. It's companionship that asks for nothing. Which re-reads the Cheers theme song: sometimes you want to go where everybody knows your name — not that everyone loves you, not that everyone needs you, just that everybody knows what you're called. blocks.label: Pitfalls & Boundaries: Pretty Places Aren't Third Places
blocks.text: The trap: these days you'll find seemingly exquisite social spaces everywhere — cafes and bars dripping with design, niche restaurants you have to book a week in advance, endless spots that photograph beautifully but hurt your butt after ten minutes. They're gorgeous, but they don't offer belonging. Compare that with Cheers and Central Perk: neither is refined. The blue-collar bar's old wooden counter is always covered in scratches, the orange sofa is old and worn, and the neurotic barista seems to be forever wiping the same cup. It's exactly that lack of polish that makes them easier to love. So the fix: don't be fooled by 'pretty' when you pick a third place. Ask yourself three questions — can I go every day? Do I need a reason? Do I need a minimum spend or a photo? Be careful: this is a high-frequency trap in daily life. As the host admits, you go once, take some photos, post them to Moments — and then, very likely, you never go back a second time. So what counts as a third place? A place you can return to again and again, with regular seats and familiar faces; no reason, no minimum spend, no photo required; standing on neutral ground, where you don't have to play a social role. blocks.label: Reality and TV: Shaping Each Other
blocks.text: Cheers was filmed in the 1980s — Americans really did go to bars back then, but Cheers made the bar-as-third-place idea clearer and more aspirational. Friends was filmed in the nineties — cafes really were rising then, but Central Perk turned the cafe-as-third-place concept into a global cultural imagination. Back to the opening question — the answer isn't either/or. Walk into any cafe today, in Beijing, Shanghai, Tokyo, or New York, and you'll see a trace of Central Perk: a window seat, a sofa you can sink into for an afternoon, a server who never rushes you out. These aren't coincidences — they're the legacy Friends and Central Perk left the world. Reality and TV shape each other, and every cafe today carries a shadow of Central Perk. And here's a way to use it: look at the cafe you keep going back to — TV shaped it, and your choice to return every day is what keeps that space genuinely alive. Take Kyoto's Rokuyosha tea shop: a kissaten tucked down an unremarkable alley, run by three generations for nearly a century. Dark-roast beans, no pour-over, no latte art, no Wi-Fi — but the function is the same: a place you can go back to, again and again. title_en: Taipei's Witch House: Thirty Years of Indie Music and Women's Spaces

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Taipei's Witch House: Thirty Years of Indie Music and Women's Spaces

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: From a shoebox storefront beneath a women's bookstore beside NTU to the birthplace of Taiwan's indie music, the Witch House was never a carefully planned project: founder Peng Yujing was a pastry apprentice who opened the shop half-willingly; a truckload of gear rescued from a shut-down livehouse accidentally turned it into a stage; and noise complaints forced the 'unplugged' rule that made its name. Thirty years on, it's like an old banyan tree — not the flashiest thing around, but always there.

blocks.label: A Chaotic Beginning: From a Cooking Dream to the Witch House
blocks.text: In 1987, Taiwan officially lifted martial law, ending 38 years of military rule. Like someone who hasn't been allowed to speak for ages finally getting room to breathe, society in the early nineties was itching to move — everyone was looking for an outlet for expression. Underground bands appeared, and livehouses built for rock fans, like Xilang, Rengou, and Mayi, slowly came into being. The key insight: a society's outlet for expression comes before business logic. Livehouses aren't just performance venues — they're physical spaces for 'speaking out.' The soil for indie music is basically the bottled-up urge to express released after martial law. Typical scenario: to understand why Taiwan's indie music burst out all at once in the nineties — you need a society that can talk before you get musicians who dare to express themselves. Quote from the show: 'Martial law had just ended after those decades, the whole society was restless, everyone was looking for an outlet for expression.' How this connects to the Witch House: it's one of the space-products of this wave of expression — but what makes it special is the three principles that reality later forced out of it. Meet the founder: Peng Yujing studied sociology at National Taiwan University, but couldn't find a job after graduating. She loved food, so she completed a cooking program, apprenticed in the pastry kitchen of the Sherwood Hotel, and dreamed of one day opening a restaurant of her own. She loved food, so she completed a cooking program, apprenticed in the pastry kitchen of the Sherwood Hotel, and dreamed of one day opening a restaurant of her own.

blocks.label: A-Feng and Scum: The Price of Rock & Roll Noise
blocks.text: A-Feng, a member of the indie band Boney Flesh — not the A-Feng from Sodagreen — founded Scum, a performance space near NTU. Unlike other livehouses that allowed full cover sets, Scum was one of the first venues to require bands on stage to play original songs. The key insight: that 'originals only' rule planted the seed of Taiwan's indie scene. But back then underground bands mostly played rock, and the ear-splitting volume drew neighbor complaints and police fines. A-Feng sank his own money in, lost a Mercedes in the process, and the venue finally went under. Typical scenario: when a 'righteous principle' collides with physical reality — noise complaints, in this case — an idea with no room for compromise gets crushed by cost. This is the cautionary tale the Witch House later took most seriously. Quote from the show: 'Scum was one of the very first places to require bands to play an original song on stage.' How this connects: Scum's original-song spirit was inherited by the Witch House, while its noise lesson was avoided by the Witch House's 'unplugged' approach. After Scum closed, A-Feng asked Peng Yujing whether he could borrow the music gear from his old venue so they could perform in her new space. It was a full truckload. Peng didn't think twice — a public space can be used in many ways, not just for food — so she agreed, and even let them handle the sound. blocks.label: The Witch House's Three Rules: Principles Forced by Reality
blocks.text: The Witch House sits in a residential area near NTU, on the ground floor, in a space so small that installing soundproofing was nearly impossible. Even with Scum's original crew running it, the full underground-band model couldn't be copied into this brand-new little room — or they'd get fined and shut down just the same. At the same time, more macho rock livehouses like Vibes were popping up. So Peng searched for the style that fit the Witch House best and made a three-point decision. The key insight: the three principles interlock into one system — unplugged solves 'whether we can survive', original music solves 'what we become', and female-first solves 'who gets to define us.' The constraints weren't treated as flaws; they were reframed into an advantage to be exploited. Quote from the show: 'Later she made a decision, including three points... none of these have to be limits — they can actually become an advantage you can use.' Unplugged was less a musical stance than a compromise forced by worrying the neighbors would complain. But at the same time it was an encouragement — an invitation to look beyond rock's loudness and find the craft of getting the audience more involved when you're performing up close. The key insight: compromise isn't retreating — it's competing on a different track. The noise restriction moved the competition from 'volume' to 'intimacy and skill', and that became the Witch House's differentiation advantage. Typical scenario: when resources, space, and compliance are all constrained, translating 'what we can't do' into 'what we can do better' is the most cost-effective way to position yourself. blocks.label: A Women's Space: From the Audience to the Stage
blocks.text: The Witch House's website keeps a timeline called the 'Time Tunnel' recording the first performances of many bands and artists since 1996. In the opening year, 1996, the stage still belonged to rock bands like Quarterback and Boney Flesh; Chen Shan-Ni only showed up at year's end. From 1997, Huang Xiaozhen, Yi Nengjing, and Chen Qizhen followed one after another, then Panai in 1998, and Lei Guangxia plus a not-yet-debuted Anpu in 1999. Also, one day each month is 'Witch Festival', when only female singers can perform. The key insight: the Witch Festival gave female creators their first stage of their own, and definitively set the Witch House apart from every other music space — on one side machismo and soundwaves, on the other stars and artistry. Typical scenario: to support an overlooked group, don't offer an 'equal invitation' — build a tilted stage instead, with a fixed time and a fixed mechanism for making room. Quote from the show: 'Female creators had their own stage for the first time, and this completely separated the Witch House's picture from other music spaces — one side is machismo and soundwaves, the other is stars and artistry.' From the start, Peng positioned the Witch House as 'a place where girls can stay out late.' The food proudly calls itself 'the most mischievous menu challenging the limits of human taste': Menstruation Iced Tea, Wine-Pool Meat-Shower, and Wild Strawberries. There's also an unwritten rule — if you dare to take off your bra and hang it on your chair, your drink is free. Peng jokes that, for hygiene reasons, they do hope everyone rotates their bras regularly. The walls are covered with posters of female rock musicians and dolls of every kind, the bathroom walls carry essays on female orgasm, and sanitary products are stocked for women. The key insight: putting 'things we're taught to feel embarrassed about' into public space is itself a feminist spatial practice — it sends the message that these things are nothing to be ashamed of. The key insight: the Witch Festival gave female creators their first stage of their own, and definitively set the Witch House apart from every other music space — on one side machismo and soundwaves, on the other stars and artistry. Typical scenario: to support an overlooked group, don't offer an 'equal invitation' — build a tilted stage instead, with a fixed time and a fixed mechanism for making room. Quote from the show: 'Female creators had their own stage for the first time, and this completely separated the Witch House's picture from other music spaces — one side is machismo and soundwaves, the other is stars and artistry.' From the start, Peng positioned the Witch House as 'a place where girls can stay out late.' The food proudly calls itself 'the most mischievous menu challenging the limits of human taste': Menstruation Iced Tea, Wine-Pool Meat-Shower, and Wild Strawberries. There's also an unwritten rule — if you dare to take off your bra and hang it on your chair, your drink is free. Peng jokes that, for hygiene reasons, they do hope everyone rotates their bras regularly. The walls are covered with posters of female rock musicians and dolls of every kind, the bathroom walls carry essays on female orgasm, and sanitary products are stocked for women. The key insight: putting 'things we're taught to feel embarrassed about' into public space is itself a feminist spatial practice — it sends the message that these things are nothing to be ashamed of.

blocks.label: Independence Beyond Music
blocks.text: The independent spirit the Witch House championed was never limited to indie music — it welcomed all kinds of creation and expression that stood apart from commerce. In 1999, Peng's German husband Yo-Yo hosted poetry readings, where Hong Hong and Xia Yu — under her pen name Li Gedi — both read their work, and some people recited with an almost rock-like explosive force, blurring the line between poetry and music. The store also staged A-Chung's glove puppet theater — glove puppetry, which originated in Fujian and grew to full development in Taiwan, is operated by hand and fingers with no human performer, relying on the backstage band; the Witch House was exactly the right venue. Stage plays and other forms followed. The key insight: 'independence' is a creative stance, and music is only one of its faces. A space that refuses to box itself in can keep holding different forms of expression. Typical scenario: keep an entry point in your space or brand for the unplanned — real distinctiveness often comes from the accidents you're willing to catch. Anpu's line: 'A small audience, the performers, and the shop together created a performance atmosphere that didn't need much defining.' Quote from the show: 'She really didn't box herself in tightly. The independent spirit she championed didn't only mean independent music... music is just one of its faces, one of its ways of expression.' For the Witch House's 20th anniversary, they held the 'Witch Festival' music festival, selling tickets completely on their own with no middleman ticketing platform — in today's terms, 'no middleman markup.' They mailed tickets to fans one by one by hand — a very handmade way of doing things. blocks.label: The Slash Space of the Livehouse World
blocks.text: The Witch House has always called itself 'the slash space of the livehouse world': it began as a cafe, then became a livehouse plus a bar. Thursday, Friday, and Saturday at nine in the evening there's always a show, with a 350-TWD cover charge that includes one drink. Later, board games were added — it doesn't rake in big money, but it doesn't die either. The key insight: from today's perspective, doing an indie stage, a cafe, a bar, and board games all at once isn't impressive — it almost sounds ordinary. But precisely because of that messy positioning, not leaning too heavily on music revenue but walking on several legs, the Witch House has managed to run to this day — and it left young creators room to breathe. Typical scenario: 'people really should live a bit messier, and a shop can try to be messier too' — multiple income streams aren't a distraction; they're redundancy by design. Quote from the show: 'Maybe it was precisely because of that messy positioning back then — not leaning too much on income from music shows but walking on many legs — that the Witch House could keep operating smoothly to this day.' Then came the crisis: a fire at the Taichung bar ALABAR claimed nine lives, and regulators finally started taking the livehouse world's long-neglected legal problems seriously. The Witch House got checked again and again, told that its 'zoning use and registered business items didn't meet the standards' — because running a livehouse wasn't exactly legal back then. Under the pressure, Peng thought: 'If the law says no, then fine — I just won't do it anymore.' The turning point was the supporters: after the news spread, fans voiced support online, dropped written opinions into the market's letterbox, and cleared the shelves of the store's merch — far beyond what Peng could have imagined. The authorities then amended the regulations to add a category for 'music performance spaces', legitimizing the livehouse business. That's how the Witch House survived the storm. blocks.label: Filter vs. Reality: Don't Pin an Era's Name on Her
blocks.text: As the hosts dug into the Witch House, their rosy filter only faded. Some netizens who visited complained it was 'chaotic, indifferent, arrogant' — the literary-space expectations crumbled one by one. The hosts get that completely — Peng herself admits the Witch House's 'grumpy face' is famous in the industry, and in an era of ever-more-polished service, it does pale next to all those refined, considerate stores. The key insight — Panai, an artist who grew out of the Witch House, offers another reading: 'The Witch House doesn't treat people differently — you're a guest, but you're still a person. The little witch who comes to work, she's a person too; she doesn't have to smile.' In this space, you're not extra great because you're a consumer, and no one becomes lesser because of the kind of work they do. Typical scenario: when you evaluate a space, separate 'service experience' from 'the value of the space' — do you expect to be served, or to be treated as a person? Quote from Panai: 'The Witch House doesn't treat people differently — you're a guest, but you're still a person. The little witch who comes to work is also a person; she doesn't have to wear a smile.' Quote from the show: 'In this space, you're not great just because you're a consumer, and people don't become lesser because of the nature of their work.' The host admits that putting the netizens' complaints and Panai's words side by side risks 'switching the subject' — but her view is: maybe it's better not to pin the name the era gave the Witch House onto her today, because there will always come a day when she falls short of the expectation. title_en: Is Obsessing Over a Place a Sickness? Inside 'Fudo Photography'

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: Is Obsessing Over a Place a Sickness? Inside 'Fudo Photography'

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: In one line: 'fudo photography' isn't the product of any photography school — it's an original concept the two hosts built from years of watching and thinking: turn your lens back on the 'fudo' you know and love best — a place's soil, climate, people, and culture — and photograph 'an obsession with a place.' Using five case studies — Alec Soth, Daido Moriyama and Kyoichi Tsuzuki, Lu Yuanmin, and a lineage from Soetsu Yanagi to Sari Shibata and Gong Le — they draw the line between fudo photography and landscape, travel, documentary, and street photography, explain why the places we know best are the easiest to overlook, and show how to carry your hometown's 'soil virtue' to any corner of the world.

blocks.label: What Is 'Fudo'? Two Layers Behind an Ancient Word
blocks.text: 'Fudo' has a very long history in Chinese, from pre-Qin classics all the way to today, and its meaning hasn't shifted much — it refers to a region's natural climate, objective landforms, and geographical environment — terrain, urban structure — along with climate change, carrying a sense of historical depth. The key insight: only time can breed a certain climate and form a certain soil structure. 'Fudo renjo' — human sentiment — adds a human layer on top of fudo: the collective memory shared by a place's people and the common human wisdom formed by living on that land. But in casual speech people usually read it as something concrete and crystallized — a festival, a specialty product, a famous sight. Why 'fudo photography' instead of 'fudo-renjo photography': it goes back to the plainer, more abstract layer — not a pure description of nature, and not a description of intangible heritage that's already been crystallized, but the vast, hard-to-put-into-words collection of spirit and civilization formed by people and nature coexisting, by people who've lived long on this land and grown together with their environment. Quote from the show: 'When people and nature coexist — or people who have long lived on this land... formed a vast, hard-to-directly-express collection of this spiritual civilization.' How this connects: this is the cornerstone of the whole episode — every case study that follows is about how to get that abstract collection into the frame. And here's the intellectual backstory: in the early 20th century, the 1930s, after studying Hegel, the Japanese philosopher Watsuji Tetsuro proposed his 'fudo theory' — a place's natural environment shapes the mental state and the national character of the people who live there. The intellectual backstory: in the early 20th century, the 1930s, after studying Hegel, the Japanese philosopher Watsuji Tetsuro proposed his 'fudo theory' — a place's natural environment shapes the mental state and the national character of the people who live there.

blocks.label: What Is Fudo Photography? Photographing Your Obsession With a Place
blocks.text: Fudo photography isn't a simple collection of pictures from old categories — landscape, portraits, street shots — but a way of seeing that goes beyond previous photographic concepts. Most importantly, it has a movement from the external world toward the spiritual world — or at least it weighs both sides equally. And it's very inclusive in scale: as big as a city or a country, as small as a district or a street — as long as people gather, share memories, and have their own climate, nature, or folk customs, it can have its own fudo. The key insight: fudo needs the thickness of time and it needs people, so it's not 'decisive moment' shooting — a single photo can barely convey fudo. When you see a fudo photograph, it naturally guides you into that world, into the inner life of the people there — carrying more information than the frame itself gives you. How to use it: to test whether a photo is fudo photography, look for that 'inward' layer — after you look at it, do you start wondering how the people in this place live, what climate and what character this neighborhood has? Quote from the show: 'It has a process of going from the external world to the spiritual world... it needs people, so it's not that decisive-moment kind of shooting... with a single photo you can hardly feel the fudo.' How it connects: it does include pictures from the old categories — landscapes focused on a region, portraits documenting people, representative street shots — but it stresses weighing both 'external world + spiritual world', and that's the decisive dividing line between it and landscape photography. Who it's for: the ideal audience for fudo photography is actually the locals — it taps into memories like 'you once walked along the Suzhou Creek.' But it's equally precious for outsiders: through photography's partial, indirect information, you get carried into the inner world of locals that an outsider could rarely reach otherwise. blocks.label: Five Case Studies: What Fudo Photography Looks Like
blocks.text: The project is defined by a clear natural boundary — the Mississippi River — yet he didn't use wide frames to shoot the river's shape, its banks, or its sights; he aimed the lens at the people living there. The key insight: he used a staged, almost directed approach, letting his subjects display the hobbies, characters, and dreams they'd accumulated in life; he also shot people-free 'empty frames' — a single sofa — where seeing the object still makes you think of its owner. The objects and people in the frame guide each other, forming a flow between them: see a man holding an airplane model at his snowy doorstep, and you think of the Mississippi, the region's climate, and one man's dreams. 'Niagara' is built around the theme of love, set against Niagara, the honeymoon capital, and shot through many couples — it reads like a poetry collection. How it differs from 'typology': he deliberately avoids lining people up against a white wall in identical compositions; instead, scenes keep shifting, and the richness and commonality of the people lead you to imagine the local spirit of the region. How to use it: choose a 'place' with a clear boundary, turn your lens from the scenery to the people who live within it, and leave information in the frame that lets the viewer do the imagining. Quote from the show: 'The objects and people in the frame both lead you to think about life in this region... the information it carries exceeds what the frame itself gives you.' And then there's Shinjuku: it stands for Japan's postwar history — a very typical location. Daido Moriyama has lived there his whole life, and what he shoots on the streets of Shinjuku is treated by the hosts as 'Shinjuku's fudo photography.' blocks.text: One-sentence conclusion: fudo photography isn't a shooting technique — it's an 'obsession with a place.' It asks you to first become familiar with it, then fall in love with it, and only then lift the camera. blocks.label: Five Pitfalls: Common Mistakes in Fudo Photography
blocks.text: First, the cause: you're unconsciously drawn to 'stimulating' scenes and capture the moments most unlike the culture you know well — a foreign journalist shooting Shanghai. The frame becomes spectacle and filter. The fix: first prove you've actually 'lived' there — genuinely engaged with it, felt its climate, gotten sick because of that climate, bought several rounds of clothes, learned to survive in it — and only then talk about photographing it. How serious is it? Fatal — locals see through it at a glance, and the moment you shoot, your unfamiliarity shows. Quote from a host: 'He might still get stimulated by the scenes of Shanghai — so there's a foreign-guest perspective.' Next pitfall: if you're shooting a common theme like 'urban disease', that's fine — but declaring 'I think one thing about Shanghai is bad' while calling it a picture of Shanghai is overgeneralization, mistaking a part for the whole. The symptom: shot from very far away, the frame shows no Shanghai people's lives — only a tiny slice — yet the title wears the name 'Shanghai', a name the whole world pays attention to. blocks.label: Post-Credits: A Photography Critique About 'Shooting Shanghai'
blocks.text: Here's the epilogue: being criticized and being discussed means the work is getting attention — many artists are magnanimous and can take in different voices; photography criticism is common in places with a developed photography culture. The core claim: the works that can support an artist are all works that 'connect with their time, with their place, and with people who can understand them.' title_en: One Year in New York: How a Pessimist Lives (725 Salon Live)

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: One Year in New York: How a Pessimist Lives (725 Salon Live)

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: On his last night before wrapping up a year of visiting scholarship in the US, host David Weng sits down live with Ouyang Bin at the 725 Salon for an open chat — from New York as 'a salad' of disconnected strangers, to the wildly different senses of time in China, Japan, and the US; from the real reason he left finance to make content, to how a pessimist finds anchors for life in a 'Chaotic Era'. It lands on his investment worldview: investing is a vote on your worldview, and his worldview is that everything runs in cycles.

blocks.label: First Impressions of New York: From Locked Cabinets to a Salad
blocks.text: He moved to New York straight from Japan, and the first impression wasn't pretty. It felt like stepping out of one operating mode of the world — an extremely ordered one — into an extremely disordered one, and the culture shock was even sharper than coming straight from China. The most concrete sign: walking into a CVS and finding some shelves locked. He hasn't seen locked cabinets in years. That unease is the most direct evidence of how a city makes you feel. Weather shapes the short-term impression, people decide the long-term one, and infrastructure is its own thing. It was only after moving to an Upper East Side co-op and getting to know people that New York became lovable. Before coming he'd set a goal — coffee chats with a hundred listeners — and last night he announced he'd made it. He moved to New York straight from Japan, and his first impression wasn't great — it felt like going from one mode of the world, an extremely ordered one, to an extremely disordered mode, and that culture shock was even sharper than coming straight from China. The most concrete, visceral sign: walking into a CVS and seeing some shelves locked up. He hadn't seen locked cabinets in Japanese convenience stores or Chinese shops in years — that unease is the most direct evidence of how he feels about a city. This is the emotional starting point for the 'salad' metaphor and the China-Japan-US comparison — physical discomfort comes first, structural insight follows. To judge a city, split your feeling into three parts: weather shapes your short-term impression, people decide the long-term one, and infrastructure is its own thing. It was only after he moved to an Upper East Side co-op and got to know people that New York became 'lovable'. 'You feel like you've gone from one operating mode of the world — an extremely ordered one — to an extremely disordered one. That culture shock might be even more obvious than if you'd come straight from China.' Before coming to New York he set a goal — coffee chats with 100 listeners — and yesterday he announced he'd done it. In nine months he traveled through more than a dozen states, meeting listeners in nearly every city.

blocks.label: China, Japan, and the US: Three Countries, Three Senses of Time
blocks.text: After living in Japan for more than two years and then coming to the US, he looked at the three countries from outside the daily grind and found them extremely, extremely different. Japan is a society living in the past: the services barely changed in twenty or thirty years, and there's still a newspaper-delivery stand. Locals feel things aren't what they used to be, but compared with everyone else, Japan moves at a glacial pace. That's why visiting Japan feels so comfortable — not much noisy new stuff. It's the polar opposite of China's future-facing buzz. America, meanwhile, is partly in the past and partly in the future: ask about AI and everyone says next week it'll be different; ask about the subway and the answer is it'll look the same in ten years. That's exactly why traveling in Japan feels so comfortable — there isn't much noisy new stuff. It's the polar opposite of China's future-facing buzz. To read a society's character, look at how much of the old way of life it keeps: newspaper stands, news kiosks, and print-magazine sales are all thermometers of a society's sense of time. 'Japan is a society that lives in the past.' 'It still keeps — there's even a newspaper-delivery stand, and every morning people still go there to pick up their papers.' The US is 'partly in the past, partly in the future': talk AI and everyone tells you 'next week it'll be different again'; talk subway and the answer might be 'in ten years it'll look the same'.

blocks.label: From Finance White-Collar to Content Creator
blocks.text: Asked why he left finance, he's quick to clarify: it wasn't a single moment of clarity, and it wasn't the FIRE script of having saved enough. It was a tug-of-war that dragged on for six months to a year. He almost joined another fund — the founder interviewed him on video for five or six hours during the pandemic — but it fell through by chance, so he finally did the thing he'd always wanted: study Japanese in Japan. And along the way he realized he didn't need to go back to a finance job. There was a real math moment: once he stopped wanting to add another zero, his savings were enough to rest for a long time. He won't hand out FIRE secrets, because he knows he rode the real-estate boom — at twenty-something, rent and a mortgage were about the same, so he bought, and the times carried him into his first capital. What drove him into content was instant feedback: every day, he could see read counts and comments moving. That's why he's unusually clear-eyed about 'windfalls'. Big transitions don't come from waiting for a 'eureka moment' — you execute the small urges you already have (learning a language, starting a project) and let reality slowly tell you the answer. 'It was a relationship of constant back-and-forth tugging.' 'You were carried along and completed an original capital accumulation … it happened while you were young and clueless.' After leaving the sovereign fund, he joined a company that 'connects financial knowledge to ordinary people' — really, he ran a WeChat public account and later started a podcast. The core driver was instant feedback: every day he could see the read counts and comments moving.

blocks.label: The 'Chaotic Era': Living in Unpredictability
blocks.text: The word comes from The Three-Body Problem. In a Chaotic Era you never know what tomorrow brings — whether the sun rises, or whether it's plus 30 degrees or minus 30. The people in the novel fold themselves into a sheet of paper and hibernate until a Stable Era comes. He and his friends first used the term for the macro picture, never expecting the macro to actually get this chaotic. The essence of a Chaotic Era is unpredictability — you can't forecast geopolitics or economic events. The market reaction is funny: since the macro can't be predicted, everyone stops watching it and turns to individual stock charts and AI. But for ordinary people the impact lands late: until it hits you, it's just news from somewhere far away; by the time the minus-30 cold snap lands on you, responding might already be too late. That's why he keeps options open — multiple currencies, multiple locations, multiple skills. The Chaotic Era explains a whole series of his choices: diversifying asset allocation, and keeping physical optionality — living in Japan for a while, staying able to move. He lived through more than three months of lockdown in Shanghai, and that feeling of 'one day you might suddenly be completely unable to move' is seared into his memory. In a Chaotic Era, don't chase prediction — build a response structure: multiple currencies, multiple locations, multiple skills. Keep the option for yourself. 'Before the Chaotic Era touches you, you always think it has nothing to do with you — it's just a news report, just something happening far away.' Ouyang Bin presses further: our parents caught the reform-and-opening wave, your generation caught real estate — how does an ordinary person avoid missing the next opportunity like that?

blocks.label: Q&A: FX Risk, Core Skills, and Deep Learning
blocks.text: A listener asks how he handles exchange-rate risk in his own allocation and how institutions deal with currency volatility. At the sovereign fund he invested across dozens of currencies, and the conclusion was that the exchange rate is the single hardest price to forecast, bar none. It's the combination of two things — RMB against the dollar — and one is already hard enough. Institutions simply don't look at FX: it stays out of monthly reviews and attribution, and year-end outlooks are almost always the most wrong forecasts in the whole firm. His home-currency principle: pick one base currency and hold foreign assets only out of real need — parents retiring in China, a possible move back. No life need, no obsessive currency bets. 'The yen will definitely rise' is a call that's cost him, but because he lives in Japan, the book loss spread across future spending basically doesn't exist. 'Nobody can predict it … so don't make it one of your predictions.' How to use it: ask yourself 'where will I actually spend money in the future?', allocate based on that need, and skip currency speculation.

blocks.label: Pitfalls & Boundary Notes
blocks.text: People naturally believe that one thing can be linearly extrapolated forever — assets always rise, tailwinds always last, trends never end. That clashes directly with the worldview that everything runs in cycles. So the fix: whenever you feel 'this time is different', treat it as a cycle signal, not a trend signal, and swap your reflex for a self-check — 'I've seen this scene before.' Getting it wrong is fatal: mistake volatility for a trend and you'll catch the knife at the peak. The same goes for narratives. Xiaohongshu is full of 'I bought SpaceX at 190 and it's now 1,000' posts, but the real world is Times Square, where a SpaceX IPO billboard and protest puppets criticizing Grok stand side by side. Before any big judgment, add ground truth — go to the scene, read primary sources, meet the people involved — then decide whether to trust the story in your feed. title_en: A 4-Hour Interview with Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's VP of Research

blocks.label: 英文标题
blocks.text: A 4-Hour Interview with Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's VP of Research

blocks.label: 本集英文简介
blocks.text: Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's first VP promoted from the research track, sits down with Zhang Xiaojun for a four-hour deep dive a month after Jensen Huang's China visit. He lays out NVIDIA's bet: Physical AI, the 'zero-billion-dollar business' (fine to make no money now, but it must be wildly influential if it succeeds), and building markets instead of fighting over existing ones. He also explains how to win GPUs for research inside a compute company, how to grow from researcher to VP, and how Cosmos collapsed from 22 models into a single Omni model. He closes with Chinese martial arts: 'the most important thing in kung fu is controlling yourself, not showing destructive power' — model competition shouldn't be a Squid Game.

blocks.label: NVIDIA's Bet and Its Boundaries
blocks.text: Cosmos isn't aimed at the video-creation market — it's aimed at Physical AI, the next revolution in Ming-Yu's eyes, because it's a genuine need: people age and can't drive and their quality of life drops sharply; plenty of jobs are labor-intensive and dangerous; nobody wants to do the chores. These physical actors that can actually change the state of the physical world need world models. NVIDIA itself is a computing company, not a solutions company — its real strength is the whole computer stack. That comes with a difficulty: it's a bit like scratching an itch through your boot, because you don't know where the pain points are. That's why he comes to China two or three times a year. And Jensen loves the 'zero-billion-dollar business' — not a business today, but billion-scale if it succeeds. You can make no money now, but when it succeeds, it has to be hugely influential. Cosmos isn't aimed at the video-creation market — it's aimed at Physical AI, the 'next revolution' in Ming-Yu's eyes, because it's a hard need: when you get old you can't drive and your quality of life drops sharply; many jobs are labor-intensive and dangerous; nobody wants to do household chores. These 'physical actors that can truly change the state of the physical world' need world models to empower them. NVIDIA is a computing company, not a solutions company — its real strength is the whole computer stack, from chips at the bottom to software. 'We're not a solutions company; our goal is to help the companies that build solutions succeed.' That brings one difficulty: 'it's a bit like scratching an itch through your boot, because you don't understand where the pain points are.' So he comes to China two or three times a year, just to understand the problems developers are actually facing. Typical use case: when judging whether a research or business direction deserves investment — first ask 'is this a big enough problem?', then ask 'does it fit my company's position in the ecosystem?' 'NVIDIA is a computing company … but we're not a solutions company; our goal is to help the companies that build solutions succeed.' (00:02:35) This is the master key to the whole interview — everything that follows, from Cosmos to generalization to building markets, unfolds on top of this bet. Jensen often says he loves the 'zero-billion-dollar business' — it's not a business yet (zero), but if it succeeds it becomes a billion-dollar one. You can make no money for now, but when it succeeds it must be very influential and enormous.

blocks.label: Accidents, Epiphanies, and Pivots
blocks.text: Grew up in Taipei, studied wireless communication at National Chiao Tung University, decided in his junior year to go to the US — his parents were shocked — then a PhD at Maryland switching to computer vision, three years at Mitsubishi Electric Research, where the year he graduated AlexNet came out, and then NVIDIA in 2016, ten years and counting. AI was an accident for him: interning at Intel Taiwan, he saw systems that could identify objects from pixels and found it magical — because he didn't understand it, it was easy to see how important it was. When everything he'd learned in his PhD suddenly stopped working, he was fine, because 'learn everything' was already a habit. He even predicted in 2016 that language would break through first, but he liked visual signals more, so he stayed. The deeper turn was from the beauty of math to the essence of problems: assumptions make math cleaner but push you further from reality. Grew up in Taipei, studied wireless communication at National Chiao Tung University in Hsinchu, decided in his junior year to go to the US (his parents were shocked), did a PhD at the University of Maryland switching to computer vision, spent three years at Mitsubishi Electric Research — the year he graduated, AlexNet appeared — then joined NVIDIA in 2016, ten years and counting. AI was an accident for him. Interning at Intel Taiwan, he saw speech and image recognition that could 'judge objects from pixels' for the first time and found it magical — 'because I didn't understand it, it was easy to understand its importance.' The SVM and graphical models he learned in his PhD suddenly 'stopped working' the year he graduated, but he'd long built the habit of 'learning everything.' As early as 2016-2017 he predicted that 'the first field to truly break through is language,' only 'he likes visual signals more, so he's stayed here.' Typical scenario: when a path dead-ends and the era shifts, how not to panic — treat 'everything I learned stopped working' as the norm, and make 'learning everything' a habit. In his junior year he told his parents he was going to study in the US: 'they were startled, because they'd known me for over 20 years and never once heard me mention going to the US to study.' (00:29:57) This trajectory explains why he became NVIDIA's first researcher to 'bring generative networks up' — it wasn't planned out; it was built one step at a time. Turn one: from the beauty of math to the essence of the problem. Early on, to prove bounds he'd make lots of assumptions — 'assumptions make your math cleaner, but they also push you further from reality.' Later he realized AI is itself an application, and he 'increasingly liked getting close to the essence of problems, without being seduced by fancy math.'

blocks.label: How to Win GPUs at NVIDIA
blocks.text: On winning GPUs: there's no place on earth where GPUs are enough, so you have to understand the problem the company is solving and explain why your work will have an impact on the company. Researchers tend to have high egos and look down on each other, but a company exists to profit its shareholders — Jensen wants to take care of the family. He saw it firsthand at Mitsubishi Electric Research: once a peer of Microsoft Research in the nineties, until the company doubted blue-sky research and a bunch of important scholars got fired. So he aligns his interest with the company's. When DALL·E came out, he wrote to Jensen: the future is already clear — image generation will run on deep learning, we must invest in GPUs. He got 1,000 A100s, a lot in the Ampere era. And he doesn't get excited about temporary model leads, because this month GPT is better, next month Anthropic, the month after open source catches up, and China's GLM, Kimi, Alibaba, DeepSeek, MiniMax keep pushing — eventually everyone's models converge. 'You have to understand the problem the company is trying to solve, then find a way to explain to the company why what you're doing will have an impact on it.' Researchers generally have high egos and look down on each other, but a company exists to make a profit for its shareholders — Jensen wants to take care of the family, and the company has to make money. He witnessed the lesson at Mitsubishi Electric Research firsthand: in the nineties it was an institution on par with Microsoft Research, but when the company changed direction and started doubting the value of blue-sky research, 'a bunch of important scholars got fired one after another.' So when doing research, 'you need to align your interest with the company's interest' — especially in a money-burning field like deep learning, you need to explain 'why this is an important investment for the company.' How to use it: before every project, answer first 'why does this matter to the company, and how does it relate to our business?' — that's not compromise, it's a survival skill. 'There is no place on this earth where GPUs are enough.' After DALL·E came out, he wrote to Jensen: 'the future is already clear — it's deep learning doing image generation … we must invest in GPUs.' He ended up getting 1,000 A100s — 'a whole lot' for the Ampere era at the time. (01:02:46) Why doesn't he get excited about a model's temporary lead? Because 'this month GPT is better, next month Anthropic is better, the month after open-source models may catch up, and China's strong players — GLM, Kimi, Alibaba, DeepSeek, MiniMax — keep breaking through, so slowly everyone's model capability ends up about the same.'

blocks.label: From Researcher to NVIDIA VP
blocks.text: 'I might be the first one, yeah' — researcher straight up to VP, a level a year in the early years. He helped NVIDIA build AI research credibility before it had AI talent, he genuinely loves shipping — turning research into products — and he earned trust step by step. Now the Cosmos team burns millions of dollars of compute a day, and that trust is exactly why he gets to lead a project this big. His biggest worry as a manager is losing touch with the fundamentals, so he stays one of the few VPs who still reads code — he reviews code, reads papers, and challenges every idea. The Cosmos paper has over 290 authors, and managing that is a tug between total alignment and individual autonomy: too aligned and you get horse-racing, too centralized and progress crawls. 'I might be the first one, yeah.' In the first few years he was promoted a level every year, all the way to VP. Three reasons: early on, when NVIDIA had no AI talent yet, he helped raise the company's AI research profile and explained how AI would affect it; he also genuinely loved shipping — turning research into products; and he earned the company's trust step by step, so it kept handing him bigger and bigger projects. The whole Cosmos team now burns millions of dollars of compute every day — 'the company only gives you this chance to lead a project this big if it has a certain level of trust in you. So aligning with the company is very important.' The risk warning: the thing he worries about most as a manager is 'losing touch with the fundamentals' — that's why he's still 'one of the few VPs who still read code', keeping on reviewing everyone's code, reading papers, and challenging each person's idea. 'What I worry about most is losing touch with the fundamentals and not understanding the core of the problem. I force myself to review everyone's code, read papers, and challenge each person's idea.' Actionable takeaway: a manager's self-freshness plan — keep a 'hands-on loop': even if you don't implement, read code and papers regularly and join technical debates, keeping your feel for the essence of problems. The Cosmos paper lists over 290 authors — just under 300. Managing a team that big is a tug between two lines: everyone aligned on the goal (or it diverges and you get horse-racing behavior) and everyone able to decide on their own (or only a few decide and progress crawls).

blocks.label: The Birth of Cosmos
blocks.text: Ten years ago, in his job talk at NVIDIA, he said the day would come when video generation ran on deep neural networks instead of traditional computer graphics. He built GANs and GauGAN — named after the painter Gauguin — and the Deep Imagination Research Group. When DALL·E appeared, he realized his ambition, courage, and resolve weren't big enough: the conditions were all there; he just didn't go do it. After Sora, he and his team wrote to Jensen — we have to do this — and Cosmos was born in March 2024. Jensen's reply: just go to Cosmos 97. Now at Cosmos 3, with 94 generations to go. His direct team is under a hundred, with a few hundred more reporting in loosely. And why video, not language? Computer-vision background, a great LLM team at NVIDIA already, and Physical AI needs actors that change the physical world. Ten years ago, in his job talk before joining NVIDIA, he said: 'one day the main compute for generating video will be deep neural networks, not traditional computer graphics.' After that, at NVIDIA he worked on GANs and GauGAN — named after the painter Gauguin — collaborated with the StyleGAN team, founded the Deep Imagination Research Group, and built Picasso, an AI foundry in partnership with Getty Images and Shutterstock. When DALL·E appeared, he realized 'my ambition wasn't big enough, I wasn't brave enough, I didn't have the resolve' — the conditions were actually all there; 'it's just because I didn't do it, so it didn't get made.' After Sora came out, he led the team to write to Jensen 'we must do this' — that's how Cosmos came to be (kicked off in March 2024, right after Sora). Jensen's reply was one line: 'just make it to Cosmos 97' — an offhand number that showed his resolve on this direction. How to use it: when you see a breakthrough bigger than you imagined, don't just regret 'I didn't think of it' — ask 'did I lack ability or resolve?' Liu's answer: both, but the resolve gap was bigger. 'When we finished Cosmos 1, we asked Jensen whether to keep going, and he told me: just make it to Cosmos 97. I'm only at 3 now, so there are still 94 generations to go.' Team size (01:37:00): his direct team is under 100 people (researchers plus engineers), with 200-300 reporting in loosely; the project split off from research and renamed itself Cosmos Lab. Three reasons: ① his background is computer vision rather than NLP, and the partners who follow him have similar backgrounds — 'we'd rather solve problems that fit me better'; ② NVIDIA already has a strong LLM team (Nemotron), and 'I don't feel I have much to contribute — Nemotron is getting better and better on its own'; ③ he sees Physical AI developing extremely fast, with many problems that need 'physical actors that can truly change the state of the physical world' to solve them.

blocks.label: From Cosmos 1 to Cosmos 3
blocks.text: For Cosmos 1, he counted up what partners needed and landed on about 22 models. In the meeting, Jensen answered with what sounded like an unrelated story: Louis Vuitton cut its displays and sales went up — too many options confuse customers and stop them from deciding. Twenty-two models would each need maintenance and support; soldiers scattered in too many places is weak, and it slows iteration. So Cosmos 1 to 2 was just better data, but 2 to 3 was a leap: folding Reason, Predict, Transfer, Parser into a single Omni model, because no matter which path you take, you're modeling the same internal representation of the world, and a foundation model is meant to absorb everything. When a founder said Cosmos 3 isn't full of innovation but engineering-validates the details, Liu replied: the details are exactly what makes some models much better than others. He cares more about the effect than revolutionary originality. When building Cosmos 1, he counted up what partners needed — 'probably 22 models' — and reported it to Jensen in a meeting. Jensen answered with what looked like an unrelated example: when LV (Louis Vuitton) reduced its product displays, sales actually went up — 'you don't want too many things confusing your consumers and stopping them from making a decision.' Too many models means each one needs maintenance and user support — 'it's exhausting; too many soldiers scatter your strength (备多则力寡), and it slows your iteration.' So Cosmos 1→2 was just a data upgrade, while 2→3 was a huge leap: folding Reason, Predict, Transfer, Parser and the rest into a single Omni model — a multimodal transformer that brings audio, video, and action together — because 'no matter which path you look from, what's modeled is the same internal representation of the world,' and the essence of a foundation model is to 'take in all streams' (纳百川), absorbing all kinds of data. How to use it: the first principle of product-line management — every extra SKU or model adds a piece of maintenance and decision cost; if users can't tell A from B, the product drags itself down. 'Too many soldiers scatter your strength (Sun Tzu) — everyone's resources are limited.' A Chinese founder building world models commented that Cosmos 3 'doesn't have much technical innovation, but it engineering-validated a lot of details.' Liu's reply: 'all the big language models are transformer-based, so you could say nobody's innovating — but those details make some models much better than others. I increasingly value the effect it can produce, and increasingly don't care whether it's a revolutionary original.' (01:51:39) Cosmos 3 uses a two-tower design: one tower handles discrete signals (understanding and reasoning, built from a Vision-Language Model), the other handles continuous signals (generation, via the diffusion path). 'We know discrete works for understanding, and continuous works for generation.'

blocks.label: 'The Matrix': Robots and the World Model
blocks.text: His vision statement on his homepage: build a Matrix for robots — a concrete way to think about what world models do. Generalization is the problem every AI must solve: can you perform well beyond your training data? For Physical AI, the hardest generalization is learning the needed operations from limited signals and applying them in a scene you've never seen — observation and action working together. The host pushes: The Matrix is about humans becoming living batteries and the awakened breaking free — what if robots awaken one day and want to break out of the virtual world? His answer has three layers. First, the world is built by people and tech is operated by people; with shared consensus it won't happen. Second, deeper: thinking and suffering drive human progress, and he's genuinely not sure silicon-made intelligence has the same thinking and suffering. Third, we need guardrails. He leaves the question open. His personal-homepage vision is 'building a Matrix for robots', to help people concretely understand what world models do. The world model helps Physical AI generalize through three handles: 'The problem any AI has to solve is generalization — can you perform very well beyond the training data you've seen?' The hardest generalization for Physical AI is 'learning the needed operations from limited signals, then applying them in a scene you've never seen' — generalization where observation and action work together. 'Most people worry that AI being too capable will take over the world … but this world is built by people, and these technologies are operated by people behind the scenes. As long as there's shared consensus, I don't think it will happen.' The host's question: The Matrix is exactly about humans becoming the machines' living batteries and the awakened ones breaking free of the virtual system — what if one day robots awaken and want to break out of this virtual world? His three-layer response: ① society is built by people and tech is operated by people, so with consensus it won't happen; ② deeper still — 'thinking and suffering are a key driver of human progress — I'm not sure intelligence made of silicon has the same thinking and suffering,' and he genuinely has doubts; ③ we need appropriate guardrails to make sure it doesn't affect the development of the normal world. Open question left open: this is an open-ended philosophical discussion — he doesn't give a firm answer, leaving the question at 'not sure silicon intelligence has the same suffering-driven motivation,' which exactly echoes his empiricist stance of 'treating models like traditional Chinese medicine.'

blocks.label: The Next CUDA?
blocks.text: In the past, software was about building logic, and CUDA helped convert the logic that applications needed into GPU computation. Future software is AI-centric — AI on top of other AI. So in his view, both Nemotron and Cosmos could be the next CUDA, because there's a huge ecosystem of services and tooling hanging off CUDA. But he won't draw an equals sign: the industry is far more complex now; many different stacks combine, and the combination may be the new CUDA, not any single model. CUDA succeeded because from day one it hunted for applications — scientific computing first, then deep learning as the killer app. Copying CUDA is a great idea, but the environment is different; you have to adapt and see clearly which important contributions you can make at which point in time. Jensen won't go hunting for nails with a hammer — he's a first-principles person. 'In the past, software was about building logic; CUDA helped convert the logic those applications needed into GPU computation. Future software is AI-centric — AI on top of other AI.' So in his view, doing Nemotron and Cosmos could both be the future CUDA — because there's a huge ecosystem of services and support hanging off CUDA. But he won't draw an equals sign between Cosmos or Nemotron and CUDA — 'the industry today has gotten far more complex; many different stacks come together, and the combination may be the new CUDA, rather than any single model being a CUDA.' The key to CUDA's success: 'from the very start it kept looking for applications — first scientific computing, then when deep learning came along it found the most important application.' Copying CUDA is a great idea, but 'the environment is different; you have to be adaptive and see clearly which important contributions you can make at which point in time.'
